Detecting subtle defect patterns in product photos when thousands of labeled inspection images are available
Predicting which subscribers will churn from years of account history with known cancellation outcomes
explain: Defect detection from labeled images and churn prediction from labeled account history both involve complex patterns that must be learned from plentiful examples, making them strong ML fits. A mandated word table and simple addition are exact deterministic operations.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A platform team first pre-trains a language model on a huge unlabeled text collection with a masked-word objective, then trains it further on a small set of support tickets labeled by resolution category for its help desk. Which statement correctly describes the two stages?
options: The first stage is self-supervised learning on unlabeled data and the second stage is supervised learning on labeled examples
Neither stage is machine learning because text is unstructured
The first stage is reinforcement learning and the second is clustering
Both stages are supervised classification on labeled tickets
explain: Masked-word pre-training derives its target from the text itself, which is self-supervised learning on unlabeled data. Training on tickets with human-assigned categories is supervised learning. Unstructured text is a standard and valid input for machine learning.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A manufacturer wants each plant's total energy consumption for next month, expressed in megawatt-hours, computed for all 300 plants in a single overnight run at the start of each planning cycle. Which pairing of problem type and inference mode is correct?
options: Classification with real-time inference for each plant on demand
Clustering with real-time inference to group plants as readings arrive
Regression (forecasting) with batch inference, because the output is a continuous future quantity for many records processed together on a schedule
Anomaly detection with batch inference to flag last month's spikes only
explain: Next month's consumption in megawatt-hours is a continuous future value, so the task is regression in a forecasting setting. Scoring all 300 plants together on a planning schedule is batch inference; no plant needs an instant on-demand answer.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hotel chain wants to use ML to reduce last-minute cancellations. The data team immediately starts training models before anyone has defined what a successful outcome looks like. Which ML lifecycle stage should the team complete FIRST?
options: Define the business problem, the target to predict, and measurable success criteria with stakeholders
Clean missing values and remove duplicate rows from the reservations data
Tune the learning rate and tree depth of the chosen algorithm
Deploy the model behind an API so the front desk can score bookings
explain: Business understanding comes first in the ML lifecycle: the team must agree on the problem, the prediction target, and how success will be measured before any data work or training, otherwise later stages optimize for the wrong goal.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An insurance company has collected three years of claims records. Before training, analysts find duplicate claims, missing claim amounts, and dates stored in inconsistent formats. Which lifecycle stage is this work part of?
options: Model deployment
Data preparation
Model monitoring
Model training
explain: Fixing duplicates, missing values, and inconsistent formats is data preparation (cleaning and transforming raw data). Training happens only after the data is clean and usable, and deployment and monitoring occur after the model is built and evaluated.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retail data scientist creates new input variables from raw transaction logs: days since each customer's last purchase, average basket size over 90 days, and the ratio of returns to purchases. Which activity is this?
options: Feature engineering
Model evaluation
Batch inference
Data collection
explain: Deriving new predictive variables from raw data is feature engineering. The raw transactions were already collected; evaluation compares finished model predictions against outcomes, and inference is using a trained model to score new data.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A bank's data science team repeatedly retrains its credit-risk model while systematically trying different learning rates, maximum tree depths, and regularization strengths, keeping whichever combination performs best on the validation set. Which lifecycle activity are they performing?
options: Model deployment
Business understanding
Hyperparameter tuning
Data collection
explain: Learning rate, tree depth, and regularization strength are hyperparameters set outside the training data, and searching for their best combination using validation performance is hyperparameter tuning, which follows initial training and precedes final evaluation.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A manufacturing company's defect-detection model has passed offline evaluation. The team now places it behind a real-time endpoint so factory systems can send it images and receive predictions in production. Which lifecycle stage is this?
options: Business understanding
Data labeling
Feature engineering
Model deployment
explain: Making a validated model available to production systems so it can score live inputs is deployment. Labeling, business understanding, and feature engineering all happen earlier, before a model is trained and evaluated.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO activities belong to the data preparation stage of the ML lifecycle? (Choose two.)
options: Imputing missing values in numeric columns
Agreeing the business success metric with stakeholders
Removing duplicate and corrupted records
Watching live prediction accuracy for drift after release
explain: Data preparation covers cleaning and readying data, including imputing missing values and removing duplicates or corrupted records. Defining success metrics is business understanding, and watching live accuracy is post-deployment monitoring.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A logistics company has a delivery-time model running in production. Analysts continuously track its prediction accuracy on live shipments and alert the team when performance degrades. Which lifecycle stage is this?
options: Model training
Data collection
Business understanding
Model monitoring
explain: Tracking a deployed model's live performance and alerting on degradation is model monitoring, the final lifecycle stage. It follows deployment and feeds back into retraining decisions when accuracy drifts.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Before launching a demand-forecasting model, an energy company compares the model's forecasts against actual consumption on data the model has never seen, to estimate how it will perform in production. Which stage is this?
options: Hyperparameter tuning
Data collection
Model evaluation
Model deployment
explain: Measuring a trained model's performance on unseen data to judge production readiness is model evaluation. It uses held-out data precisely so the estimate is not inflated by data the model already learned from.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An education company wants an ML system for student dropout risk. Before building anything, leadership and data scientists agree the project succeeds if advisors can identify at-risk students at least four weeks earlier than today, with success measured on advisor interventions. Which stage does this describe?
options: Business understanding
Feature engineering
Model monitoring
Data preparation
explain: Translating a business goal into an ML problem with a clear, measurable definition of success is business understanding. It frames every later decision, from which data to collect to which metric the model is judged against.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A government agency documents its planned ML workflow. Which sequence lists the lifecycle stages in the CORRECT order?
options: Training, business understanding, data collection, deployment, evaluation, monitoring
Data preparation, deployment, business understanding, evaluation, training, monitoring
Business understanding, data collection and preparation, training and tuning, evaluation, deployment, monitoring
Deployment, monitoring, business understanding, training, evaluation, data preparation
explain: The lifecycle runs: define the business problem, collect and prepare data, train and tune the model, evaluate it on held-out data, deploy it, then monitor it in production. Deploying or evaluating before training, or defining the problem after building, breaks that logic.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An agriculture company installs soil-moisture sensors, subscribes to a weather data feed, and exports five seasons of yield records from its farm management system to build a training dataset. Which lifecycle stage is underway?
options: Hyperparameter tuning
Model monitoring
Model evaluation
Data collection
explain: Gathering raw data from sensors, external feeds, and existing systems is data collection. Preparation, training, and evaluation all depend on this data existing first.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A media company converts a categorical genre field into one-hot encoded columns and creates a new variable: total watch time divided by account age. Which activity has the team performed?
options: Feature engineering
Model monitoring
Model deployment
Data collection
explain: Encoding categorical variables and deriving ratio variables from existing fields is feature engineering: creating informative inputs for the model. The data was already collected, and the model has not been deployed or monitored yet.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: What is the primary purpose of the training dataset in supervised learning?
options: To produce the final, unbiased estimate of production performance
To let the model learn patterns and relationships from labeled examples
To select hyperparameters after the model is finished
To score live customer requests in production
explain: The training dataset is what the algorithm learns from: it adjusts its internal parameters to fit the patterns in those labeled examples. Final performance estimation is the test set's job, and scoring live requests is inference, not training.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An energy company trains several candidate demand models, then uses a separate held-out dataset to compare them and pick the best hyperparameters before any final testing. What is that separate dataset called?
options: The inference dataset
The validation dataset
The labeling dataset
The production dataset
explain: The validation set is used during development to compare model versions and tune hyperparameters. Keeping it separate from the test set preserves the test set for one final, unbiased evaluation of the chosen model.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A healthcare team has finished tuning its readmission model. It now runs the model exactly once on a dataset that played no role in training or tuning, to report an unbiased estimate of real-world performance. Which dataset is this, and why is it used last?
options: The feature store, because it holds the newest data
The validation set, because it was used for tuning
The training set, because it is the largest
The test set, because it was never used in any earlier decision
explain: The test set is reserved until the end and used once, precisely because no training or tuning decision touched it, so its score is an unbiased estimate of performance on unseen data. Reusing validation data for the final report would overstate performance.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Why should a team avoid repeatedly tuning a model against its test set?
options: Because tuning automatically deletes the test data after each run
Because hyperparameters can only be changed before any data is loaded
Because test sets are legally restricted to a single use per year
Because the model gradually adapts to the test set, so the test score stops being an unbiased estimate of performance on new data
explain: Every tuning decision informed by the test set leaks information about it into the model, so the model effectively overfits the test set and its score becomes optimistic. The test set must stay untouched until one final evaluation.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A bank builds a model to predict loan defaults within 12 months of origination. One input feature is 'total collections fees charged,' which is only recorded after a loan has already defaulted and been sent to collections. Why will this model fail in production?
options: The feature makes the model an unsupervised learning problem
The feature leaks the target: it is only known after the outcome it is meant to predict, so it will not exist at prediction time
The feature is categorical and should have been encoded
The feature has too many missing values to be useful
explain: This is data leakage: the collections-fee feature is a consequence of default, unavailable when a new application must be scored. Offline metrics look excellent because the feature nearly encodes the answer, but the model cannot use it on genuinely new applications.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO practices help a team prevent data leakage? (Choose two.)
options: Splitting data first and fitting preprocessing steps only on the training portion
Fitting data normalization on the entire dataset before splitting it
Adding a column derived directly from the target variable as an input feature
Removing any feature that would not be available at the moment a prediction is made
explain: Leakage is prevented by using only features available at prediction time and by splitting data before fitting preprocessing, so statistics from validation or test data never influence training. Target-derived features and pre-split preprocessing are themselves classic leakage sources.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A real estate team randomly shuffles 15 years of housing data before splitting it into training and test sets for a price-trend forecasting model. A reviewer objects to the random split. Why?
options: Random splits let future information leak into training, so the model is partly tested on the past it has already seen the future of; time-based data should be split chronologically
Shuffled data cannot be used with regression algorithms
Shuffling makes the dataset too large to train on
Chronological splits are only needed for image data
explain: With time-ordered data, random shuffling places future records in training and past records in test, leaking future information and producing unrealistically good scores. A chronological split, training on earlier data and testing on later data, mirrors real forecasting.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A sports analytics team has only 800 labeled matches, too few to spare a large holdout set, but still needs a reliable performance estimate and to use its data efficiently. Which technique should the team use?
options: Evaluate the model on the training set several times and average the results
Discard half the data so the test set is bigger
Train on all 800 matches and report the training accuracy
K-fold cross-validation, rotating which fold is held out for validation
explain: K-fold cross-validation splits the data into folds and rotates the validation fold, so every record is used for both training and validation across rounds. This gives a more reliable estimate from a small dataset than a single small holdout, without wasting data.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A legal-tech model classifies contracts as compliant or non-compliant. On a test set of 200 contracts, it classifies 170 correctly. What is the model's accuracy?
explain: Accuracy is correct predictions divided by total predictions: 170 divided by 200 equals 0.85, or 85%. The other values come from dividing incorrectly or reporting the error rate (30 of 200 wrong equals 15%) instead of accuracy.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A fraud model reviews 1,000 transactions. It flags 50 as fraud: 40 really are fraud and 10 are legitimate. It also misses 20 fraudulent transactions. What is the model's precision?
explain: Precision is TP divided by (TP + FP): the model flagged 50 transactions, of which 40 were truly fraud, so precision is 40/50 = 80%. Recall would be 40/(40+20) = 67%; that is the distractor value, measuring missed fraud rather than flag accuracy.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hospital evaluates a cancer-screening model on 200 patients who have the disease. The model correctly identifies 180 of them and misses 20. What is the model's recall?
explain: Recall is TP divided by (TP + FN): 180 divided by (180 + 20) equals 90%. Recall measures how many actual positive cases the model catches, which is the critical concern in screening, where a missed case delays treatment.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retailer has a heavily imbalanced churn dataset: only 3% of customers churn. Leadership wants ONE summary metric for model selection that balances catching churners against not flooding the retention team with false alarms. Which metric best fits?
options: RMSE, because churn is a numeric outcome
Accuracy, because it uses every prediction in the test set
MAE, because it averages absolute errors
F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall
explain: F1 balances precision and recall in a single number, which suits imbalanced classification where accuracy is dominated by the majority class. RMSE and MAE are regression metrics and do not apply to a churn yes/no classification.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: In a payments fraud model, a legitimate transaction that the model correctly allows through without flagging it is an example of which confusion-matrix outcome?
options: A true positive
A false negative
A false positive
A true negative
explain: A true negative is a negative case (legitimate transaction) correctly predicted as negative (not flagged). A false negative would be fraud the model missed, and a false positive would be a legitimate transaction wrongly flagged.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: On a manufacturing line, a defect model flags a finished part as defective, but inspection shows the part is perfectly good and it is scrapped anyway. In confusion-matrix terms, what happened?
options: A false positive, because a good part was incorrectly predicted defective
A true negative, because the part was actually good
A true positive, because the model made a prediction
A false negative, because a defective part escaped
explain: A false positive is a negative case (a good part) incorrectly predicted as positive (defective). It wastes a good part and inspection effort, which is why teams watch false-positive rates when precision matters.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A screening program for a serious but treatable disease states that missing a true case is far worse than sending a healthy patient for one extra confirmatory test. Which metric should the team prioritize when tuning the model?
options: Recall, to minimize missed true cases
Precision, to minimize false alarms
MAE, to minimize average error size
Accuracy, because the dataset is balanced
explain: Recall measures the share of true cases the model catches, so prioritizing recall minimizes false negatives — the missed cases the program considers most costly. Extra false positives only cost a confirmatory test, an acceptable trade-off here.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An email provider finds that its spam filter's worst failure is sending a customer's legitimate invoices and job offers to the spam folder. Which metric should the provider prioritize?
options: AUC, because it ignores the decision threshold
F1, regardless of the cost balance
Recall, so no spam is ever missed
Precision, so that messages flagged as spam really are spam
explain: Precision is TP/(TP+FP): it measures how trustworthy a positive (spam) flag is. Prioritizing precision reduces false positives, the legitimate mail wrongly filed as spam, even if a little more spam slips through to the inbox.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Only 1% of an insurer's claims are fraudulent. A model that labels EVERY claim as legitimate reports 99% accuracy, yet the fraud team calls it useless. Why?
options: Because 99% accuracy means the test set leaked into training
Because accuracy ignores the minority class: the model catches zero fraud, so its recall for fraud is 0% despite the high accuracy
Because accuracy can never exceed the size of the test set
Because the model must be underfitting its training data
explain: With extreme class imbalance, always predicting the majority class yields high accuracy while detecting none of the rare cases that matter. Precision, recall, and F1 for the fraud class expose the failure that accuracy hides.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO statements about evaluation metrics are correct? (Choose two.)
options: F1 is the simple arithmetic average of precision and accuracy
Precision equals TP divided by (TP + FP)
The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall
Recall equals TP divided by (TP + FP)
explain: Precision is TP/(TP+FP), and F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which punishes extreme imbalance between them. Recall is TP/(TP+FN), not TP/(TP+FP), and F1 does not involve accuracy.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A bank compares two credit-default classifiers using ROC curves. Model X has an AUC of 0.92 and Model Y has an AUC of 0.61. What does this tell the bank?
options: Model Y has higher precision at every threshold
Model Y will be cheaper to run in production
Model X separates defaulters from non-defaulters far better across decision thresholds; Model Y is only slightly better than random guessing
Model X is 92% accurate on the test set
explain: AUC measures ranking/discrimination across all thresholds: 0.92 indicates strong separation between classes, while 0.61 is barely above the 0.5 of a random classifier. AUC is not accuracy and says nothing directly about cost or precision at a specific threshold.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An energy company forecasts hourly electricity demand in megawatts. A few very large forecast misses cause expensive emergency power purchases, so the team wants an error metric that penalizes large errors disproportionately. Which metric should they choose?
options: Recall
RMSE, because squaring errors weights large misses more heavily
Precision
Accuracy
explain: RMSE squares each error before averaging, so a few very large misses dominate the score — exactly the behavior the team wants for regression forecasts. Accuracy, precision, and recall are classification metrics and do not apply to numeric predictions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A logistics company predicts delivery times in hours and wants an error metric that stakeholders can read directly as 'on average, our prediction is off by about X hours,' without extra sensitivity to rare huge misses. Which metric fits best?
options: AUC
MAE, the mean absolute error in the original units
Precision
F1 score
explain: MAE averages absolute errors in the same units as the target (hours), making it directly interpretable, and it does not square errors, so rare huge misses do not dominate it the way they dominate RMSE. AUC, F1, and precision are classification metrics.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A model's precision is 0.80 and its recall is 0.60. What is its F1 score (rounded to two decimal places)?
explain: F1 = 2 x (precision x recall) / (precision + recall) = 2 x (0.80 x 0.60) / 1.40 = 0.96 / 1.40 = about 0.69. The 0.70 distractor is the plain arithmetic mean, which is not how F1 is calculated; the harmonic mean sits lower when the two inputs differ.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A fraud team LOWERs the score threshold at which transactions are flagged for review. What is the expected effect on the confusion matrix?
options: Precision rises and recall falls
Both precision and recall always rise together
Recall rises because more fraud is caught, while precision typically falls because more legitimate transactions are flagged
The number of true negatives increases
explain: Lowering the flagging threshold catches more actual fraud (higher recall, fewer false negatives) but also flags more legitimate transactions (more false positives), which lowers precision. Threshold choice is a deliberate trade-off between the two metrics.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO metrics are used to evaluate a REGRESSION model that predicts a continuous numeric value? (Choose two.)
options: AUC (area under the ROC curve)
Precision
MAE (mean absolute error)
RMSE (root mean square error)
explain: RMSE and MAE both measure the size of numeric prediction errors for regression. Precision and AUC are classification metrics: precision depends on a confusion matrix, and AUC evaluates class ranking, neither of which fits continuous outputs.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A support-ticket classifier is tested on 100 tickets with these results: 30 true positives, 50 true negatives, 10 false positives, and 10 false negatives. What is its accuracy?
explain: Accuracy is (TP + TN) divided by total predictions: (30 + 50) / 100 = 80%. Counting only true positives (30%) ignores the correctly rejected tickets, which are also correct predictions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hiring platform needs to compare several resume-screening classifiers fairly, without committing to one decision threshold yet, because the legal team has not finalized how cautious the cutoff must be. Which metric best supports this comparison?
options: AUC, which summarizes discrimination across all possible thresholds
Training loss on the full dataset
MAE, which averages threshold errors
Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold, fixed in advance
explain: AUC evaluates how well a classifier ranks and separates classes across every threshold, so models can be compared before a specific cutoff is chosen. Accuracy at one fixed threshold would bake in an assumption the team has explicitly not made yet.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retail marketing team uses a model to select customers for a discount offer. The model selects 60 customers: 45 of them are true positives who respond to the offer, and 15 are false positives who do not respond. What is the model's precision?
explain: Precision is TP divided by all predicted positives: 45 divided by (45 + 15) equals 75%. It answers 'of everyone the model selected, how many were correct selections,' which is what the marketing team needs to judge wasted spend.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A logistics provider's late-delivery alert model is evaluated: it correctly alerts on 70 late shipments and fails to alert on 30 late shipments. What is the model's recall for late deliveries?
explain: Recall is TP divided by (TP + FN): 70 divided by (70 + 30) equals 70%. The 30 missed shipments are false negatives, and recall directly measures how many of the true late deliveries the model caught.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: During training of a retail forecasting model, training error keeps falling epoch after epoch, but validation error falls, then starts rising steadily. The team stops the run at the point where validation error was lowest and keeps that model version. Which technique did they use?
options: Data augmentation
Feature selection
Early stopping
Transfer learning
explain: Early stopping halts training when validation performance stops improving and begins to worsen, keeping the best checkpoint. Rising validation error alongside falling training error is the classic signature of the model beginning to overfit.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO actions are appropriate remedies when a model is overfitting its training data? (Choose two.)
options: Making the model substantially more complex
Simplifying the model or reducing the number of input features
Evaluating the model only on its training data
Applying regularization to penalize overly complex solutions
explain: Regularization and simplification both constrain a model that has memorized training noise, improving generalization to new data. Adding complexity worsens overfitting, and judging a model on its training data hides the problem rather than fixing it.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hospitality company models nightly room demand with a single straight-line relationship to price, but actual demand curves sharply around holidays and local events. The model performs poorly on BOTH training and new data. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add stronger regularization to simplify the model further
Use a more expressive model and add features such as holidays and events, because the current model underfits
Evaluate the model on a larger test set only
Remove the price feature entirely
explain: Poor performance on both training and unseen data signals underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the real pattern. Increasing model capacity and adding informative features addresses it; more regularization would make the model even simpler and worse.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A data scientist adds a regularization term to a regression model's training objective, so the model is penalized for assigning very large weights to its features. What is the main purpose of doing this?
options: To make training finish in fewer epochs
To discourage overly complex fits and improve generalization to unseen data
To convert the regression problem into a classification problem
To guarantee the model achieves zero training error
explain: Regularization penalizes large weights and excessive complexity, trading a little training accuracy for better performance on new data. It is a standard defense against overfitting, not a speed optimization or a problem conversion.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A bank's model achieves 61% accuracy on its training data and 60% on unseen data. A second model achieves 99% on training data and 72% on unseen data. Which statement is correct?
options: The second model is better because its training accuracy is highest
The first model is overfitting and the second is underfitting
The first model underfits (it cannot capture the pattern even in training), while the second overfits (a large train-test gap)
Both models generalize equally well
explain: Low accuracy on both training and test data means the first model underfits: it never learned the pattern. The second model's 27-point gap between training and test performance is the hallmark of overfitting, even though its test score is the higher of the two.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An agriculture team uses 5-fold cross-validation while developing a crop-yield model. What is the main benefit of this approach over a single train-validation split?
options: It guarantees the model will never overfit
It trains five production models at once
It eliminates the need for a final test set in all cases
It produces a more reliable performance estimate because every data point is used for both training and validation across the folds
explain: Cross-validation rotates the validation fold so all data contributes to both training and validation, averaging out the luck of one particular split. It improves estimate reliability but does not by itself prevent overfitting or replace final testing.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A streaming service's recommendation model memorizes the viewing history of its training users and performs noticeably worse for new users. The team can license a much larger, representative dataset of viewing behavior. Why would this help?
options: More data converts the problem into unsupervised learning
A larger dataset automatically removes the need for a validation set
More representative training data generally reduces overfitting, because the model must learn patterns that hold broadly instead of memorizing a small sample
A larger dataset guarantees 100% accuracy for new users
explain: With more varied, representative examples, memorizing individual records stops working and the model is forced toward general patterns, reducing overfitting. It does not remove the need for validation or guarantee any specific accuracy.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A model built by an education company predicts exam scores with high error on the training set AND equally high error on new students. Training longer and tuning the learning rate barely changes the results. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple or lacks informative features for this problem
Concept drift in the production environment
Data leakage in the training pipeline
A decision threshold set too low
explain: High error on training data itself means the model cannot even fit known examples: underfitting, usually from insufficient capacity or weak features. Leakage inflates scores rather than depressing them, drift affects deployed models over time, and thresholds apply to classification decisions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hospitality pricing model scores 99% accuracy in training but only 68% on new bookings. An engineer proposes adding many more features and layers so training accuracy can reach 100%. Why is this the WRONG direction, and what should the team do instead?
options: The model needs a lower decision threshold before any other change
Training accuracy is capped by law at 99%, so the team should stop training
The gap signals overfitting; adding capacity will widen it, so the team should simplify the model or apply regularization and validate with cross-validation
The gap already signals underfitting, so the team should collect a smaller dataset
explain: A 31-point train-test gap is overfitting: the model memorizes training bookings instead of learning general pricing patterns. More features and layers increase memorization capacity; simplification, regularization, more data, and cross-validation are the corrective direction.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO conditions can cause a deployed model's performance to degrade even though the model itself has not changed? (Choose two.)
options: The production data is no longer representative of the population the model was trained on
The real-world relationship between the inputs and the outcome changes over time
The test set is kept locked away and used only once
The model is retrained on fresh, representative data every week
explain: A static model degrades when incoming data stops resembling its training data or when the underlying input-outcome relationship shifts over time (drift). Regular retraining on fresh representative data counteracts degradation, and a protected test set does not affect production performance.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Why do teams monitor ML models continuously AFTER deployment instead of relying only on pre-launch evaluation?
options: Because data and behavior change over time, so a model that was accurate at launch can silently degrade in production
Because evaluation results expire after 30 days under AWS policy
Because monitoring replaces the need to evaluate models before launch
Because live traffic uses a different programming language than training
explain: Pre-launch evaluation is a snapshot. In production, input data and real-world patterns shift, so continuous monitoring is what detects silent degradation and triggers investigation or retraining before business impact grows.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: After a major shift to remote work, a bank's spending-pattern model degrades: customers' transaction behavior now relates to income and location differently than it did in the historical training data. Which phenomenon is this?
options: Underfitting, because the model is too simple
A false positive problem in the confusion matrix
Data leakage, because future data entered the training set
Concept drift, because the relationship between the inputs and the predicted outcome has changed
explain: Concept drift is a change in the underlying relationship between features and the outcome, here driven by a lasting change in customer behavior. The input distributions may look similar, but what they imply has changed, so the old model systematically errs.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retail demand model was trained mostly on desktop web orders. After a successful mobile app launch, most orders now arrive from mobile with different basket sizes and session patterns, though what drives demand has not changed. The model's accuracy slips. What type of drift is this?
options: Concept drift only, because the outcome definition changed
Underfitting caused by the app launch
Label leakage from the mobile app
Data drift, because the distribution of the input data changed while the underlying demand relationship stayed the same
explain: Data drift means the statistical distribution of production inputs differs from training inputs — here, a new dominant channel with different patterns. Concept drift would require the relationship between inputs and demand itself to have changed.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A manufacturing company wants a systematic way to detect drift: production feature values will be compared automatically against the statistical baseline captured from the training data, with alerts when distributions diverge beyond a threshold. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Re-labeling the original training data with a new workforce
Manually reviewing a sample of predictions once a year
Automated model monitoring that compares live data distributions to the training baseline and alerts on divergence
Lowering the model's decision threshold until alerts stop
explain: Drift detection works by comparing live input (and prediction) distributions against a baseline established from training data, alerting when they diverge. Manual annual reviews are too slow, and relabeling or threshold changes do not measure distribution shift.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO statements best describe the purpose of MLOps? (Choose two.)
options: To replace data scientists with a single fully autonomous system
To store raw training files in a shared spreadsheet for manual tracking
To monitor production models and trigger retraining or rollback when performance degrades
To automate and standardize the ML lifecycle, including versioned pipelines for training, deployment, and retraining
explain: MLOps applies DevOps-style automation and discipline to ML: reproducible, versioned pipelines plus production monitoring with retraining or rollback triggers. Its goal is reliable operation at scale, not eliminating human oversight or tracking work manually in spreadsheets.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An insurance churn model's monitored F1 score has fallen below the team's agreed threshold for two consecutive weeks as customer behavior evolves. What is the MOST appropriate next step in a well-run ML lifecycle?
options: Delete the model and return to manual processes permanently
Raise the alert threshold so the dashboard stops flagging the issue
Ignore it, because models always recover on their own
Retrain the model on recent, representative data and validate the new version before promoting it
explain: Sustained monitored degradation is the trigger for retraining on fresh, representative data, followed by validation and controlled promotion of the new version. Silencing alerts or ignoring decay leaves a stale model making production decisions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which statement best defines MLOps?
options: A set of practices that combines ML system development with reliable, automated operations across the model lifecycle
A labeling workforce used to annotate training data
A pricing model for on-demand inference endpoints
A type of neural network architecture for time-series data
explain: MLOps is the discipline of applying DevOps principles — automation, versioning, CI/CD, and monitoring — to machine learning systems so models can be built, deployed, and maintained reliably and repeatedly.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A data scientist wants ONE integrated environment to write notebooks, access data, train models, tune them, and deploy endpoints without stitching together separate tools. Which SageMaker capability provides this unified workspace?
options: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Studio
explain: Amazon SageMaker Studio is the unified, web-based IDE for the end-to-end ML workflow, bringing notebooks, training, tuning, and deployment together. Canvas is a separate no-code tool for business users, and Ground Truth and Feature Store each serve one specific function.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Business analysts at a logistics company understand their shipment data well but do not write code. They want to build a model that forecasts late deliveries and generate predictions themselves. Which SageMaker capability should they use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
explain: SageMaker Canvas provides a visual, no-code interface so business analysts can build ML models and generate predictions without writing code or having ML expertise. The other options serve data engineers or ML engineers performing preparation, orchestration, or monitoring.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A media startup wants to launch quickly using prebuilt, ready-to-deploy models and end-to-end solution templates, including foundation models it can customize, instead of building everything from scratch. Which SageMaker capability fits best?
options: Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Clarify
explain: SageMaker JumpStart offers prebuilt models, foundation models, and complete solution templates that can be deployed or fine-tuned with minimal effort. Autopilot builds a custom model from the customer's own tabular data rather than supplying prebuilt solutions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retail data team spends most of its time manually writing transformation code to clean and aggregate sales data from several sources before training. They want a visual, low-code tool to build and export these preparation flows. Which SageMaker capability should they use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
explain: SageMaker Data Wrangler provides a visual interface to import, clean, transform, and analyze data from multiple sources and export the preparation flow for training. It targets exactly the repetitive data-preparation work the team describes.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Several teams at a bank keep rebuilding the same customer features (30-day average balance, transaction counts) separately for training and for live scoring, and the two versions sometimes disagree. Which SageMaker capability provides a central place to store, share, and reuse features consistently for both training and inference?
options: Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
explain: SageMaker Feature Store is a central repository for storing, sharing, and serving ML features, with online and offline stores so the same feature definitions feed both training and real-time inference. That consistency is what eliminates the disagreement between separately built feature versions.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A healthcare company needs 200,000 chest X-ray reports labeled by trained annotators, with a workflow that routes uncertain cases to human specialists and automatically labels the straightforward cases. Which SageMaker capability provides this labeling workflow?
options: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
explain: SageMaker Ground Truth builds data-labeling workflows combining human labelers with automated labeling, routing low-confidence cases to humans. Autopilot builds models from already-labeled data, and Model Monitor watches deployed models; neither manages annotation workforces.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO SageMaker capabilities let users build ML models with little or no code? (Choose two.)
options: Amazon SageMaker Canvas, a visual no-code interface for business users
Amazon SageMaker Autopilot, which automates model building and tuning from tabular data
Hand-coding a distributed training job on raw EC2 instances
Writing custom training scripts in SageMaker Studio notebooks
explain: Canvas gives non-coders a visual interface to build models, and Autopilot automates algorithm selection, training, and tuning so users supply data rather than code. Writing scripts in notebooks or on EC2 is the opposite of the no-code requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An insurance company uploads a labeled dataset of past claims and wants AWS to automatically explore algorithms, train candidate models, and tune them to find the best performer, with full visibility into how the winner was built. Which SageMaker capability should the company use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Autopilot
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler
explain: SageMaker Autopilot is Amazon's AutoML capability: it automatically preprocesses tabular data, selects algorithms, trains and tunes multiple candidates, and ranks them, producing notebooks that show how the best model was created. The other options handle labeling, feature storage, or data preparation only.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A deployed fraud model must be watched continuously so the team is alerted when live transaction data or prediction patterns drift away from the baseline captured at training time. Which SageMaker capability does this?
options: Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
explain: SageMaker Model Monitor continuously monitors deployed models for data drift, concept drift, and quality degradation against a training baseline and raises alerts. JumpStart supplies prebuilt models, Canvas is a no-code builder, and Ground Truth labels data.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An ML team wants to turn its manual sequence of data preparation, training, evaluation, and conditional deployment steps into a repeatable, versioned workflow that runs automatically whenever new data arrives. Which SageMaker capability should the team use?
options: Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store
Amazon SageMaker Clarify
Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks run by hand
explain: SageMaker Pipelines is the CI/CD and workflow-orchestration capability for ML: it defines the steps of the lifecycle as a repeatable, versioned pipeline with automation and conditional execution. Running notebooks by hand is exactly the manual process the team wants to replace.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A streaming company discovers its churn model performs far worse in production than offline. Investigation shows the features computed in the live scoring path use different logic than the features the model was trained on. Which SageMaker capability directly addresses this training-serving skew?
options: Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth, to relabel the churn data
Amazon SageMaker Feature Store, so training and inference read the same centrally defined features
Amazon SageMaker Canvas, so analysts can rebuild the model visually
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, to swap in a prebuilt model
explain: Training-serving skew comes from inconsistent feature computation between training and inference. Feature Store removes it by serving the same centrally stored, versioned feature definitions to both paths, which none of the other options is designed to do.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A retail company wants to automatically identify objects, scenes, and faces in its product photos and customer-uploaded images, and detect inappropriate content, without building its own computer vision model. Which AWS service should it use?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Textract
explain: Amazon Rekognition provides prebuilt image and video analysis: object and scene detection, facial analysis, celebrity and face recognition, text in images, and content moderation. Comprehend analyzes text, Textract extracts document data, and Kendra is enterprise search.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO statements correctly describe AWS speech-related managed AI services? (Choose two.)
options: Amazon Transcribe converts spoken audio, such as call recordings, into text
Amazon Lex converts written text into lifelike spoken audio
Amazon Textract converts speech in videos into subtitles
Amazon Polly converts written text into lifelike speech in multiple languages and voices
explain: Amazon Transcribe is speech-to-text, turning audio such as call recordings into transcripts, and Amazon Polly is text-to-speech, turning text into lifelike speech. Lex builds conversational chatbots; it does not synthesize speech, and Textract extracts data from documents, not audio.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An accounting firm scans thousands of paper invoices and tax forms. It needs the printed text, the values in form fields, and the contents of tables extracted as structured data for its systems. Which AWS service is designed for this?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Textract
Amazon Transcribe
explain: Amazon Textract goes beyond basic OCR: it extracts text, handwriting, tables, and key-value form fields from scanned documents as structured data. Polly and Transcribe handle speech, and Rekognition analyzes images for objects and faces rather than document structure.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A hospitality group wants a chatbot on its website and phone line that can hold a conversation, understand that a guest wants to change a reservation, and ask follow-up questions for the missing details. Which AWS service is built for this?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Lex
Amazon Personalize
explain: Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces using automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding, managing intents, slots, and multi-turn dialog — exactly what a booking-change chatbot needs. Comprehend only analyzes text; it does not run conversations.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Employees at a government agency waste hours searching shared drives, wikis, and document repositories for policy answers. The agency wants an intelligent search service that answers natural-language questions by searching across those enterprise sources and ranking the most relevant passages. Which AWS service fits?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Personalize
explain: Amazon Kendra is an intelligent enterprise search service: it indexes content across repositories and uses natural language understanding to return relevant answers and ranked passages to questions. The other services handle recommendations, speech, and text analytics rather than enterprise search.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: An online sports retailer wants to show each shopper real-time product recommendations such as 'fans who viewed this jersey also bought,' generated from browsing and purchase behavior, using the same technology class as retail recommendation engines. Which AWS service should it use?
options: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Lex
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Personalize
explain: Amazon Personalize builds real-time personalized recommendations from user interaction data such as views, clicks, and purchases, without the retailer building its own recommender. Kendra is search, Rekognition is image analysis, and Lex is conversational interfaces.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A social media startup must screen millions of user-uploaded photos each day for explicit or unsafe content before the photos become visible to other users. Which AWS service provides this capability as a managed API?
options: Amazon Comprehend sentiment analysis
Amazon Polly speech synthesis
Amazon Rekognition content moderation
Amazon Textract document analysis
explain: Amazon Rekognition includes content moderation that detects explicit, suggestive, and violent content in images and video at scale through an API. Comprehend analyzes text sentiment, Textract reads documents, and Polly generates speech; none of them moderate images.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: Which TWO use cases are matched to the CORRECT AWS managed AI service? (Choose two.)
options: Translating product manuals between languages with Amazon Polly
Generating lifelike spoken narration from a script with Amazon Transcribe
Detecting personally identifiable information and named entities in customer emails with Amazon Comprehend
Extracting line items from tables in scanned loan application forms with Amazon Textract
explain: Textract extracts tables and form data from scanned documents, and Comprehend performs NLP on text including entity and PII detection. Narration from text is Polly, not Transcribe (which is speech-to-text), and text translation is Amazon Translate, not Polly.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A legal firm processes thousands of contracts and needs to automatically pull out party names, dates, jurisdictions, and monetary amounts, and to classify each document's overall tone in client correspondence. Which AWS service provides this text analytics capability?
options: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Amazon Comprehend is the NLP service for text: it extracts entities such as people, dates, organizations, and amounts, plus key phrases, sentiment, and language. Rekognition works on images, Kendra is search, and Transcribe converts speech to text.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A call center wants searchable text transcripts of recorded support calls, including which speaker said what and recognition of product names from its own industry vocabulary, so analysts can mine the calls for quality issues. Which AWS service meets all these requirements?
options: Amazon Lex with built-in intents
Amazon Comprehend with topic modeling
Amazon Polly with custom lexicons
Amazon Transcribe with speaker diarization and custom vocabulary
explain: Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text and supports speaker identification (diarization) and custom vocabularies for domain terms such as product names. Polly works in the opposite direction (text to speech), and Lex and Comprehend do not transcribe recorded audio.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A news publisher wants its articles to be listenable: readers can press play and hear each article read aloud in a natural-sounding voice. Which AWS service converts the article text into speech?
options: Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
Amazon Lex
Amazon Comprehend
explain: Amazon Polly is the text-to-speech service, converting written text into lifelike speech in many voices and languages. Transcribe does the reverse (speech to text), Lex powers chatbots, and Comprehend analyzes text without producing audio.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: A global hotel chain publishes its booking policies, help articles, and guest communications in English and needs them rendered accurately in Spanish, French, and Japanese for its international sites. Which AWS service should it use?
options: Amazon Lex
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Polly
explain: Amazon Translate is the managed neural machine translation service for translating text between languages at scale, which is exactly the hotel chain's requirement. Polly produces spoken audio, Comprehend analyzes text, and Lex builds conversational bots.
domain: Domain 1: Fundamentals of AI and ML

q: What is a foundation model?
options: A small model trained for one specific task on a small dataset
A large machine learning model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
A hardware chip designed for AI workloads
A database schema used to store training data
explain: Foundation models are large models pre-trained on vast, broad datasets. They learn general representations of language (or other modalities) that can be adapted - through prompting, fine-tuning, or RAG - to a wide range of tasks.

q: In generative AI, what is a token?
options: A security credential used to access a model API
A type of neural network layer
A hardware accelerator for training
The basic unit of text a model processes, such as a word, part of a word, or character
explain: Models break text into tokens - words, subwords, or characters. Token counts determine how much text fits in a request and are commonly the basis for usage pricing.

q: What are embeddings in the context of AI models?
options: Numerical vector representations of data that capture meaning and relationships
Encrypted passwords stored in a database
Physical chips embedded in servers
Backup copies of trained models
explain: Embeddings convert data such as text into dense numerical vectors where similar meanings sit close together. They power semantic search, recommendations, and the retrieval step of RAG.

q: In a foundation model, what do "parameters" refer to?
options: The API timeout limits
The learned weights and values the model adjusts during training - a rough measure of model size and capacity
The billing settings for model usage
The number of users allowed to access the model
explain: Parameters (weights) are the internal values a model learns during training. A higher parameter count generally means greater capacity to capture complex patterns, though bigger is not automatically better for every task.

q: What is the transformer architecture known for?
options: It is the neural network architecture underlying most modern large language models, using attention mechanisms
It is a data compression algorithm
It is a database replication method
It is a cloud deployment pattern
explain: The transformer architecture, introduced in 2017, uses self-attention mechanisms to process sequences efficiently. It is the foundation of most modern large language models.

q: What does a model's "context window" determine?
options: The maximum amount of text, in tokens, the model can consider in a single request
The number of concurrent users
The training time required
The geographic regions where the model is available
explain: The context window is the maximum number of tokens (input plus output) a model can process at once. Larger windows allow longer documents, longer conversations, and more in-prompt context.

q: Diffusion models are primarily used to:
options: Detect network intrusions
Translate text between languages
Compress large files
Generate images by progressively refining random noise into coherent visuals
explain: Diffusion models generate images (and other media) by learning to reverse a gradual noising process - iteratively refining random noise into a coherent image guided by a text prompt.

q: A model that can process and generate both text and images is called:
options: A multimodal model
A binary model
A linear model
A unimodal model
explain: Multimodal models handle multiple data modalities - such as text, images, and audio - within a single model, enabling tasks like describing an image or generating an image from text.

q: What happens during pre-training of a foundation model?
options: The model is deployed to production
The model learns general patterns from massive, broad datasets before being adapted to specific tasks
The model is fine-tuned on a small company dataset
The model's outputs are evaluated by humans
explain: Pre-training exposes the model to vast amounts of broad data so it learns general language and world patterns. Later adaptation steps - such as fine-tuning or prompting - specialize it for specific tasks.

q: What is a "hallucination" in generative AI?
options: A billing error
A type of prompt injection attack
A hardware malfunction in the GPU
When a model generates plausible-sounding but false or fabricated information
explain: Hallucinations are confident but incorrect outputs - the model produces fluent text that is factually wrong. Common mitigations include RAG (grounding in real data), human review, and guardrails.

q: What does the "temperature" inference parameter control?
options: The randomness and creativity of the model's output - lower values give more deterministic responses
The model's context window size
The physical heat of the server
The cost per API call
explain: Temperature controls output randomness: a low temperature produces focused, deterministic responses, while a high temperature produces more creative and varied outputs.

q: A developer sets "max tokens" to 50 for a summarization task. What is the effect?
options: The model will process at most 50 input documents
The model's generated response is limited to about 50 tokens in length
The model will cost 50 cents per call
The model retries the request up to 50 times
explain: Max tokens caps the length of the model's generated output. It is used to control response length and manage cost and latency.

q: Top-p (nucleus) sampling is used to:
options: Control output diversity by sampling from the smallest set of most-likely tokens whose probabilities sum to p
Encrypt the model's response
Rank training datasets by quality
Select which cloud region hosts the model
explain: Top-p sampling limits each token choice to the most probable tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p, balancing coherence and creativity. Top-k sampling similarly restricts choices to the k most likely tokens.

q: In generative AI, what is a prompt?
options: A hardware component
The input text or instructions given to a model to guide its output
A type of encryption key
A billing invoice for model usage
explain: A prompt is the input provided to a generative model - instructions, context, examples, or questions - that shapes what the model generates.

q: What is prompt engineering?
options: Designing physical prompts for theater productions
The practice of crafting effective inputs to guide a foundation model toward desired outputs
Building data centers
Writing code to train models from scratch
explain: Prompt engineering is the discipline of designing and refining prompts - instructions, context, and examples - to get accurate, useful outputs from a foundation model without retraining it.

q: Asking a model a question with no examples - just the instruction - is called:
options: Chain-of-thought prompting
Fine-tuning
Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
explain: Zero-shot prompting provides only the task description with no examples, relying on the model's pre-trained knowledge to handle the task.

q: Including several input-output examples in a prompt to show the model the desired pattern is called:
options: Few-shot prompting
Zero-shot prompting
Model distillation
Pre-training
explain: Few-shot prompting includes a few examples demonstrating the task, which helps the model match the desired format, style, and behavior.

q: Asking a model to "think step by step" and show its reasoning before answering is an example of:
options: Temperature scaling
Zero-shot prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
Token chunking
explain: Chain-of-thought prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps from the model, which often improves accuracy on complex reasoning, math, and multi-step problems.

q: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) improves responses by:
options: Deleting the model's outdated training data
Increasing the temperature parameter
Retrieving relevant information from an external knowledge source and including it in the prompt so the model grounds its answer in real data
Retraining the model from scratch on new data
explain: RAG retrieves relevant documents (typically via embeddings and vector search) and adds them to the prompt. This grounds responses in current, factual, or proprietary data and reduces hallucinations - without retraining the model.

q: What is fine-tuning?
options: Increasing server capacity
Adjusting billing settings
Deleting old model versions
Further training a pre-trained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset to specialize its behavior
explain: Fine-tuning continues the training of a pre-trained model on domain- or task-specific data, adapting it to specialized terminology, tone, or tasks.

q: RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) is used to:
options: Compress model files
Speed up GPU hardware
Align model behavior with human preferences by training on human rankings of outputs
Translate models between languages
explain: In RLHF, humans rank or rate model outputs, a reward model learns those preferences, and the language model is optimized against it - improving helpfulness, honesty, and safety.

q: What is the purpose of guardrails for a generative AI application?
options: To reduce token costs to zero
To physically protect servers
To increase the model's parameter count
To apply safeguards that filter harmful inputs and outputs and enforce content policies
explain: Guardrails - such as Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock - apply safety policies to a generative AI application: filtering harmful content, blocking denied topics, and redacting sensitive information.

q: Which methods can be used to evaluate a generative AI model's output quality?
options: Measuring the server's CPU temperature
Counting the model's training hours
Automated metrics (such as ROUGE or BLEU) and human evaluation
Only counting the number of parameters
explain: Generative outputs are evaluated with automated metrics that compare outputs to references (ROUGE for summarization, BLEU for translation) and, crucially, with human evaluation of quality, relevance, and safety.

q: A "stop sequence" in a model inference request is used to:
options: Shut down the model server
Cancel the customer's subscription
Tell the model to stop generating when it produces a specified string DOMAIN 3 - APPLICATIONS OF FOUNDATION MODELS
Prevent the model from being fine-tuned
explain: Stop sequences are strings that signal the model to end generation - useful for controlling output format, for example stopping after a single answer in a templated prompt.

q: Which statement best describes a foundation model?
options: A rule-based expert system
A small model trained for one narrow task
A database of vector embeddings
A model trained on broad data at scale that can be adapted to many downstream tasks
explain: Foundation models are trained once on massive, broad datasets and then adapted - via prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning - to many tasks.

q: In a large language model, a token is:
options: A type of neural network layer
A password used for API authentication
The smallest unit of text the model processes
A compressed copy of the training data
explain: Tokens are the smallest text units (words or word pieces) a model reads and generates. The context window is measured in tokens.

q: A chatbot confidently states that a product launched in 2019, but the product does not exist. This is an example of:
options: Data drift
Overfitting
Model quantization
A hallucination
explain: A hallucination is confident, plausible-sounding output that is factually incorrect - a core limitation of generative AI.

q: A developer wants highly deterministic, repeatable answers from a model for an invoice-classification task. Which temperature setting is most appropriate?
explain: Temperature controls randomness. A value of 0 makes output deterministic and focused right for factual, repeatable tasks. Higher values add creativity and variation.

q: Which model type generates images by starting from random noise and progressively refining it?
options: Transformer
Support vector machine
Diffusion model
Decision tree
explain: Diffusion models create images by denoising random noise step by step. This is the technique behind text-to-image generation.

q: Embeddings are best described as:
options: Checkpoints saved during model training
Encrypted copies of prompts stored by AWS
Human-written labels attached to training data
Numerical vector representations of text that capture semantic meaning
explain: Embeddings convert text into vectors where similar meanings sit close together, enabling semantic search and RAG retrieval.

q: The key innovation of the transformer architecture is:
options: Backpropagation
The self-attention mechanism
Decision forests
Token billing
explain: Transformers - the architecture behind modern LLMs - use self-attention to weigh the importance of different words in context.

q: A developer sets a system prompt: "You are a banking assistant. Never give financial advice." The system prompt's role is to:
options: Extend the context window
Fine-tune the model's weights
Encrypt the user's prompts
Set the persona, rules, and context for the whole conversation
explain: The system prompt gives persistent instructions - persona, tone, and guardrails - that shape every response in the conversation.

q: An image prompt includes "blurry, watermarked, low-resolution" to keep those qualities out of the output. This is a:
options: System prompt
Few-shot example
Negative prompt
Stop sequence
explain: A negative prompt tells the model what to avoid - a common technique for steering image (and text) generation away from unwanted traits.

q: A team generates a report by prompting for an outline, then a draft from the outline, then edits to the draft - each step's output feeding the next prompt. This is:
options: Batch inference
Prompt chaining
Model distillation
Reward modeling
explain: Prompt chaining breaks a complex task into steps, where each step's output becomes the next step's input - improving quality on multi-stage work.

q: Which inference parameter restricts the model to only the k most likely next tokens?
options: Max tokens
Temperature
Top-p
Top-k
explain: Top-k sampling considers only the k highest-probability next tokens; temperature controls randomness, and top-p uses a cumulative-probability cutoff instead.

q: A support team reuses a prompt skeleton with {customer_name} and {ticket_text} placeholders across thousands of tickets. This is a:
options: Prompt template
Embedding
Vector index
Fine-tuned model
explain: Prompt templates are reusable prompt structures with placeholders, keeping prompts consistent across many similar requests.

q: Reviewers rank pairs of model responses by quality, and those rankings train a reward model used to further tune the LLM. This describes:
options: Prompt chaining
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
Supervised pre-training
Model distillation
explain: RLHF aligns models with human preferences: human rankings train a reward model, and the LLM is then optimized against it.

q: An invoice-extraction model gives differently worded answers on every run, breaking downstream parsing. The best fix is to:
options: Lower the temperature toward 0
Increase max tokens
Add negative prompts
Raise the temperature
explain: Temperature near 0 makes output deterministic and focused - exactly what factual extraction tasks need; higher temperatures add creative variation.

q: How does fine-tuning differ from continued pre-training?
options: Fine-tuning uses labeled task examples; continued pre-training uses unlabeled domain text
Continued pre-training needs no data at all
Fine-tuning trains a model from scratch
They are two names for the same technique
explain: Fine-tuning adapts a model with labeled examples for a specific task, while continued pre-training teaches domain knowledge from unlabeled text.

q: A company adapts a Bedrock model to understand internal jargon by training it further on unlabeled company documents. This is:
options: RAG
Continued pre-training
Fine-tuning
Prompt chaining
explain: Continued pre-training extends a foundation model with unlabeled domain data - the right choice for teaching terminology and domain knowledge rather than a specific task.

q: A foundation model trained in 2023 confidently answers questions about 2025 events with made-up details. This limitation is its:
options: Temperature setting
Knowledge cutoff
Context window
Overfitting
explain: A model only knows what was in its training data. Its knowledge cutoff is where that data ends anything newer is unknown to it, so it may hallucinate.

q: Before storing documents for RAG, they are typically split into smaller passages. This step is called:
options: Fine-tuning
Reward modeling
Chunking
Distillation
explain: Chunking splits documents into small retrievable passages; each chunk is then embedded and stored so the retriever can find the most relevant pieces.

q: A team has reviewers blindly compare outputs from two candidate models and pick the better response each time. This is:
options: Human evaluation
An automatic metric
Benchmark testing
Unit testing
explain: Human evaluation uses people to judge output quality - often by comparing or rating responses complementing automatic metrics like ROUGE.

q: Images created by Amazon Titan Image Generator carry invisible watermarks. Their purpose is to:
options: Identify the content as AI-generated
Speed up generation
Encrypt the images
Compress the image files
explain: Titan Image Generator embeds invisible watermarks so AI-generated images can be identified later - a transparency and safety feature.

q: Amazon Nova is:
options: A prompt engineering library
Amazon's family of foundation models for text, image, and video
A vector database service
A family of ML training chips
explain: Nova is Amazon's own foundation-model family (text, image, and video understanding and generation), available on Bedrock.

q: AWS Trainium and AWS Inferentia are:
options: Custom AWS chips for ML training and inference
Prompt template libraries
Types of Bedrock guardrails
Foundation models on Bedrock
explain: Trainium accelerates model training and Inferentia accelerates inference - purpose-built silicon that lowers generative AI compute costs.

q: A developer wants inline code suggestions and explanations inside their IDE. Which Amazon Q offering fits?
options: Amazon Kendra
Amazon Q Business
PartyRock
Amazon Q Developer
explain: Q Developer is the generative AI assistant for software development (IDE code suggestions, explanations); Q Business serves business users answering questions over company data.

q: A team wants deterministic answers for data extraction but creative variety for brainstorming, using one model. They should:
options: Use the same temperature for both tasks
Disable the context window
Adjust temperature per task: low for extraction, higher for brainstorming
Fine-tune two separate models
explain: Temperature is a per-request setting: near 0 for factual, repeatable tasks and higher for creative ones - no retraining needed.

q: A retail company uses one large pretrained model to summarize product reviews, translate listings, and answer shopper questions. Which property of a foundation model makes this possible?
options: It contains a separate hand-coded rule set for each retail task
It was built to perform only one narrow classification task
It requires no input data because it stores every product catalog
It was trained on broad data and can be adapted to many downstream tasks
explain: Foundation models are pretrained at scale on broad, diverse data, so the same base model learns general language and reasoning patterns that can be adapted through prompting or fine-tuning to many different tasks.

q: A bank compares a traditional ML churn model with a foundation model. Which statement is the most accurate difference?
options: A foundation model can never be adapted after pretraining is complete
Traditional models and foundation models are always trained on the same amount of data
A traditional model is usually trained for one specific task, while a foundation model is pretrained broadly and then adapted
A traditional model always generates new text, images, and audio content
explain: Traditional ML models are typically built and trained for a single defined task such as churn prediction. A foundation model is pretrained once on broad data and then adapted to many tasks, which is the core distinction.

q: During pretraining, a healthcare technology team exposes a model to a very large corpus of unlabeled text. What is the model primarily learning during this phase?
options: A fixed list of approved medical diagnoses for one hospital
The exact answers to the questions it will be asked after deployment
How to bill insurance claims in a specific software system
General patterns, structure, and relationships in language from the data itself
explain: Pretraining on unlabeled data is self-supervised: the model learns general patterns and relationships, such as predicting the next token, without needing humans to label every example first.

q: A manufacturing firm wants defect-report summaries but has only a small set of labeled examples. Why might starting from a foundation model help?
options: Pretraining removes the need to evaluate the adapted model at all
The model guarantees perfect accuracy on factory data it has never seen
Prior pretraining gives the model general knowledge, so adaptation can succeed with far less task-specific data
The firm must still collect millions of labeled defect reports first
explain: Because a foundation model already learned general patterns during pretraining, adapting it with prompting or fine-tuning usually requires much less labeled, task-specific data than training a model from scratch.

q: Which statement best describes a foundation model at a conceptual level?
options: A large model trained on broad data at scale that serves as a base for many applications
A single-purpose sensor model that detects one type of manufacturing defect
A database that stores documents so applications can retrieve them by keyword
A small lookup table that returns prewritten answers to known questions
explain: A foundation model is a large model, typically with billions of parameters, trained on broad data at scale. Its generality is what lets many different applications build on the same base.

q: An education startup avoids training a language model from scratch and instead adapts an existing foundation model for tutoring. What is the main cost and time benefit of this approach?
