options: The startup no longer needs any subject-matter review of the tutor responses
Adaptation eliminates all inference costs for the life of the application
The existing model automatically complies with every education regulation
Pretraining is reused, so the startup avoids the massive data and compute cost of creating the base model
explain: Pretraining a foundation model requires enormous data and compute. Reusing that pretrained base and only adapting it is far cheaper and faster than repeating the full pretraining process.

q: A media company is evaluating foundation models for several content tools. Which TWO characteristics are typical of foundation models? (Choose two.)
options: They are pretrained on large, broad datasets
They can be used for only one task and cannot be adapted
They contain no learned parameters and rely only on rules
They can be adapted to a wide range of downstream tasks
explain: Foundation models are defined by large-scale pretraining on broad data and by adaptability: the same base can support many downstream tasks through prompting, fine-tuning, or other adaptation methods.

q: An insurance team asks why pretraining data for a foundation model does not need a label for every document. Which explanation is correct?
options: Human reviewers label each document during the inference phase instead
The training objective can be derived from the data itself, such as predicting the next token in a sequence
Pretraining uses only data that regulators have already certified
The model memorizes a label that is hidden inside every document
explain: Self-supervised pretraining creates its own learning signal from unlabeled data, for example by hiding or predicting the next token, so no human-provided label is needed for each document.

q: A logistics company previously built separate models for route-note summarization, email drafting, and shipment Q&A. What changes when it adopts a single foundation model?
options: The company must convert all three tasks into image classification problems
One broadly pretrained base can support all three language tasks with different prompts or adaptation
The foundation model can only draft emails, so the other tasks must be dropped
Each task still requires a completely separate pretraining run from random weights
explain: A foundation model provides a shared, general-purpose base. Different prompts, retrieval, or light fine-tuning can specialize that same base for summarization, drafting, and question answering.

q: A government agency hears that a foundation model has billions of parameters. What do those parameters represent in practical terms?
options: The learned numerical weights that encode patterns the model picked up during training
The number of documents stored in the agency document management system
The number of separate applications that have been built on the model
The number of users who are allowed to query the model each day
explain: Parameters are the learned weights inside the model that are adjusted during training. Their values encode the patterns the model learned, and large foundation models have billions of them.

q: A hospital system must decide between training a traditional model from scratch and adapting a foundation model for clinical note summarization. Which trade-off should drive the decision?
options: Foundation models never need validation on clinical data before use
Training from scratch is always cheaper than adapting any pretrained model
A traditional model will automatically understand unstructured clinical notes better
Adapting reuses general language ability but still requires domain validation, privacy controls, and evaluation
explain: Adaptation saves the cost of building general language ability from scratch, but it does not remove the need to validate outputs on representative clinical data and to apply appropriate privacy and safety controls.

q: An agriculture company uses a foundation model to answer grower questions in English and Spanish and to draft field reports. Which capability is it relying on?
options: The model requires a new pretraining run for each new report format
Generalization from broad pretraining lets one model handle varied languages, formats, and tasks
The model was hand-programmed with a separate rule for every crop question
The model only works in the single language used in its first prompt
explain: Broad pretraining exposes a model to many languages, styles, and task formats, giving it general abilities that transfer across use cases instead of being limited to one narrow format.

q: Which task is a generative foundation model, rather than a traditional predictive model, most directly designed to perform?
options: Sorting historical invoices into paid and unpaid categories
Creating a new draft marketing email from a short instruction
Assigning every existing customer to exactly one predefined segment
Calculating a credit score from a fixed set of numeric fields only
explain: Generative models produce new content such as text, images, or code. Traditional predictive models mainly classify, score, or forecast from existing data rather than generating new content.

q: A legal technology team plans to adapt a foundation model for contract work. Which TWO approaches are valid ways to adapt the base model to the task? (Choose two.)
options: Deleting the pretrained weights and starting again from random values
Storing contracts in a relational database and calling that pretraining
Prompting the model with instructions and examples for contract summaries
Fine-tuning the model on labeled examples of the desired contract outputs
explain: A pretrained base can be adapted at inference time through prompting and examples, or more deeply through fine-tuning on task examples. Neither requires discarding the pretrained weights.

q: An energy company asks how a foundation model differs from the large dataset it was trained on. Which answer is correct?
options: The model and the dataset are the same thing stored in two formats
The dataset is a compressed copy of the model that can generate text
The dataset makes predictions, while the model only stores training examples
The model is the learned system that can generate or process new inputs; the dataset was the training material
explain: The training dataset is the material used during learning. The foundation model is the resulting system of learned weights that can respond to new inputs it was not explicitly given as examples.

q: A real estate platform needs listing descriptions, neighborhood summaries, and answers about listings from one AI investment. Which foundation model trait best supports this plan?
options: It is limited to returning exact passages copied from its training data
It cannot process inputs that differ from its pretraining examples
It performs best when every output follows one rigid template forever
It transfers learned language skills across related tasks without building a new model for each one
explain: Transfer of general learned ability is central to foundation models: skills learned in broad pretraining carry over to many related downstream tasks, reducing the need for separate models.

q: A sports media team says its foundation model was pretrained once but is updated for a new commentary style without full retraining. Which concept does this illustrate?
options: Adaptation can build on pretrained knowledge instead of repeating full pretraining for every change
Commentary style is controlled entirely by the network bandwidth available
A model style can only change if its training dataset is deleted
Pretraining happens automatically every time a user submits a prompt
explain: The value of a pretrained base is reuse: prompting, fine-tuning, or similar adaptation can change behavior for a new style or task without paying the full cost of pretraining again.

q: A bank is concerned that a foundation model might behave unpredictably on a task unlike anything in its evaluation set. Which property of broad pretraining explains both the opportunity and this risk?
options: The model was explicitly programmed for every banking task in advance
The model can only repeat training examples word for word, so risk is zero
Unpredictability comes only from the user interface, never from the model
General learned abilities can transfer to new tasks, but performance on untested tasks is not guaranteed
explain: Generalization lets foundation models handle tasks they were not specifically built for, but that same generality means behavior on novel, untested tasks must be evaluated rather than assumed.

q: Which description of pretraining is most accurate?
options: It is a pricing tier that gives a model a larger context window at inference
It is the initial large-scale training phase where a model learns from broad data before task adaptation
It is the final user acceptance test performed after a model is deployed
It is the process of writing prompts that users will send to the model
explain: Pretraining is the first, large-scale training phase on broad data. Later steps such as fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment build on the pretrained model that this phase produces.

q: A hospitality group uses the same foundation model for guest-message translation and itinerary drafting, but performance on legal disclaimers is weak. What is the most reasonable conclusion?
options: Foundation models perform identically on every task, so the test must be wrong
A general base does not guarantee strong performance on every specialized task; targeted adaptation and evaluation may be needed
The group should assume legal text is safe because other tasks work well
Weak results prove the model was never pretrained on any data
explain: A foundation model is general, not uniformly expert. Strong results on common tasks do not guarantee quality on specialized content, which may need adaptation, retrieval, and its own evaluation.

q: An insurer is selecting a base model for claims correspondence. Which TWO factors are most relevant to whether the foundation model will adapt well? (Choose two.)
options: The model ability to follow instructions and handle the required languages
The number of office locations the insurer operates in each state
The color scheme chosen for the claims portal user interface
The breadth and quality of the data used to pretrain the model
explain: Adaptation quality depends heavily on what the base model learned in pretraining and on practical abilities such as instruction following and language coverage that match the target use case.

q: A university researcher wants a model that can caption photos, draft study notes, and answer reading questions from one base system. Which choice best fits?
options: Use only a keyword search index, because it generates new explanations on demand
Use a spreadsheet macro, because it learns patterns from large unlabeled corpora
Train three unrelated traditional models and forbid any shared components
Use a foundation model, because its broad pretraining supports adaptation across these tasks
explain: The shared requirement is a reusable, general base. A foundation model fits because one pretrained system can be adapted across captioning, drafting, and question answering tasks.

q: A logistics executive asks why foundation models are sometimes called a platform shift in AI. Which response is best?
options: They remove the need for any application development on top of the model
They let every company avoid evaluating models for its own use cases
Many products can be built from the same pretrained base instead of each product training a model from scratch
They are only useful to the single team that performed the pretraining
explain: Foundation models change the development pattern: one expensive pretrained base becomes a platform that many teams and products adapt, rather than every application starting model development from zero.

q: A retailer fine-tunes a foundation model and finds it performs worse on general product questions than the base model did. What does this outcome demonstrate?
options: Specializing a model can trade off some general performance, so both task and general behavior should be re-evaluated
The base model must have had no parameters before the fine-tuning began
Adaptation always improves every capability of a foundation model
Fine-tuning results prove pretraining never contributed any useful knowledge
explain: Specialization can shift model behavior and sometimes degrade other abilities. Teams should evaluate the adapted model on the target task and on important general behaviors before deploying it.

q: A retailer pastes a product description into a language model and the system first breaks the text into smaller units. What are those units called?
options: Tokens are encrypted passwords that protect a model during training
Tokens are the final answers a model stores after each conversation
Tokens are the user accounts that are allowed to access the model
Tokens are the text chunks a model splits input into before processing it
explain: Before processing text, a language model splits it into tokens, which are chunks such as words, parts of words, or punctuation. The model works with these token units rather than reading the raw text directly.

q: A healthcare chatbot encounters a rare drug name it has not seen as a whole word. How does tokenization most likely handle the name?
options: The model rejects any word that did not appear as a whole word in training
The tokenizer deletes unfamiliar terms so they cannot affect the output
The term is converted into a single image token and removed from the text
The term is split into subword tokens that the model can combine to represent it
explain: Tokenization is often subword-based, so an uncommon term can be split into several familiar pieces. The model can represent rare or new words by combining the tokens for those pieces.

q: A developer is surprised that a 100-word legal clause consumes more than 100 tokens. Which explanation is correct?
options: Only English letters become tokens; numbers and punctuation are ignored
One token can represent a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or a character sequence
Every word in every language is always represented by exactly one token
A token is always longer than a paragraph but shorter than a document
explain: Tokens are not the same as words. Short words may be one token, while long words, punctuation, code symbols, and text in some languages can require several tokens each.

q: A banking assistant performs well on short chats but forgets details from the start of very long sessions. Which model property explains this limit?
options: It is the number of days a model retains a user conversation on a server
It is the maximum price a customer can be charged for one request
It is the physical screen size used to display a chatbot conversation
It is the maximum amount of token content the model can consider at one time
explain: The context window is the total amount of token content the model can consider at once for a request, covering the input it receives and, depending on the model, the output it generates.

q: A long customer support conversation exceeds a model context window. What is the direct practical consequence for the application?
options: The conversation is paused until the vendor releases a larger model
Older content may be truncated or summarized so the conversation fits the window
The model converts the extra text into embeddings and loses nothing at all
The model automatically expands its window without any cost or latency effect
explain: When content exceeds the window, the application must decide what to include: earlier turns may be dropped, truncated, or summarized so the total input fits within what the model can process.

q: An insurance team chooses a model variant with a much larger context window for policy reviews. What benefit does it gain?
options: It makes every request faster regardless of how much text is supplied
It guarantees the model will never produce an incorrect statement
It lets the model consider more input, such as longer documents or more conversation history, in one request
It removes the need to chunk any document before retrieval is used
explain: A larger context window lets a model consider more material in one request, such as a longer document or conversation history, instead of requiring the text to be split into separate calls.

q: A media company wants to paste entire episode archives into every prompt. Which trade-off of using a very large context window should it consider?
options: Context length has no relationship to token-based pricing models
Sending more context generally costs more and can add latency, so relevant context should be selected carefully
A larger window eliminates the need for retrieval or summarization in all cases
A larger window permanently stores documents inside the model weights
explain: Larger windows are useful but not free: processing more input tokens generally raises cost and can increase latency, so teams include only relevant context rather than everything available.

q: A logistics firm notices its chatbot bill rises when answers become verbose and prompts include long manuals. Which pricing factor explains this?
options: Only the number of employees using the application affects the price
Pricing is based only on the size of the building where servers run
Pricing is a flat fee that never changes with prompt or answer length
Both input tokens processed and output tokens generated contribute to usage-based cost
explain: Token-based pricing typically charges for the text processed as input and the text produced as output. Long prompts, long retrieved passages, and verbose responses therefore all raise the bill.

q: An education provider wants to lower token-based inference costs without changing models. Which action most directly reduces cost?
options: Repeat the system instructions multiple times in every request
Send the entire knowledge base with each individual user question
Trim redundant prompt content, limit irrelevant context, and control output length
Ask the model to produce the longest possible answer to every question
explain: Cost is driven by total tokens processed. Removing redundant instructions, trimming irrelevant retrieved text, and capping unnecessary output length directly reduce the tokens the provider must process.

q: A hospitality company is forecasting its generative AI spending. Which TWO factors most directly increase token-based cost for a request? (Choose two.)
options: A long input prompt that contains extensive retrieved context
The physical size of the end user laptop screen
The time zone in which the end user submits the request
A long generated response with many output tokens
explain: Token consumption drives generative AI cost, so a very long input context and a very long generated response both increase what a token-priced service charges for a request.

q: What is an embedding in the context of generative AI?
options: Embeddings are the error messages a model returns when a prompt fails
Embeddings are human-written labels that must be attached to every document
Embeddings are compressed copies of documents that users can read directly
Embeddings are numeric vector representations that capture the meaning of content
explain: An embedding represents text, an image, or another item as a list of numbers called a vector. That numeric form lets software measure how close two items are in meaning.

q: A retailer finds that a search for comfortable running shoes returns sneakers described as cushioned trainers, with no shared keywords. How did embeddings enable this result?
options: Only documents that share identical keywords can ever be close as vectors
Embeddings place items randomly so search results vary on every run
Vector closeness is determined only by which author wrote each document
Items with similar meaning tend to have vectors that are close in the embedding space
explain: Embedding models map meaning into vector space, so content with similar meaning ends up with vectors that point in a similar direction, even when the exact words used are different.

q: A support team uses cosine similarity to compare a question embedding with help-article embeddings. What does a cosine similarity near 1 indicate?
options: A value of zero always means two passages have identical meaning
It measures the physical distance between two data centers
It compares vector direction, and values near 1 indicate the embeddings are highly similar in meaning
It counts how many identical words appear in two documents
explain: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors. A value near 1 means the vectors point in a very similar direction, which for embeddings indicates strong semantic similarity.

q: A manufacturer wants search that finds a relevant manual passage even when a technician phrases a question with completely different words. Which approach best meets this need?
options: Translating every manual into a second language before searching it
Increasing the keyword list until it contains every possible synonym manually
Embedding the question and passages, then retrieving passages whose vectors are most similar in meaning
Fine-tuning the model on the manuals every time a new ticket arrives
explain: Keyword search misses paraphrases because it relies on exact terms. Embedding search represents the question and passages by meaning and retrieves the nearest vectors, finding relevant text phrased differently.

q: What is the role of a vector database in a generative AI application?
options: It is a spreadsheet used to schedule model retraining jobs each week
It is a graphics library that renders charts from model training metrics
It stores embeddings and supports fast similarity search to find semantically related content
It is a backup system that keeps copies of model weights in cold storage
explain: A vector database is built to store embeddings and perform fast similarity searches over them, returning the nearest, most semantically relevant items for a query vector.

q: In a retrieval system for energy utility documents, how do embeddings connect a user question to source passages?
options: Embeddings are used only to change the color of the returned answer text
The question embedding is matched against chunk embeddings to retrieve the most relevant passages for the prompt
The model is retrained from scratch whenever a relevant chunk is found
The vector store replaces the language model and writes answers by itself
explain: Retrieval-augmented generation works by embedding the question and stored chunks, finding the chunks whose embeddings are closest in meaning, and passing those chunks to the model as grounding context.

q: An agriculture team is told its embedding model produces 1,024-dimension vectors. What does the dimension count describe?
options: Each dimension is one numeric value in the vector that helps represent meaning
Dimensions count how many languages a document has been translated into
A dimension is one document stored in the vector database
Dimensions are the number of users who can query a vector store at once
explain: An embedding vector contains many numeric values called dimensions. More dimensions can capture richer distinctions in meaning, at the cost of more storage and computation.

q: A streaming service already stores embeddings for its catalog. Which TWO additional uses can those embeddings support? (Choose two.)
options: Encrypting model weights so they cannot be copied by competitors
Translating speech audio into a written transcript in real time
Semantic search that finds relevant content despite different wording
Grouping similar support tickets together by topic for trend analysis
explain: Because embeddings capture meaning, they power semantic search that tolerates different wording and content grouping tasks such as clustering similar items together for analysis or recommendations.

q: A government knowledge assistant returns irrelevant passages even though its embeddings are from a strong model. A review finds each stored chunk contains several unrelated policy topics. Which diagnosis is most likely correct?
options: Chunk size affects retrieval quality because overly large chunks mix topics and overly small chunks lose needed context
Larger embedding dimensions always make irrelevant results disappear
The vector database is unnecessary once a large context window exists
Cosine similarity fails whenever a corpus contains more than 1,000 chunks
explain: Splitting documents into chunks that are too large mixes topics and weakens similarity matching, while chunks that are too small lose context. Chunk sizing is a retrieval-quality design choice, not an unlimited-window problem.

q: A real estate search team plans to embed listings now and user queries at runtime. Which requirement is essential for the similarity search to work?
options: Any embedding model can be mixed with any other because all vectors are identical
Similarity search works only when the query is longer than the stored text
Stored passages and the user query must be embedded with the same model so their vectors are comparable
Queries should never be embedded; only stored documents need vectors
explain: The same embedding model must be used for stored content and for the incoming query, because vectors from different models live in different spaces and their similarity scores are not comparable.

q: A hotel group wants a Spanish guest question to retrieve help content written in French. How can a multilingual embedding model support this?
options: Semantically equivalent text in different languages can map to nearby vectors in a shared embedding space
The system keyword-matches only documents written in the same language
Each language needs a completely separate foundation model to be searched
The model translates every answer back into English before embedding it
explain: Multilingual embedding models are trained so that passages with the same meaning in different languages map close together, enabling cross-language retrieval without translating every document first.

q: A recruiter uses embeddings to shortlist resumes for a role description. Which process is the system following?
options: The assistant uses only the file creation date to estimate candidate quality
The assistant sorts resumes alphabetically and presents the first twenty
The assistant compares the job description vector with resume vectors and ranks the closest matches highest
The assistant counts how many times each resume repeats the exact job title
explain: Embeddings make meaning computable: the assistant can embed the request and each resume, then rank resumes by vector similarity to find the closest skill matches rather than exact keyword overlap.

q: A sports analytics chatbot includes 40 retrieved pages per question, and bills and latency climb while answer quality stalls. What is the best explanation?
options: Latency depends only on the number of users, never on prompt length
Including extra irrelevant context increases input tokens, which raises cost and can increase response time
Irrelevant passages always improve answers by giving the model more to read
Retrieved context is free because only generated output is ever processed
explain: Input size is a real cost and latency driver because the model must process every input token. Relevant retrieved passages, rather than the whole manual, keep quality while controlling both effects.

q: A legal team needs to estimate whether a brief will fit in a model context window before submitting it. What is the most reliable approach?
options: Use the model tokenizer to count tokens, because window limits and pricing are measured in tokens
Estimate fit by counting characters and dividing by the number of pages
Count only the words in the document headings and ignore the body text
Assume every document page equals exactly 500 tokens for every model
explain: A rough estimate uses the model tokenizer to count tokens, because token count, not page count or word count alone, determines how much fits in the window and how usage is billed.

q: A translation service correctly translates a sentence where the word bank means a river bank in one case and a financial institution in another. Which transformer mechanism most directly supports this?
options: It weighs the relevance of tokens to each other so context shapes the meaning of each word
It stores every conversation permanently inside the model weights
It processes text one character per day to improve translation quality
It deletes words that appear more than once in a sentence
explain: Self-attention lets the model weigh how relevant each token is to the others in the sequence. That helps it use surrounding words to resolve meaning, such as which entity a pronoun refers to.

q: A research team chooses a transformer model partly because it trains efficiently on very large text corpora. Which architectural property is responsible?
options: Transformers must read tokens strictly one at a time with no parallel work
Transformers remove the need for any training data at inference time
Transformers store sequences in a vector database before generating text
Transformers process tokens in parallel, which speeds training on large datasets
explain: Earlier sequence models processed tokens largely in order, which limited parallelization. Transformers can process tokens in a sequence in parallel during training, making large-scale training much more efficient.

q: A language product uses an encoder-decoder transformer for translation. Which description of the two parts is correct?
options: The encoder generates images while the decoder stores them in a database
The decoder runs before any input exists and guesses the source text
The encoder represents the input and the decoder generates the output based on that representation
Both parts only classify inputs and neither can generate a sequence
explain: In an encoder-decoder design, the encoder builds a rich representation of the input, and the decoder uses that representation to generate the output sequence, which fits tasks such as translation.

q: A support chatbot reads, The technician updated the server because it was failing, and correctly identifies what it refers to. Which transformer concept explains this behavior best?
options: The model counts letters in the pronoun to decide the answer
The model ignores all nouns and translates pronouns in isolation
Attention lets the model focus on relevant earlier tokens, such as the noun a pronoun refers to
The model looks up pronouns in a fixed table written by its developers
explain: Attention scores are computed between tokens so the model can focus on the most relevant earlier words. For a pronoun, the model can attend strongly to the noun the pronoun most plausibly refers to.

q: An energy company needs a 40-page operational report condensed into a one-page brief for executives. Which LLM capability should it use?
options: Physically mailing the report to every shareholder in the company
Rendering the report as a photorealistic image of an office
Composing a background music track for the earnings presentation
Summarizing the report into a shorter version that keeps the main findings
explain: Summarization is a core LLM capability: the model reads longer source text and produces a shorter version that preserves the main points, which is exactly what condensing a report requires.

q: A hotel chain drafts a guest welcome message in English and needs the same message in Spanish and German. Which statement about using an LLM for this is correct?
options: The model must be retrained from scratch for each new message it translates
The same LLM can generate the original text and translate it because it learned multilingual language patterns
Translation requires the model to be converted into a diffusion model first
Only a separate traditional model can ever produce text in Spanish
explain: LLMs learn language patterns across many languages during pretraining, so a general model can draft an original message in one language and translate it into another within the same workflow.

q: A software firm is scoping what a large language model can do for its teams. Which TWO tasks are core LLM capabilities? (Choose two.)
options: Predicting tomorrow weather by reading satellite hardware directly
Summarizing long documents into concise briefs
Controlling a factory robot arm with physical precision
Generating code from a natural language description of the function needed
explain: Large language models are capable of both condensing longer text into summaries and producing working code from natural language descriptions, among many other language tasks.

q: A retailer wants incoming support messages automatically labeled as billing, shipping, returns, or product help. Which LLM capability is this?
options: The model translates every ticket into three other languages
The model assigns each ticket to a predefined category based on its content
The model creates an image representing the mood of each ticket
The model generates a marketing slogan for each ticket category
explain: Classification with an LLM assigns input text to one of the categories the requester defines. The model reads each ticket and returns the label that best fits its content.

q: A student asks an AI tutor to explain why the sky is blue in simple terms and receives a direct explanation. Which LLM capability is being demonstrated, and what caveat applies?
options: An LLM answers questions by returning the embedding vector of the question
Question answering requires the model to browse a physical library
An LLM can only answer questions that appear word for word in training
An LLM can generate answers to questions using the prompt and any context supplied with it
explain: An LLM answers questions by generating a response grounded in the question and any context provided. Accuracy is not guaranteed, so important answers should be verified, but question answering is a core capability.

q: An engineering team asks how a transformer knows word order if attention looks at token relationships across a sequence. Which answer is most accurate?
options: The attention mechanism runs only on the first and last tokens of a text
Every token is replaced by its position number before training begins
Position information is added so the model can account for token order in a sequence
Transformers assume word order never affects meaning in any language
explain: Because attention is computed without relying only on word order, transformers use positional information to represent where each token sits in the sequence, preserving order-sensitive meaning.

q: A media team types a description of a mountain sunrise and receives a newly created image. If the generator is a diffusion model, how was the image produced?
options: They start from random noise and iteratively refine it into an image guided by a prompt
They convert an image into an embedding and never produce a picture
They draw images one pixel at a time following hand-written artist rules
They cut and paste pieces of existing photographs stored in a database
explain: Diffusion models generate images by beginning with random noise and progressively removing noise in steps, guided by a text prompt or other conditioning, until a coherent image emerges.

q: A game studio increases the number of diffusion steps for its concept art and notices better detail but slower generation. Which trade-off does this illustrate?
options: Step count has no effect on either quality or generation time
More steps always make image generation both faster and cheaper
More denoising steps can improve detail but increase generation time and cost
Fewer steps guarantee the highest possible image detail in all cases
explain: More denoising steps generally allow finer refinement of the image, which can improve detail and prompt adherence, but each additional step adds computation, latency, and cost.

q: Which statement best describes a multimodal model?
options: It can process or generate more than one modality, such as text combined with images
It is a model that was trained by several different companies at once
It is a model that can only accept typed text and return typed text
It is a model that stores data in several different database systems
explain: A multimodal model can work with more than one type of input or output, such as understanding an image together with a text question and responding in text about what the image shows.

q: A banking analyst uploads a screenshot of a revenue chart and asks a model which quarter grew fastest. Which model type and ability are required?
options: The analyst should first delete the chart because LLMs cannot use images
The analyst must convert the chart into audio before any model can use it
A multimodal model can take the chart image plus the question and answer about the visual data
Only a diffusion model can answer questions about an existing chart image
explain: A multimodal model can jointly process an image and a related text question, reasoning over the visual content, such as reading values and trends from a chart, rather than treating the image as plain text.

q: A design team is learning how diffusion image generation works. Which TWO statements about the process are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It requires a human artist to draw each intermediate step manually
It starts from random noise rather than from a finished image
It copies the single closest photograph from its training set unchanged
It progressively denoises over multiple steps to form a coherent image
explain: Diffusion generation begins with noise rather than a finished image, and the model refines that noise over multiple iterative denoising steps, typically guided by a text prompt, to form the final image.

q: An agriculture research group reads about generative adversarial networks for synthetic crop images. How does a GAN work at a conceptual level?
options: A classifier labels images while a second classifier deletes the labels
Two translators compete to produce the shortest summary of a document
A database and a search index race to return the fastest query result
A generator creates samples while a discriminator tries to distinguish real from generated samples
explain: In a GAN, the generator creates synthetic samples and the discriminator tries to tell real samples from generated ones. This adversarial feedback pushes the generator toward more realistic outputs.

q: A streaming service compares GANs and diffusion models for promotional artwork. Which comparison is most accurate?
options: GANs start from noise and denoise it, while diffusion models use a discriminator
Diffusion models iteratively denoise from noise for image generation, while GANs learn through a generator-discriminator contest
GANs and diffusion models are the same method with two different names
Diffusion models classify images, while GANs only summarize text documents
explain: Each family has a different strength: diffusion models are widely used for high-quality text-guided image generation, while GANs use adversarial training between a generator and a discriminator and were an earlier leading approach.

q: A news archive needs a written description generated for each photograph so the photos become searchable. Which capability is this?
options: It converts the photo into an audio file describing the scene aloud
It takes an image as input and generates a textual description of its content
It is a text-to-image task performed only by diffusion models
It removes the background from a photo without producing any text
explain: Image captioning takes an image as input and produces descriptive text as output. It is an image-to-text task commonly performed by multimodal models, not text-to-image generation.

q: A logistics developer describes a function that sorts shipments by delivery date and receives draft Python code. Which statement about this capability is correct?
options: An LLM can draft code from a description, and the code should be reviewed and tested before use
LLMs cannot produce code because code is not a form of text
Code generation requires converting the request into an image first
The model guarantees generated code is secure and error-free
explain: Generating code from a description is a core LLM capability because code is a formal text language. Generated code should still be reviewed and tested like any other code before use.

q: An insurance call center wants a one-paragraph summary of each recorded call transcript plus answers to staff questions about the call. Which pairing of LLM capabilities fits?
options: Transcription alone answers staff questions without any language model
Summarization condenses the call, and question answering uses the transcript content to respond to staff queries
Each staff question requires retraining the model on the full transcript
The model must be a diffusion model because calls contain spoken audio
explain: The same underlying LLM capabilities support both tasks: summarization condenses the long transcript, and question answering lets staff query its content, especially when the transcript or retrieved passages are supplied as context.

q: A university lecturer is listing defining traits of transformers. Which TWO traits belong on the list? (Choose two.)
options: A built-in rule that output must always be a translated sentence
Self-attention that lets each token weigh the relevance of other tokens
Parallel processing of tokens in a sequence during training
A requirement to store all training data in a vector database
explain: Self-attention, which lets tokens attend to one another for context, and the ability to process sequence tokens in parallel during training are defining characteristics of the transformer architecture.

q: A legal firm needs to classify clauses by risk type, not generate new contracts. An architect proposes an encoder-focused transformer. Which reasoning is sound?
options: An encoder-only model is the standard choice for generating long original stories
A multimodal model is required before any text can be classified
An encoder-focused model suits understanding and classification, while generation usually relies on decoder components
Encoder and decoder models are interchangeable for every task by definition
explain: Encoder-only models build rich representations of input text, which suits understanding tasks like classification. Generating long new sequences is typically the role of decoder-based or encoder-decoder designs.

q: A patient-facing assistant accepts a photo of a skin rash together with a written description of symptoms. Why is a multimodal model appropriate here?
options: The assistant is a diffusion model because it received an image as input
A multimodal model can consider the photo and the text together when formulating its response
The assistant can use only the text and must ignore the uploaded photo
The assistant converts the photo to a token price before answering
explain: A multimodal assistant can combine the image and the written symptom description, using both signals together to suggest relevant information, though medical use still requires professional oversight.

q: A real estate agent gives an LLM three bullet points about a house and receives a polished listing email. Which capability produced the email?
options: The model produces new, coherent draft copy based on the brief and instructions given
Text generation means converting the brief into an embedding vector only
The model can only fill in a single missing word, not draft a full email
The model retrieves the exact email a competitor sent last year
explain: Text generation is the LLM capability of producing new, coherent text that follows the instruction, such as drafting complete marketing copy from a brief outline of points to cover.

q: A retail platform team is planning its first foundation model project. Which sequence best represents the foundation model lifecycle?
options: Evaluation of a model that has not yet been trained on any data
Writing user prompts, which replaces all training and evaluation stages
Pretraining, adaptation, evaluation, deployment, and then feedback-driven iteration
Deployment first, followed by pretraining only if users complain about quality
explain: The foundation model lifecycle starts with large-scale pretraining, then moves through adaptation such as fine-tuning, evaluation of the adapted model, deployment to users, and ongoing feedback and iteration.

q: A healthcare company has adapted a model for discharge-note summaries and is deciding whether it is ready for clinicians. What should happen before deployment?
options: The only valid evaluation is asking the model whether it thinks it is accurate
Evaluation means counting how many servers are needed to host the model
Candidate models should be evaluated on representative tasks for quality and safety before deployment
Evaluation is optional because pretrained models are always production ready
explain: Evaluation before deployment measures whether outputs meet quality, safety, and task requirements on representative examples. Skipping it means weaknesses are discovered by customers instead of by the team.

q: A student asks an AI assistant for sources on a research topic, and it confidently provides a journal citation that cannot be found anywhere. What is this failure called?
options: The assistant refused to answer because the topic was too broad
The assistant summarized a real article more briefly than requested
The assistant translated the reading list into another language
The assistant confidently cited a journal article that does not actually exist
explain: A hallucination is generated content that sounds fluent and confident but is factually incorrect or invented. Fabricated references are a classic example because the citation looks plausible but does not exist.

q: A banking assistant trained with data through last year gives outdated answers about a regulation issued this month. Which limitation explains this?
options: The model charges more for questions about recent events
The model was trained on data up to a cutoff date and has no built-in knowledge of later events
The model deletes older training data whenever a new law is passed
The model refuses to discuss any event from the current year
explain: A model knowledge reflects its training data up to a cutoff point. Events after that point are not in its training, so it cannot reliably describe them without an external source of current information.

q: An insurance company wants to reduce invented policy details in its chatbot answers. Which mitigation most directly addresses hallucination risk?
options: Supplying retrieved passages from authoritative internal documents as context for the answer
Asking the model to answer faster so it has less time to invent details
Raising the temperature so the model produces more varied policy wording
Removing all source documents so the model relies only on pretraining
explain: Grounding generation in retrieved, authoritative source passages gives the model verified facts to base its answer on and lets users check citations, which reduces invented details compared with relying on model memory alone.

q: Two staff members at a logistics firm run the identical prompt on different days and receive noticeably different wording and one different recommendation. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The model intentionally changes answers to test whether staff are paying attention
Sampling during generation means the same prompt can yield different outputs on different runs
Inconsistent answers prove the users typed completely different questions
The model must have been retrained between the two runs
explain: Generative models sample from probable outputs, so repeated runs of the same prompt can produce differently worded or even substantively different responses. This variability is expected behavior, not a sign the prompt changed.

q: A hiring tool built on a language model drafts job descriptions that consistently use language discouraging some applicant groups. Which root cause and response are most accurate?
options: Training data can carry historical biases that the model reproduces, so outputs need group-level evaluation and review
A model trained on more data is automatically free of any bias
Bias can only enter a model through the final user prompt it receives
Bias is a hardware problem caused by the type of chip used for inference
explain: Models learn patterns from training data, which can include historical and societal biases. Outputs should be tested across relevant groups and reviewed so biased patterns are detected and addressed before and after deployment.

q: A legal research team wants practical safeguards against hallucinated case summaries. Which TWO safeguards should it adopt? (Choose two.)
options: Increase output randomness to make invented details harder to notice
Prevent users from seeing any source or citation for an answer
Require human review of high-impact outputs before they are used
Ground answers in retrieved, trusted source material
explain: Grounding answers in retrieved trusted sources and keeping human review for consequential outputs are both established hallucination mitigations. Neither raising randomness nor hiding sources from users reduces invented content.

q: After selecting a pretrained model, a media company trains it on labeled examples of its own headline style. Where does this step belong in the lifecycle?
options: Fine-tuning is a user interface setting that changes the screen layout
Fine-tuning further trains a pretrained model on task-specific examples to adapt its behavior
Fine-tuning is the stage where a model is first exposed to any data at all
Fine-tuning happens instead of pretraining and always uses unlabeled data
explain: Fine-tuning occurs after pretraining: it further trains the pretrained model, usually on smaller, task-specific examples, so its behavior, tone, or format better fit a particular application.

q: Once a hospitality chatbot is live, guests report that it mishandles early check-in requests. What does the feedback stage of the lifecycle call for?
options: Collecting user feedback and monitoring outputs to guide improvements in the next iteration
Returning the model to pretraining even for a minor wording complaint
Deleting all usage data so problems cannot be traced to the system
Freezing the system permanently so no weakness is ever addressed
explain: Deployment is not the end of the lifecycle. User feedback, error reports, and monitoring reveal weaknesses that teams use to improve prompts, data, retrieval, or the model itself in later iterations.

q: A traveler asks a standalone LLM for todays live flight prices. Which limitation applies if the model has no tools or retrieval connected?
options: It stores today's prices in its parameters from yesterday's conversations
It can read any live website as long as the user names the site
It updates its knowledge continuously every time any user asks a question
It has no built-in access to real-time data unless connected to retrieval or external tools
explain: A base LLM generates from patterns learned in training and from the context it is given. Without retrieval, tools, or a live data connection, it has no built-in access to real-time information such as current prices.

q: A finance team finds that an LLM explains a loan concept well but makes errors in a multi-step interest calculation. Which limitation does this show?
options: Arithmetic errors happen only when the user writes the numbers in words
LLMs calculate arithmetic internally with guaranteed exact results
Language models can be unreliable at multi-step arithmetic, so results should be verified or handled by a calculation tool
A model that writes fluent explanations can never make a numeric error
explain: LLMs generate plausible text by predicting tokens, which is not the same as performing exact calculation. Multi-step arithmetic and similar precise tasks should be verified or delegated to a calculator or code tool.

q: An education platform is choosing between a large model for essay feedback and a smaller model for simple quiz hints. Which trade-off should guide the choice?
options: The largest model is always the cheapest because it needs fewer retries
Latency and cost are identical for every model size and task type
Smaller models outperform larger models on every complex reasoning task
Larger models may offer higher quality but usually bring higher cost and latency than smaller models
explain: Model choice is a trade-off: larger, more capable models often produce better quality on complex tasks but cost more per request and respond more slowly than smaller models, which may be sufficient for routine work.

q: A government communications team is documenting known LLM limitations for its staff guide. Which TWO limitations should it include? (Choose two.)
options: It can browse the live internet by default with no tools or retrieval
Its knowledge is limited to information available up to its training cutoff
It is guaranteed to produce mathematically exact answers to any calculation
It can reproduce biases present in its training data in generated outputs
explain: A fixed knowledge cutoff and the ability to produce biased output are both well-known LLM limitations. Built-in live internet access and guaranteed freedom from arithmetic errors are not properties of a standalone LLM.

q: A streaming service needs to judge whether generated show descriptions are accurate and appealing before launch. Which evaluation approach is most appropriate?
options: Checking only whether the model responded within one second
Counting the number of words in each output and preferring the longest
Human reviewers rating outputs for accuracy, relevance, and tone against defined criteria
Asking the model to grade itself with no external criteria or reviewers
explain: Open-ended generation has no single correct answer, so evaluation commonly combines human reviewers rating outputs against criteria with benchmark tasks, rather than relying only on exact-match metrics.

q: An accounting firm needs its assistant to reflect tax guidance issued this year, after its model knowledge cutoff. Which solution addresses this without retraining the model?
options: Retrieve current guidance from an up-to-date knowledge source and ground the answers in it
Wait for the vendor to pretrain a completely new model next year
Fine-tune the model every morning on the days new tax documents
Tell users the assistant cannot help with any tax question at all
explain: Retrieval supplies current information at request time, so the answer can reflect this year guidance without retraining the model. The underlying model cutoff does not change; the retrieved context fills the gap.

q: A manufacturing engineer follows a model multi-step troubleshooting derivation that reads confidently but contains one wrong intermediate step, leading to a bad conclusion. Which lesson is most important?
options: If the final answer sounds certain, earlier steps do not need checking
A model can produce a plausible but flawed step in multi-step reasoning, so critical work should be broken down and verified
Reasoning errors only occur when the model response is very short
A confident, well-formatted explanation proves every reasoning step is correct
explain: Fluent, confident reasoning text is still generated token prediction and can contain a subtle wrong step that invalidates the conclusion. Critical multi-step work needs decomposition, tool use, and verification rather than trust in presentation style.

q: Six months after launch, a retail assistant answers product questions noticeably worse as the catalog changes. Which TWO lifecycle practices should have caught and addressed this? (Choose two.)
options: Monitoring is only needed during the first hour after a model launches
Using collected feedback to update retrieval content, prompts, or the model in the next iteration
Once deployed, a model should never be changed for any reason
Tracking quality signals from real usage to detect emerging failure patterns early
explain: After deployment, teams monitor real outputs, quality signals, and user feedback for problems such as declining accuracy, new failure patterns, or changing user needs, then use what they learn to iterate on the system in the next cycle.

q: A science communicator asks why a model invented a plausible-sounding but false statistic. Which explanation of hallucination is most accurate?
options: Hallucinations are caused only by typos in the user prompt wording
The model predicts plausible next tokens from learned patterns, which can produce fluent text that is not factually grounded
The model deliberately fabricates facts to mislead its users
The model copies its answers from a single unreliable website each time
explain: Hallucinations arise because the model generates the most plausible-sounding continuation based on learned patterns, not because it looks facts up in a verified internal database before answering.

q: A sports media company is building its pre-launch evaluation plan for a generative assistant. Which THREE activities belong in the evaluation stage? (Choose three.)
options: Having human reviewers rate responses for helpfulness and accuracy
Safety testing for harmful, biased, or policy-violating outputs
Setting the production auto-scaling policy for inference servers
Running benchmark tasks and test sets to measure output quality
explain: Evaluation of a generative model typically combines benchmark or test-set measurement, human rating of output quality, and safety testing for harmful or policy-violating content before the model is released.

q: A bank tests its assistant by asking the same fee question in three different phrasings and receives three different fee amounts. What does this result demonstrate?
options: Differing facts across paraphrased questions reveal an inconsistency weakness that should be tested and reduced
Paraphrase sensitivity is impossible in any generative model
Inconsistency can only be fixed by giving the model a larger screen
The model is working correctly because every wording deserves a different fact
explain: Wording changes should not change the underlying facts in an answer. Variation across paraphrases signals a robustness problem that teams should measure with paraphrase test sets and address before relying on the system.

q: A language-learning app collects thumbs-up and thumbs-down ratings plus corrections on tutor responses. How is this feedback used in the model lifecycle?
options: Feedback is stored only to increase the size of the training invoice
A single thumbs-down rating automatically retrains the model instantly
Feedback matters only if every user agrees on the same complaint
Reviewed user feedback identifies failure patterns that guide improvements to prompts, data, or the model
explain: User corrections and ratings are feedback signals. Teams review them to find failure patterns and then improve prompts, retrieval content, fine-tuning data, or guardrails in the next iteration of the system.

q: A logistics company runs a large foundation model for a simple yes-or-no shipment label check millions of times a day, and costs are high. Which evaluation of the choice is best?
options: A foundation model is the lowest-cost option for every workload by default
Latency never matters for customer-facing classification workloads
Cost differences disappear when a task is run millions of times
A smaller task-specific model can be cheaper and faster for narrow, high-volume classification than a large foundation model
explain: For simple, high-volume classification, a smaller fine-tuned traditional model is often cheaper and faster at inference, while the foundation model strength is broad generative work. Matching the tool to the task controls cost.

q: A pharmaceutical team plans two adaptation steps for a pretrained model: more training on unlabeled research text, then training on labeled question-answer examples. Which pairing is correct?
options: Continued pretraining is performed by end users every time they chat
Fine-tuning and continued pretraining are two names for the identical process
Deployment is the stage where a model first learns from raw text data
Continued pretraining adapts a model on more unlabeled domain data, while fine-tuning trains it on task-specific examples
explain: Continued pretraining, fine-tuning, evaluation, and deployment are distinct lifecycle stages. Continued pretraining adapts a model on additional unlabeled domain data, while fine-tuning uses task examples to shape specific behavior.

q: A retail company wants to experiment with several foundation models from different providers through one API, without provisioning or managing any servers. Which service meets these requirements?
options: Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs
Amazon EC2 with self-hosted models
AWS Lambda with custom model code
Amazon Bedrock
explain: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed, serverless service that gives API access to foundation models from multiple providers through a single API. The company does not provision servers or manage infrastructure, unlike self-hosting on EC2 or building custom training jobs.

q: A bank is evaluating Amazon Bedrock and is concerned that prompts sent by its employees will be used to train the base foundation models for other customers. Which statement is correct?
options: Prompts are shared with the model provider that supplied the chosen model
Data submitted to Amazon Bedrock is not used to train the underlying base foundation models
Only anonymized prompts are used to retrain base models each month
Customer data is used to train base models unless the company opts out in writing
explain: With Amazon Bedrock, customer inputs and outputs are not used to train the original base foundation models and are not shared with model providers. This privacy design is a key reason regulated industries can use managed foundation models.

q: A media company expects a steady, predictable volume of foundation model requests every day and wants a reserved capacity option with more predictable performance than pay-as-you-go access. Which Amazon Bedrock option should the company choose?
options: On-demand throughput
Spot model access
Provisioned Throughput
Model playground access
explain: Provisioned Throughput in Amazon Bedrock lets customers purchase reserved model units for a specific model, providing consistent throughput for steady, predictable workloads. On-demand throughput is pay-as-you-go and better suited to variable or getting-started usage.

q: A startup is testing a new support assistant and has unpredictable, spiky traffic. The team wants to start without any capacity commitment and pay only for tokens processed. Which Amazon Bedrock pricing model fits best?
options: Dedicated hosted endpoints billed hourly
Provisioned Throughput with a one-year commitment
On-demand throughput
Reserved model units
explain: On-demand throughput on Amazon Bedrock is serverless and pay-as-you-go based on tokens processed, with no capacity commitment. It is the natural starting point for spiky or experimental workloads, while Provisioned Throughput suits steady high-volume traffic.

q: A product team wants business users to try prompts against different foundation models in the AWS Management Console before writing any code. Which Amazon Bedrock feature should they use?
options: Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Bedrock model evaluation jobs
Bedrock Guardrails
Bedrock playgrounds
explain: Amazon Bedrock playgrounds in the console let users experiment with prompts and compare models interactively, including chat, text, and image playgrounds, before committing to code. Knowledge Bases, Guardrails, and evaluation jobs serve different production purposes.

q: A team is choosing a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock for a new application. Which factors should drive the decision? (Choose two.)
options: How well the model performs on the team's representative evaluation tasks
The design of the model provider's logo
The model's cost and latency profile for the expected workload
The physical size of the servers the team must install to run the model
explain: Model selection on Bedrock should be evidence-based: measured performance on tasks like the team's own, plus the cost and latency the workload can support. Bedrock is serverless, so the team installs no model servers, and branding plays no role in fitness for the task.

q: Which tasks are good fits for the Amazon Nova family of models on Amazon Bedrock? (Choose two.)
options: Physically compressing data stored in Amazon S3
Generating text, images, and video content at a strong price-performance point
Understanding text, images, and video inputs for multimodal applications
Replacing an AWS account root user for billing administration
explain: Amazon Nova is Amazon's family of foundation models on Bedrock, spanning understanding models that process text, image, and video inputs and creative models that generate images and video, positioned for strong price-performance. Nova does not administer AWS accounts or compress storage.

q: An insurance company wants a model family on Amazon Bedrock that was built by Amazon and includes options for text generation and image generation. Which family should the company evaluate?
options: Amazon Polly voices
A self-trained model in Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Titan
Meta Llama only, hosted outside Bedrock
explain: Amazon Titan is Amazon's own foundation model family available through Amazon Bedrock, including text models and the Titan Image Generator. Polly is a text-to-speech service, not a foundation model family, and Llama is a third-party family from Meta.

q: A healthcare startup wants to build a generative AI feature but has no ML infrastructure team. The startup wants AWS to manage the servers, scaling, and model hosting entirely. Which characteristic of Amazon Bedrock meets this need?
options: Bedrock requires a dedicated cluster for each prompt
Bedrock requires customers to patch the underlying GPU hosts
Bedrock is serverless, so model access is through APIs with infrastructure managed by AWS
Bedrock only runs inside a customer data center
explain: Amazon Bedrock is serverless and fully managed: customers call model APIs and AWS handles the underlying infrastructure, scaling, and availability. That removes the need for an ML infrastructure team just to access foundation models.

q: A government agency wants to compare responses from Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, and Amazon Titan models for the same citizen-service prompts before selecting one. Which capability of Amazon Bedrock supports this?
options: Exclusive access to only Amazon-built models
Automatic conversion of every model into a Titan model
A single API that provides access to models from multiple providers
A requirement to sign a separate contract and build a separate integration for each provider inside Bedrock
explain: A core value of Amazon Bedrock is choice: one API gives access to foundation models from Amazon and leading third-party providers such as Anthropic and Meta, so teams can evaluate and switch models without rebuilding their application for each provider.

q: An education company built a prototype that calls a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock. Traffic grows 20x, and latency-sensitive requests now compete with long batch summarization jobs. What is the MOST appropriate Bedrock action?
options: Stop using Bedrock and train a model from scratch
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the steady, latency-sensitive workload and keep batch work on demand
Increase the temperature for all requests
Move all traffic to the console playground
explain: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for a model, giving predictable performance for steady production traffic, while on-demand remains suitable for flexible batch work. Temperature affects randomness, not capacity, and the playground is for experimentation, not production.

q: What is the primary purpose of Amazon Bedrock?
options: To train graphics processors in AWS data centers
To manage employee payroll for AI teams
To provide a managed way to build generative AI applications using foundation models through APIs
To replace Amazon S3 as the default object store
explain: Amazon Bedrock exists to make foundation models easy to use: managed API access to models from multiple providers, plus features such as knowledge bases, agents, guardrails, and evaluation for building generative AI applications without managing infrastructure.

q: A real estate firm wants its application to switch from one foundation model to another on Amazon Bedrock if a better model is released. Which design benefit does Bedrock provide for this?
options: Models are interchangeable because Bedrock locks the firm into a single model forever
A consistent API across models reduces the code changes needed to evaluate or swap models
Switching models always requires retraining from scratch
Bedrock automatically rewrites the firm's business logic for each model
explain: Because Bedrock presents different models through a common API and console experience, teams can test a new model and swap it in with far less integration work than managing separate provider integrations. Business logic and prompts may still need tuning, but the access pattern stays consistent.

q: A manufacturing company wants a lightweight Amazon-built model on Bedrock for high-volume ticket tagging, and a more capable Amazon-built option for complex document understanding that includes video. Which pairing is correct?
options: Titan Text for tagging; Nova understanding models for complex multimodal document and video understanding
Polly for tagging; Transcribe for video understanding
Nova for tagging; a rules engine for video understanding
Rekognition for tagging; Lex for document understanding
explain: Amazon Titan text models suit tasks such as classification and summarization, while Amazon Nova understanding models handle multimodal inputs including images and video for more complex understanding. Polly, Transcribe, Rekognition, and Lex are purpose-built services, not Bedrock model families for this pairing.

q: Which statements about Amazon Bedrock are true? (Choose two.)
options: It provides access to foundation models from multiple providers, including Amazon models such as Titan and Nova
It offers both on-demand and provisioned throughput options for model inference
It can only be used from the AWS Management Console and has no API
Customers must manage the servers that host the foundation models
explain: Amazon Bedrock is fully managed and serverless, offers on-demand and Provisioned Throughput inference options, and provides models from multiple providers including Amazon Titan and Nova through APIs and SDKs as well as console playgrounds. Customers never manage the hosting servers.

q: A hospitality group wants to add a text-generation feature to its booking app in days, not months, and does not want to train any model. Which approach has the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Collect labeled data and train a custom model in Amazon SageMaker AI
Call a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock using on-demand throughput
Build a rules engine that contains a handwritten reply for every possible guest question
Buy GPU servers and host an open-source model in a company data center
explain: Calling a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock on demand requires no training and no infrastructure management, so it is the fastest, lowest-overhead path to a text-generation feature. Training a custom model or self-hosting adds weeks of work and ongoing operations.

q: A sports media editor uses the Amazon Bedrock console to test headline-generation prompts on two different models side by side before the development team integrates anything. Which feature is the editor using?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Bedrock model import
The Bedrock playgrounds for interactive model experimentation
Agents for Amazon Bedrock
explain: Bedrock playgrounds provide an interactive console environment to run prompts, adjust parameters, and compare models before writing integration code. Provisioned Throughput is a capacity purchase, and Agents orchestrate multi-step tasks in applications, not manual prompt testing.

q: An energy company will run a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock for a customer-facing assistant. The workload is new, volumes are unknown, and finance wants no upfront commitment. Which starting choice is MOST appropriate?
options: On-demand throughput, then reassess once real usage patterns are known
A one-year reserved capacity purchase before launch
Self-hosting to avoid any usage-based billing
Provisioned Throughput with the maximum model units available
explain: For a new workload with unknown volume, on-demand throughput avoids upfront commitments and charges only for use; the company can move steady traffic to Provisioned Throughput later once patterns are proven. Buying maximum reserved capacity up front risks paying for unused capacity.

q: A banking team wants the lowest-cost Amazon foundation model that still handles simple text classification well, and plans to test it in Amazon Bedrock. Which principle should guide the selection?
options: Select a model based only on the provider's brand
Avoid testing and commit to one model for all future tasks
Evaluate smaller, task-appropriate models first, because model choice strongly affects both cost and latency
Always select the largest model because cost does not vary by model
explain: On Bedrock, price and latency vary significantly by model, and smaller models often perform simple tasks such as classification just as well as large ones at a fraction of the cost. Evaluation on representative prompts, not brand or size alone, should drive the choice.

q: Which Amazon Bedrock capability lets a team reserve model units for a specific foundation model to support a known production workload?
options: Prompt templates
Provisioned Throughput
Automatic model evaluation
Model playgrounds
explain: Provisioned Throughput is the Bedrock feature for purchasing reserved model units dedicated to a chosen model, which supports consistent throughput for production workloads. Playgrounds, prompt templates, and evaluation do not reserve inference capacity.

q: A retail data team wants to generate product images for an online catalog using an Amazon-built image model available through Amazon Bedrock. Which model should the team use?
options: Amazon Titan Image Generator
Amazon Nova Micro for text only
Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe
explain: Amazon Titan Image Generator is Amazon's image generation foundation model on Bedrock, used to create and edit images from text prompts. Polly synthesizes speech and Transcribe converts speech to text; neither generates catalog images.

q: A company is designing a generative AI application on Amazon Bedrock and wants to keep its proprietary prompts and responses private from model training pipelines. Which Bedrock property addresses this requirement directly?
options: Bedrock deletes the application after each request
Bedrock does not use customer data to train the base foundation models
Bedrock anonymizes data by publishing it after 30 days
Bedrock requires customers to encrypt models themselves before every call
explain: A foundational Bedrock design point is that customer data is not used to train the base foundation models, which keeps proprietary prompts and responses out of shared training pipelines. This is distinct from optional fine-tuning, where a customer deliberately supplies training data for its own customized model.

q: A developer team wants to invoke foundation models from application code in Python with minimal setup on AWS. Which combination is correct?
options: Install the model weights into the application's container image
SSH into the foundation model host and run the model binary directly
Use the Amazon Bedrock API or AWS SDK from the application code; no model servers need to be provisioned
Create an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group for each model before any call
explain: Bedrock is consumed programmatically through its API and the AWS SDKs, so application code simply makes inference requests; AWS hosts and scales the models. There is no host to log into and no model weights for the customer to install or scale.

q: Employees at an insurance company waste time searching policy manuals, wikis, and shared drives. Leadership wants a generative AI assistant that answers employee questions using only company data sources. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon Q Developer
PartyRock
Amazon Q Business
Amazon Bedrock playgrounds
explain: Amazon Q Business is the enterprise generative AI assistant that connects to company data sources such as documents, wikis, and applications so employees can ask questions and get answers grounded in company content. Q Developer targets software development tasks instead.

q: A software team wants an AI assistant inside the IDE that suggests code, explains errors, and helps refactor functions. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Q Business
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Comprehend
explain: Amazon Q Developer is the generative AI assistant for developers, providing code suggestions, explanations, debugging help, and refactoring support in IDEs, the CLI, and the AWS Console. Q Business is aimed at business users working with company data, not coding.

q: A bank wants two different assistants: one so staff can query internal procedures, and one so engineers can modernize legacy Java applications. Which pairing is correct?
options: Amazon Q Business for staff questions over company data; Amazon Q Developer for code transformation and developer assistance
Amazon Q Developer for staff questions; Amazon Q Business for Java upgrades
Amazon Lex for both use cases
PartyRock for both use cases
explain: Amazon Q Business serves business users with answers grounded in enterprise data, while Amazon Q Developer serves engineers with coding help and transformation agents that can modernize workloads such as Java upgrades. Swapping them mismatches each product's purpose.

q: An operations manager wants Amazon Q Business to do more than answer questions, such as filing a ticket in the company's ITSM tool from the chat interface. Which Q Business capability enables this?
options: Image generation models
Plugins that connect Q Business to third-party applications to take actions
Provisioned Throughput units
GPU instance scheduling
explain: Amazon Q Business supports plugins for popular third-party applications, letting users complete actions such as creating a support ticket from within the assistant experience. Plugins extend Q Business beyond question answering into workflow actions on connected systems.

q: A healthcare provider connects Amazon Q Business to its document repositories. A nurse asks about a discharge procedure and receives an answer that only reflects documents she is authorized to see. Which Q Business characteristic is demonstrated?
options: Q Business ignores document permissions for convenience
Q Business respects existing access controls so answers reflect only data the user is permitted to access
Q Business trains a public model on the hospital's documents
