Q Business requires all documents to be made public first
explain: Amazon Q Business honors the access controls of connected data sources, so each user's answers are grounded only in content that user is authorized to view. It does not make private documents public or use them to train public models.

q: Which data sources can Amazon Q Business connect to when building an enterprise assistant? (Choose two.)
options: Physical paper files that were never digitized
Only data typed manually into the chat window
Company documents stored in Amazon S3 and connected repositories
Enterprise applications and wikis through built-in connectors
explain: Amazon Q Business uses connectors to index content from sources such as Amazon S3, SharePoint, Confluence, and business applications, then grounds answers in that indexed content with citations. Undigitized paper and chat-only input are not indexed enterprise sources.

q: A developer asks Amazon Q Developer to convert a .NET Framework application to .NET Core and to upgrade Java 8 code to a newer version with minimal manual effort. Which Q Developer capability is being used?
options: Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon Q Business plugins
PartyRock app sharing
Code transformation agents that automate application modernization tasks
explain: Amazon Q Developer includes transformation capabilities and agents that automate large modernization jobs, such as Java version upgrades and .NET migrations, analyzing code and applying changes with developer review. This is a developer-assistant capability, distinct from Q Business data question answering.

q: A new engineer wants help understanding an unfamiliar codebase, generating unit tests, and documenting functions while working in the IDE. Which assistant is designed for this workflow?
options: Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Textract
Amazon Personalize
Amazon Q Business
explain: Amazon Q Developer works where developers work, including the IDE, and helps explain code, generate tests and documentation, and suggest implementations in context. Q Business answers questions over business data for general employees instead.

q: A logistics company is deciding between Amazon Q Business and building directly on Amazon Bedrock. The company wants a ready-made employee assistant over its documents with minimal development. Which choice has the LEAST development effort?
options: Deploying Amazon Q Business with connectors to the company documents
Training a foundation model from scratch
Building a custom RAG pipeline on Amazon Bedrock
Writing a custom search engine and chat UI
explain: Amazon Q Business is a packaged application: connect data sources, configure the assistant, and employees can use it, which is far less development than assembling a custom retrieval and chat solution on Bedrock. Bedrock offers more control when a custom application is truly required.

q: Which tasks can Amazon Q Business help employees with? (Choose two.)
options: Summarizing and drafting content based on company information
Answering questions grounded in connected company documents and data
Provisioning GPU servers for model training
Compiling application code inside an IDE as the primary user experience
explain: Amazon Q Business is the employee-facing assistant over enterprise data: it answers questions grounded in connected sources and can summarize and draft content from that information. Hands-on coding assistance in the IDE is Amazon Q Developer's role, and Q Business does not provision training infrastructure.

q: A media company's non-technical producer wants to build a small generative AI app, such as a headline brainstorming tool, by describing widgets in a browser, with no code and no AWS account setup for app building. Which option fits?
options: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
PartyRock
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Bedrock Provisioned Throughput
explain: PartyRock is a no-code playground built on Amazon Bedrock where anyone can assemble generative AI apps from widgets, experiment, and share them without writing code. JumpStart is a SageMaker hub for deploying models, and Q Developer is a coding assistant.

q: What is PartyRock best described as?
options: A fine-tuning service for Titan models
A billing tool for foundation model usage
A production database for generative AI apps
A no-code Amazon Bedrock playground for building and sharing experimental generative AI apps
explain: PartyRock is an AWS-built, no-code playground powered by Amazon Bedrock that lets users create small generative AI apps by combining widgets and models, then share those apps with others. It targets experimentation and learning rather than production enterprise deployment.

q: A data science team wants to deploy a pre-trained foundation model from a catalog inside Amazon SageMaker AI, then fine-tune it on company data within the same environment. Which SageMaker feature should the team use?
options: PartyRock
SageMaker JumpStart
SageMaker Ground Truth
Amazon Q Business
explain: SageMaker JumpStart is the hub inside Amazon SageMaker AI that provides pre-trained foundation models and solution templates that can be deployed and fine-tuned in SageMaker. Ground Truth is for data labeling, not model deployment from a catalog.

q: How does SageMaker JumpStart differ from Amazon Bedrock for foundation models?
options: Bedrock requires customers to deploy every model to a SageMaker endpoint first
JumpStart provides models and solutions to deploy and fine-tune within SageMaker AI, while Bedrock provides serverless API access to models without managing endpoints
JumpStart models can only run on premises
There is no difference; they are two names for the same service
explain: Both routes expose foundation models, but the operating model differs: JumpStart deploys models into your SageMaker environment where you manage endpoints and can fine-tune, while Bedrock offers serverless, API-based access with infrastructure fully managed by AWS.

q: A teacher wants students to remix and share simple generative AI apps during a workshop without learning cloud infrastructure. Which tool is MOST appropriate?
options: Provisioned Throughput on Amazon Bedrock
SageMaker JumpStart, because every student should deploy an endpoint
PartyRock, because apps are built with widgets in a browser and can be shared by link
Amazon Q Developer transformation agents
explain: PartyRock is designed for exactly this kind of low-barrier experimentation: browser-based, widget-driven app building on Bedrock models with easy sharing. Deploying endpoints or buying provisioned capacity would add cost and complexity far beyond a workshop's needs.

q: Which capabilities belong to Amazon Q Developer? (Choose two.)
options: Inline code completion and chat assistance in supported IDEs
Reserving foundation model throughput for production APIs
Indexing the company HR wiki for all employees
Agents that help with tasks such as feature development and code transformation
explain: Amazon Q Developer focuses on software development: inline code suggestions and chat in the IDE, plus agents for feature development, documentation, testing, and code transformation. Indexing company content for employees is Q Business, and reserving throughput is a Bedrock function.

q: A government agency wants citations in employee-facing answers so staff can verify which source document an answer came from. The agency deploys an assistant over its policy library. Which service provides this grounded, cited question answering over agency data?
options: Amazon Q Business
Amazon Polly
SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Q Developer
explain: Amazon Q Business answers questions using connected enterprise data and provides source attribution so users can verify the documents behind an answer. Q Developer targets coding tasks, Polly is text-to-speech, and JumpStart deploys models rather than serving employee Q&A.

q: A startup CTO asks for the fastest way for the engineering team to get AI help with code reviews, explanations of AWS errors, and generating infrastructure-as-code snippets. Which recommendation is correct?
options: Give every engineer access to Amazon Q Developer in the IDE and console
Connect Amazon Q Business to the code repository and use it as the code reviewer
Use SageMaker JumpStart to fine-tune a model before any developer help is available
Give every engineer PartyRock accounts for code review
explain: Amazon Q Developer is purpose-built for these tasks and is available immediately in IDEs and the AWS Console, assisting with code, troubleshooting, and AWS guidance. Q Business and PartyRock are not code review tools, and fine-tuning is unnecessary to start getting developer assistance.

q: An agriculture cooperative wants to evaluate foundation models available in Amazon SageMaker AI, including models it can fine-tune and deploy to its own endpoints for a crop-disease assistant. Which starting point should the team use?
options: Amazon Lex intents
SageMaker JumpStart model catalog
Amazon Q Business connectors
The Bedrock console playground only
explain: SageMaker JumpStart provides a catalog of pre-trained foundation models and built-in solutions inside SageMaker AI that teams can evaluate, fine-tune, and deploy to endpoints they control. The Bedrock playground is useful for quick tests but does not deploy SageMaker endpoints.

q: A hospitality chain pilots an idea for a generative AI itinerary builder. A marketing analyst with no coding experience assembles a working demo in an afternoon and shares it with executives by link. Which tool MOST likely produced the demo?
options: PartyRock
Amazon Bedrock Agents
SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Q Developer
explain: PartyRock lets non-developers assemble generative AI demos from widgets in a browser and share them by link, making an afternoon no-code pilot realistic. The other options require development work, endpoint deployment, or application engineering.

q: A company already uses Amazon SageMaker AI for custom ML. A team now wants a curated catalog of foundation models, example notebooks, and one-click deployment options inside that same platform. Which feature meets the need?
options: SageMaker Clarify
Amazon Q Business
SageMaker JumpStart
SageMaker Data Wrangler
explain: SageMaker JumpStart is the ML hub within SageMaker AI offering pre-trained models, foundation models, and end-to-end solutions with notebooks and streamlined deployment. Clarify addresses bias and explainability, and Data Wrangler prepares data; neither is a model catalog.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes Amazon Q Business from Amazon Bedrock?
options: Q Business is a foundation model, while Bedrock is a chatbot
Q Business is a ready-to-use assistant application over company data, while Bedrock is a platform service developers use to build custom generative AI applications with foundation models
Q Business replaces the need for any data sources
Bedrock is only for business users, while Q Business is only for developers
explain: The distinction is product versus platform: Amazon Q Business is a finished assistant application grounded in enterprise data, whereas Amazon Bedrock is the underlying managed platform of models and features that developers use to build their own generative AI applications.

q: A developer team lead wants an AI agent in the development workflow that can implement a described feature across multiple files, run tests, and propose the changes for review. Which service offers this kind of software development agent?
options: Amazon Q Business
Amazon Lex
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon Comprehend
explain: Amazon Q Developer includes software development agent capabilities that can turn a feature description into code changes across a repository, run tests, and present the result for developer review. Lex builds conversational bots and Comprehend analyzes text; neither implements software features.

q: A retailer's marketing team spends days writing first drafts of product descriptions for thousands of items. Which generative AI benefit applies MOST directly?
options: Generative AI eliminates the need for product data
Generative AI can physically photograph the products
Generative AI can guarantee every description is legally compliant without review
Generative AI can create original draft content quickly, which humans then review and refine
explain: Content creation is a core generative AI strength: models draft descriptions, articles, and marketing copy at scale so humans can edit rather than start from a blank page. Outputs still need review for accuracy and compliance, and the model cannot replace source product data or photography.

q: A bank wants to predict, for each loan applicant, a precise probability of default based on structured historical data, and regulators require a stable, explainable score. Which approach fits best?
options: A diffusion model that generates an image of the applicant
A large language model prompted with the applicant's story
A rules-free chatbot with high temperature
A traditional predictive ML model, such as a classification model trained on labeled loan outcomes
explain: Predicting a calibrated numeric probability from structured data with explainability requirements is a classic traditional ML classification task. Generative models produce fluent text, not stable, auditable probability scores, and high temperature would make outputs less consistent.

q: A streaming service wants two things: a ranked list of titles each viewer is most likely to watch, and a short written synopsis in each viewer's preferred tone. Which pairing is correct?
options: Traditional ML recommendations for the ranked list; generative AI for drafting the synopsis text
Generative AI for both, because ranking is a language task
Generative AI for the ranking; a spreadsheet formula for the synopsis
A rules engine for both, because neither involves patterns in data
explain: Ranking items by predicted preference is predictive ML, the domain of recommendation models. Drafting fluent, tone-adjusted synopsis text is generative AI. Matching each sub-problem to the right technique is the key design judgment.

q: An insurance company receives thousands of damage photos with free-text claim notes and wants the key facts, such as date, location, and damage type, pulled into structured fields. Which generative AI capability is MOST relevant?
options: Exact premium calculation using actuarial tables
Physical repair of the damaged property
Data extraction and structuring of unstructured text
Guaranteed fraud verdicts with no human review
explain: Foundation models excel at reading unstructured text and extracting named facts into structured fields, which speeds claims intake. Setting the premium itself is a separate actuarial calculation, and extraction output should still be validated rather than treated as a final verdict.

q: A hospital wants a tool that drafts summaries of long doctor-patient visit transcripts so clinicians can review and sign them faster. Which statement about generative AI fits this use case?
options: Generative AI summaries are always accurate, so review is unnecessary
Only a rules-based system can shorten text
Summarization is a strength of generative AI, but a clinician must verify the summary before it enters the record
Summarization requires training a model from scratch on hospital data first
explain: Summarization is one of the most common and effective generative AI applications. In healthcare the output is a draft: hallucination risk means a qualified clinician must verify content before it becomes part of the medical record.

q: A manufacturer must decide whether a machine will fail in the next 24 hours, using years of numeric sensor readings with known failure events. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Use an image generation model to picture the failure
Ask a chatbot to guess based on the machine's brand
Prompt a foundation model with a paragraph describing the machine
Train a predictive ML model on the labeled time-series sensor data
explain: Failure prediction from labeled numeric sensor history is supervised predictive ML: the model learns patterns that precede failures. A language model prompted with prose cannot reliably learn from raw time-series signals and would not produce a dependable risk estimate.

q: Which business problems are strong fits for generative AI? (Choose two.)
options: Summarizing long support call transcripts into short case notes
Drafting personalized email responses to common customer questions for agent review
Determining the exact interest due on a loan for a legal filing
Calculating payroll tax to the exact cent using fixed statutory formulas
explain: Drafting personalized responses and summarizing transcripts are generative strengths: fluent language output where a human can review. Exact payroll and interest calculations are deterministic arithmetic governed by fixed formulas, where traditional software, not a probabilistic language model, must produce the authoritative number.

q: A logistics firm wants a customer support chatbot that answers questions about shipment policies in natural conversation and handles follow-up questions. Why is generative AI a good fit for the conversational part?
options: It makes the bot's answers legally binding
It guarantees the bot never needs access to company policy documents
It understands varied phrasing and generates fluent, context-aware replies rather than matching fixed scripts only
It removes the need for any human escalation path
explain: Generative AI handles the open-ended language of support conversations: customers phrase the same question many ways, and the model can respond fluently using conversation context and grounded policy content. Human escalation and grounded data sources remain necessary parts of a responsible design.

q: A law firm wants to know a foundation model's key limitation before using it to research case law. Which limitation should the firm plan around?
options: The model refuses to discuss any legal topic
The model cannot process more than one sentence at a time
The model only works when the office Wi-Fi is disconnected
The model can produce confident but fabricated citations, so every citation must be verified against real sources
explain: Hallucination is the central limitation for legal research: models can invent plausible-looking case citations that do not exist. Grounding with retrieval from real databases and mandatory human verification are the standard mitigations.

q: An education company asks a foundation model detailed questions about a regulation published last month, and the answers are vague and partly wrong. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The temperature was set too low
The model's training data has a knowledge cutoff and does not include very recent events
The questions were too short
The model needs a larger monitor
explain: Foundation models know what was in their training data up to a knowledge cutoff; events after that point are not known and the model may guess. Supplying current documents through retrieval is the practical fix, not changing display hardware or prompt length.

q: A finance team tests a foundation model on multi-step arithmetic for expense reports and finds occasional wrong totals despite confident explanations. Which limitation does this reveal, and what is the best design response?
options: The model is broken; replace it with an image model
Arithmetic errors mean the prompts need more creative temperature
Language models are probabilistic text generators and can be unreliable at exact calculation; delegate arithmetic to a calculator or code tool
The team should let the model approve its own totals
explain: Large language models generate plausible text token by token and are not reliable calculators, especially over many steps. Robust designs let the model handle language while deterministic tools or code perform the arithmetic, a pattern also used by AI agents.

q: A team is planning a customer-facing generative AI feature. Which limitations of foundation models should the team explicitly plan around? (Choose two.)
options: The model may generate confident but incorrect information that needs verification
The model can certify that its own outputs are correct
The model guarantees exact, auditable arithmetic on every request
The model's built-in knowledge stops at a training cutoff, so recent facts need an external source
explain: Two limitations must be designed for: hallucination, where outputs sound confident but are wrong, and the knowledge cutoff, where events after training are unknown without retrieval. Foundation models do not guarantee exact arithmetic and cannot certify their own outputs.

q: A government benefits office has a strict rule: an application is complete only if three specific documents are present, with no judgment involved. Which solution is MOST appropriate for the completeness check?
options: A recommendation model trained on past applicants
A generative AI model asked to decide completeness creatively
A simple deterministic rules-based check, because the criteria are fixed and must be applied identically every time
A diffusion model
explain: When criteria are fixed, explicit, and must be applied identically, deterministic rules are cheaper, auditable, and more reliable than a probabilistic model. Generative AI earns its place on variable language tasks, not on exact rule enforcement.

q: A media company wants a generative AI system to write match reports. Editors notice the model sometimes invents quotes from players. Which combination best addresses this known limitation?
options: Remove all human editors to reduce inconsistency
Ground the model in verified match data and transcripts, and keep editorial review before publication
Raise the temperature and publish faster
Ask the model to promise not to invent quotes and trust the promise
explain: Invented quotes are hallucinations. Grounding generation in retrieved, verified source material plus human editorial review directly reduces fabrication risk. A model's promise in its own output is not a control, and higher temperature increases variability.

q: Which scenarios are better served by traditional predictive ML than by generative AI? (Choose two.)
options: Scoring transactions for fraud probability from structured transaction features
Brainstorming names for a new product line
Predicting which customers are likely to churn next quarter from usage history
Writing a friendly first draft of a customer apology letter
explain: Fraud scoring and churn prediction produce numeric risk estimates from structured historical data, which is predictive ML's core strength. Drafting letters and brainstorming names are open-ended language creation tasks where generative AI excels.

q: A hospitality brand wants each guest to receive a welcome message that references their past stays, reason for travel, and local events. Which generative AI value is being applied?
options: Physical room cleaning automation
Exact revenue accounting
Personalization of content at scale
Guaranteed occupancy forecasting
explain: Generative AI can personalize language content for each recipient by weaving supplied context, such as stay history and trip purpose, into a natural message at a scale humans could not hand-write. The underlying facts still come from the company's systems, and forecasting occupancy remains a predictive task.

q: A bank's developers use an AI coding assistant to generate boilerplate code, explain legacy functions, and draft unit tests. Which category of generative AI value is this?
options: Network routing optimization
Physical document storage
Code assistance that accelerates developer productivity
Automated loan approval
explain: Code assistance is a well-established generative AI value area: models generate and explain code and tests, speeding development while engineers review the output. It does not approve loans or manage physical storage or networks.

q: An energy utility compares two designs for outage notifications. Design A uses templates with fixed fields. Design B uses generative AI to compose messages. When is Design B clearly justified?
options: When the utility wants to avoid reviewing any message content ever
When messages must adapt tone and detail to each customer's situation, language, and outage context beyond what fixed templates can express
When there is only one possible message the utility will ever send
When every message must be word-for-word identical for legal reasons
explain: Generative composition earns its complexity when content must adapt: different customer situations, languages, and levels of detail. If a message must be identical and legally fixed, a template is safer and simpler, and generated messages still warrant oversight.

q: A sports league wants a foundation model to answer fan questions about this week's injuries and trades, information that changes daily. What is the model's main limitation and the standard remedy?
options: The model answers too slowly; buy a bigger screen for the support team
The model cannot read questions in English; translate all questions first
The model has no limitation; its training includes future events
The model's knowledge is frozen at training time; connect it to current data through retrieval so answers use fresh facts
explain: A foundation model's built-in knowledge stops at its training cutoff, so daily-changing facts require retrieval from a current source at question time, the RAG pattern. Translation and hardware do not address stale knowledge.

q: A real estate platform finds that a foundation model gives slightly different answers to the same factual question across runs. Which property of generative AI explains this, and how should the platform respond for factual features?
options: The platform's servers are overheating; add cooling
The model is learning secretly between calls; delete the account
Generation is probabilistic, so outputs vary; use low temperature and grounding for factual answers
Models are deterministic databases; no response is needed
explain: Generative models sample tokens probabilistically, so identical prompts can yield different wording or even different facts. For factual features, teams lower temperature, ground answers in retrieved data, and validate outputs rather than assuming database-like consistency.

q: An agriculture firm wants to classify satellite images of fields into crop types using thousands of labeled examples, producing a consistent category per image. Which approach fits best?
options: A generative model asked to write poems about each field
A text-to-speech service
A text chatbot asked to imagine the crop type
A traditional ML computer vision classification model trained on the labeled images
explain: Consistent category prediction from labeled image examples is supervised computer vision, a traditional ML strength with measurable accuracy. Asking a language model to improvise categories gives unvalidated, inconsistent results for an operational decision.

q: A legal team needs a clause-by-clause comparison of two contracts and a plain-English summary of the differences. Which approach is MOST suitable?
options: A demand-forecasting model, because contracts contain dates
A generative AI model, because the task is language understanding and summarization over provided documents
A rules engine with one rule per possible clause, written in advance
An image generation model, because contracts are often scanned
explain: Comparing and summarizing provided text is squarely a language task where foundation models add value, especially when the documents are supplied in context. Forecasting models and image generators do not perform textual legal analysis, and pre-writing a rule for every clause is impractical.

q: Which statement about generative AI limitations is accurate?
options: Outputs reflect patterns in training data and can reproduce biases present in that data
Fine-tuning removes all possibility of biased output
A larger model can never produce a wrong answer
Models understand facts the way humans do and can certify their own answers
explain: Foundation models learn statistical patterns from training data, so biases in that data can surface in outputs, and no model size guarantees correctness. Responsible use requires evaluation, grounding, guardrails, and human oversight for consequential decisions.

q: A travel assistant does more than answer questions: given a goal, it checks the calendar, searches flights, compares options, and books the chosen flight. What type of system is this?
options: A keyword search index
A diffusion model
A static FAQ page
An AI agent that reasons, plans, and uses tools to complete multi-step tasks
explain: An AI agent combines a foundation model with planning and tool use: it breaks a goal into steps, calls external tools and APIs such as calendars and booking systems, observes results, and continues until the task is complete. A single prompt-response chatbot does not do this.

q: What distinguishes an AI agent from a plain chatbot that only generates text responses?
options: Agents never use foundation models
Agents can plan multi-step actions and invoke tools or APIs to affect external systems, not just reply with text
Chatbots can book meetings, but agents cannot
Agents are always larger models than chatbots
explain: The defining difference is action: agents reason about a goal, decide on steps, and call tools, APIs, and data sources to carry out work in the world, checking results as they go. A plain chatbot's output ends at the text it returns.

q: An agent for a logistics company must check warehouse inventory before promising a delivery date. The model decides it needs current stock data and requests a call to the inventory API with specific parameters, then uses the returned value in its answer. What is this capability called?
options: Image diffusion
Tokenization
Tool use, also known as function calling
Temperature sampling
explain: Tool use or function calling lets a model request that the application execute a defined function, such as an inventory API call, with model-chosen parameters, and then incorporate the returned result. This is how agents ground actions and answers in live systems.

q: A banking agent follows this loop: interpret the request, decide the next step, call a tool, review the tool's output, and repeat until the customer's address change is completed across two systems. Which agentic concept does this loop illustrate?
options: One-shot zero-shot prompting only
Batch inference with no feedback
Reasoning and acting in iterative steps, using observations from tool results to choose the next action
Continued pre-training
explain: Agents work in a reason-act-observe loop: they plan a step, act through a tool, observe the outcome, and adapt the next step accordingly until the goal is met. This iterative loop, not a single prompt, is what lets agents handle multi-step, branching tasks.

q: A development team keeps writing custom integration code for every new tool it connects to its agents. Which standard is designed to reduce this work?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Top-p sampling
Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard way to connect models and agents to tools and data sources
Amazon S3 versioning
explain: Model Context Protocol is an open standard that defines a common way for AI applications and agents to connect to external tools, data, and services, so a tool built once as an MCP server can be reused by many MCP-compatible clients instead of bespoke integrations for each one.

q: Which statements describe the Model Context Protocol (MCP) correctly? (Choose two.)
options: It helps the same tool integration be reused across different MCP-compatible agents and applications
It provides a standardized interface for agents to discover and call external tools and access data
It replaces the need for foundation models in an agent
It is a pricing model for foundation model tokens
explain: MCP standardizes how applications expose and consume tools and context: servers offer tools and data through a common protocol, and any compatible client or agent can use them, improving reuse. MCP is not a pricing scheme and agents still rely on a foundation model for reasoning.

q: An enterprise wants to run production AI agents that need a secure hosted runtime, conversation memory across sessions, controlled access to tools, and managed identity for calling other systems. Which AWS offering is designed for this?
options: PartyRock
Amazon Polly
SageMaker Canvas
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
explain: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides infrastructure for deploying agents in production, including a runtime for agent workloads, memory, a gateway for tool access, and identity management, so teams do not have to build that plumbing themselves. PartyRock is a no-code experiment playground, not production agent infrastructure.

q: A support agent built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore remembers a returning customer's open issue and preferences from last week's conversation. Which AgentCore component most directly provides this?
options: AgentCore billing reports
AgentCore Memory, which stores short-term and long-term context for agents
The Bedrock console playground
Provisioned Throughput units
explain: AgentCore Memory gives agents both in-session context and longer-term retained memory across interactions, enabling continuity such as recalling a prior issue. Throughput and playgrounds do not provide agent memory.

q: A company wants its agents to call existing enterprise APIs and Lambda functions as tools through one managed access point, rather than wiring each tool into each agent separately. Which Amazon Bedrock AgentCore component fits?
options: Amazon Lex slot types
Titan Image Generator
AgentCore pricing page
AgentCore Gateway, which turns APIs and functions into tools agents can discover and call
explain: AgentCore Gateway provides a managed way to expose existing APIs and Lambda functions as tools that agents can call, centralizing tool access instead of custom per-agent wiring. It complements the AgentCore runtime, memory, and identity components.

q: A regulated insurer will let an agent retrieve policy data from internal systems. Auditors require that the agent call those systems with a verifiable, scoped identity rather than shared credentials. Which AgentCore capability addresses this?
options: PartyRock sharing links
AgentCore Identity, which manages authenticated, scoped identities for agents and their tool calls
Automatic prompt templates
The model's temperature setting
explain: AgentCore Identity provides identity and credential management for agents so tool and API calls are authenticated and scoped to what the agent is allowed to do, supporting audit and least-privilege requirements. Temperature and prompt templates have nothing to do with caller identity.

q: Which capabilities are part of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore at a conceptual level? (Choose three.)
options: Physical warehouse robots for logistics customers
Identity management for agents calling tools and systems
Memory so agents retain context across interactions
A runtime for deploying and running agents
explain: AgentCore's core building blocks are a runtime to host agents, memory for short- and long-term context, a gateway for tool access, and identity for secure calls. It is a software platform for agents, not a robotics product.

q: A hotel chain has a traditional chatbot built on Amazon Lex that handles fixed intents such as booking lookups and check-in times. Guests now ask open-ended questions about amenities and local attractions that the intent model handles poorly. What is the MOST effective enhancement?
options: Add more keyword rules for every possible guest question
Combine Lex's conversational framework with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock so open-ended questions get generative, grounded answers while structured intents stay reliable
Replace the bot with a printed FAQ at the front desk
Raise the bot's speech rate so answers finish sooner
explain: A hybrid design keeps Lex's strengths, structured intents, speech, and dialog management, and adds a Bedrock foundation model for the open-ended language questions Lex's intent model cannot anticipate. Hand-writing rules for every phrasing does not scale, which is the original problem.

q: How does a traditional intent-based chatbot differ from a generative AI chatbot?
options: Traditional bots recognize predefined intents and follow scripted flows, while generative bots compose flexible responses using a foundation model
There is no difference in how the two produce responses
Traditional bots never use natural language understanding
Generative bots can only answer yes-or-no questions
explain: Intent-based bots such as classic Amazon Lex designs classify each message into predefined intents and slots and respond from scripted flows, which is reliable but brittle. Generative chatbots use a foundation model to interpret varied phrasing and compose answers, trading some predictability for flexibility.

q: A government agency needs a voice-enabled phone assistant that understands spoken requests and manages multi-turn dialogs for common services. Which AWS service provides the conversational interface with automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding?
options: Amazon Translate
Amazon Textract
Amazon Lex
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces with automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding, supporting voice and text bots with multi-turn dialog management. Textract extracts document data and Rekognition analyzes images; neither runs conversations.

q: An airline designs a customer assistant: Amazon Lex manages the conversation flow and identity verification, and a Bedrock foundation model answers free-form questions about travel policies using retrieved documents. Which statement best describes this architecture?
options: Lex is being used as the foundation model
The foundation model should also handle payment card storage directly
Bedrock replaces the need for any dialog design
The design pairs a conversational framework with generative AI, using each for what it does best
explain: This is the standard hybrid pattern: Lex provides structured dialog, speech, and flow control, while Bedrock supplies flexible, document-grounded answers for open-ended questions. Neither component is the other, and sensitive functions like payments stay in controlled systems, not the model.

q: A retailer's agent must refund an order. The model determines the refund steps, calls the order API to verify the purchase, calls the payment API to issue the refund, and confirms the result to the customer. Which agent characteristics are demonstrated? (Choose two.)
options: Tool use to act on external systems
Multi-step task execution toward a goal
Diffusion-based image generation
Training a new foundation model during the conversation
explain: The scenario shows the two hallmarks of an agent: carrying out a multi-step plan and using tools, here the order and payment APIs, to change state in external systems and report back. No image generation or model training occurs during the interaction.

q: A company wants an agent that can work with several enterprise systems. Which design elements support reliable tool use by the agent? (Choose two.)
options: Defining each tool with a clear name, purpose, and input parameters the model can supply
Returning tool results to the model so it can decide the next step
Giving the model direct database passwords in the system prompt
Hiding all tool errors so the model assumes every action succeeded
explain: Reliable tool use depends on well-described tools whose parameters the model can fill, and on feeding tool results back so the agent can observe outcomes and adapt. Concealing errors breaks the reason-act-observe loop, and embedding passwords in prompts is a security anti-pattern.

q: A developer connects an agent to a database tool, a web search tool, and a ticketing tool, all exposed through the same standard protocol, and a second agent application reuses the same tool servers without new integration code. Which technology enables this reuse?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Continued pre-training
Top-k sampling
Model Context Protocol (MCP)
explain: MCP standardizes the interface between AI applications and tool or data servers, so one MCP server implementation can serve many compatible agents and clients. Sampling parameters and throughput options affect generation and capacity, not tool interoperability.

q: A manufacturer deploys agents to monitor equipment alerts and open maintenance tickets. Before go-live, the safety team asks what happens if an agent misinterprets an alert. Which design practice is MOST appropriate?
options: Give the agent unrestricted write access to all plant systems to move faster
Remove all logging so the agent cannot be second-guessed
Scope the agent's tool permissions, require approval for high-impact actions, and log agent actions for review
Let the agent approve its own high-impact actions to avoid delays
explain: Production agents need guardrails proportional to their ability to act: least-privilege tool access, human approval for consequential actions, and audit logging of what the agent did and why. Unrestricted access and self-approval remove the controls that make agentic automation safe.

q: A startup built a prototype agent in a notebook and now needs to run it reliably for thousands of users with session isolation and scaling handled by AWS. Which AgentCore component should the startup use?
options: AgentCore Runtime, a managed environment for deploying and running agent workloads
Amazon Q Business connectors
PartyRock widgets
The Titan Image Generator
explain: AgentCore Runtime is the managed hosting environment for agents, providing the isolation and scaling needed to move from a prototype to production traffic. PartyRock is for no-code experiments, and the other options serve unrelated purposes.

q: What is function calling in the context of foundation models?
options: A billing report listing API calls
A way for users to phone the model provider
A method for renaming model parameters
A feature where the model outputs a structured request to invoke a defined function with arguments, and the application executes it and returns the result
explain: In function calling, the model selects a function from those the developer provided and emits structured arguments; the application runs the function, returns the output to the model, and the model uses it to continue. It is the mechanism behind most tool-using agents.

q: A sports retailer wants an assistant that can answer product questions, check live stock, and place an order when the customer confirms. A simple question-answering bot already exists. What must be added to make it an agent?
options: A higher temperature for more creative answers
Planning and tool access so the assistant can check inventory and call the ordering system to complete the purchase
A larger logo on the chat window
More canned responses in the FAQ list
explain: Agency comes from the ability to plan steps and act through tools: verifying stock via an inventory system and submitting the order via the ordering system, with customer confirmation. Cosmetic changes and more canned text leave it a passive question answerer.

q: A research team compares two designs. Design 1: a model answers questions about documents. Design 2: an agent that searches for documents, reads them, drafts a brief, and sends it for approval. Which statement is MOST accurate?
options: Design 1 is an agent because it uses documents
Design 2 is agentic because the system pursues a goal through planned steps and tools, while Design 1 is a single-purpose question-answering application
Both designs are identical because both use a foundation model
Design 2 cannot use a foundation model
explain: Using a foundation model does not by itself make a system an agent. Design 2 qualifies because it decomposes a goal, uses tools such as search and messaging, and sequences steps toward a deliverable, all orchestrated around the model.

q: An enterprise architect wants a single sentence to explain MCP to executives. Which sentence is MOST accurate?
options: MCP is a dashboard for monitoring agent spending
MCP is a foundation model sold by AWS for agent workloads
MCP is a standard protocol that lets AI agents connect to tools and data through reusable integrations instead of one-off custom code for every pairing
MCP is a method for compressing prompts to save tokens
explain: Model Context Protocol is about interoperability: it defines a common way for agents and AI applications to discover and use tools and data sources, so integrations are built once and reused. It is a protocol, not a model, compression method, or dashboard.

q: A bank prototypes a generative assistant for branch staff using Amazon Lex for guided dialogs and Amazon Bedrock for summarizing customer-submitted documents. Which benefit does the Bedrock component add that Lex alone does not?
options: Predefined slot filling for account numbers
Telephony network connectivity
Open-ended language understanding and generation, such as free-form summarization of arbitrary documents
Automatic speech recognition for phone calls
explain: Lex provides speech recognition, intent handling, and slot filling for structured dialogs. Bedrock adds the generative capability: understanding and summarizing arbitrary free-form documents that were never anticipated as fixed intents, which is why the two are paired.

q: A logistics company evaluates whether to let an agent autonomously re-route shipments during storms. The agent would reason over weather data, call routing tools, and notify customers. Which evaluation is MOST sound before launch?
options: Judge the agent only by how fluent its customer messages sound
Pilot the agent with human approval on routing changes, measure its decisions against dispatcher outcomes, and expand autonomy only where it proves reliable
Remove dispatchers from the process during the pilot to get clean data
Launch fully autonomous immediately because agents never make mistakes
explain: Sound agent deployment is graduated: constrain autonomy, compare agent decisions with trusted human outcomes, and widen scope based on evidence. Fluency of messages says nothing about routing quality, and assuming agents are infallible invites operational harm.

q: Which description best fits an AI agent's planning capability?
options: Planning is a billing feature that forecasts token usage
The agent breaks a goal into ordered sub-tasks, decides which tools each sub-task needs, and adjusts the plan when intermediate results change the situation
Planning means choosing the model's temperature once at deployment
The agent memorizes a single script and repeats it for every request
explain: Planning is the agent's ability to decompose a goal into steps, sequence them, select tools, and re-plan when observations differ from expectations. A memorized script is the opposite of adaptive planning, and temperature or billing are unrelated settings.

q: What is Amazon Bedrock?
options: A video streaming service
A database migration tool
A fully managed service for building generative AI applications with foundation models through a single API, without managing infrastructure
A physical data center location
explain: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed service that provides access to high-performing foundation models from Amazon and third-party providers through one API, with serverless inference - no infrastructure to manage.

q: Which statement about Amazon Bedrock is true?
options: It is serverless - customers access models via API without managing infrastructure
It requires training models from scratch
It only works with open-source models
Customers must provision and manage GPU servers to use it
explain: Bedrock is serverless: AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, and customers invoke models through APIs on a pay-as-you-go basis.

q: What is SageMaker JumpStart?
options: A billing dashboard
A code editor
A machine learning hub offering pre-trained models and solution templates that can be deployed in SageMaker AI with a few clicks
A certification exam
explain: SageMaker JumpStart provides pre-trained, open-source and proprietary models plus end-to-end solution templates for fast deployment, evaluation, and fine-tuning within SageMaker AI.

q: Amazon Q is best described as:
options: A generative AI-powered assistant for work, including business data Q&A; and developer assistance
A message queueing service
A quantum computing service
A DNS service
explain: Amazon Q is a generative AI assistant: Q Business answers questions and generates content using company data, while Q Developer assists with coding tasks such as code generation and debugging.

q: What is PartyRock?
options: A server operating system
A database engine
An AWS playground for experimenting with generative AI app building using foundation models, without writing code
A music streaming application
explain: PartyRock, built by AWS, is a no-code playground where anyone can build, experiment with, and share generative AI apps powered by Amazon Bedrock foundation models.

q: What do Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock enable?
options: Video rendering
Fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation - connecting foundation models to company data sources so responses are grounded in that data
Training foundation models from scratch
Manual server configuration
explain: Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock provide fully managed RAG: they ingest your data sources, create embeddings, store them in a vector database, and retrieve relevant context at query time.

q: What are Agents for Amazon Bedrock used for?
options: Breaking down complex tasks, orchestrating multi-step workflows, and calling APIs and data sources to complete actions
Compressing log files
Monitoring server CPU usage
Managing IAM users
explain: Agents for Amazon Bedrock extend foundation models beyond text generation: they reason about tasks, break them into steps, retrieve information, and invoke APIs or company systems to carry out actions.

q: What do Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock provide?
options: Content filters, denied-topic blocking, PII redaction, and configurable safety policies for generative AI applications
Backup services
Physical security for data centers
Network firewalls
explain: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock implement responsible AI policies directly in applications: content filters for harmful categories, denied topics, word filters, and sensitive information (PII) redaction on inputs and outputs.

q: How can you evaluate a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock?
options: By counting parameters only
Using automatic evaluation with metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU, or human evaluation workflows
It cannot be evaluated
By measuring network latency only
explain: Model evaluation on Amazon Bedrock supports automatic metrics-based evaluation and human-based evaluation, helping teams compare models and prompts on their own datasets before committing.

q: A company wants to customize a Bedrock model with its own labeled examples to improve task-specific performance. Which approach fits?
options: Fine-tuning on Bedrock with task-specific labeled data
Increasing the temperature
Changing the AWS Region
Continued pre-training
explain: Fine-tuning adapts a pre-trained model using labeled, task-specific examples. Continued pre-training, by contrast, uses large volumes of unlabeled domain data to build broad domain knowledge.

q: When should you choose continued pre-training over fine-tuning?
options: When you want the model to absorb broad domain knowledge from large amounts of unlabeled domain data
When you have labeled examples of the exact task
When you want to eliminate inference costs
When you want shorter outputs
explain: Continued pre-training feeds the model large volumes of unlabeled domain text (for example, financial documents) so it gains deep domain expertise; fine-tuning then specializes it with labeled task examples.

q: A company needs current, factual answers from proprietary documents without retraining a model. The best approach is:
options: Fine-tuning
RAG (for example, Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock)
Increasing max tokens
Continued pre-training
explain: RAG grounds responses in retrieved documents at query time - ideal for current or proprietary knowledge that changes often. Fine-tuning bakes knowledge into model weights and is a poor fit for frequently changing facts.

q: Amazon Transcribe is used to:
options: Convert speech to text
Convert text to lifelike speech
Translate documents between languages
Recognize faces in photos
explain: Amazon Transcribe is automatic speech recognition - it converts speech to text, including real-time streaming transcription with features like speaker identification.

q: Amazon Polly is used to:
options: Transcribe meetings
Convert text into lifelike speech
Forecast sales
Detect objects in images
explain: Amazon Polly is a text-to-speech service that turns text into natural-sounding spoken audio, with many voices and languages.

q: A company needs to translate its website content into 20 languages. Which AWS AI service fits?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Translate
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Amazon Translate provides fast, high-quality neural machine translation between supported languages - the right purpose-built service for website localization.

q: Amazon Rekognition provides:
options: Demand forecasting
Image and video analysis - object, scene, and face detection, and content moderation
Text-to-speech conversion
Chatbot frameworks
explain: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video: object and scene detection, facial analysis, celebrity recognition, and detection of unsafe content.

q: A support team wants to detect customer sentiment in thousands of product reviews. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Translate
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Polly
Amazon Forecast
explain: Amazon Comprehend is an NLP service for text analysis: sentiment detection, entity extraction, key phrases, language detection, and topic modeling - no ML expertise required.

q: A company wants to build a conversational chatbot with automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Lex
Amazon Personalize
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Amazon Lex builds conversational interfaces - chatbots and voice bots - with automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding, the same technology behind Alexa.

q: A bank needs to extract text and data from scanned loan application PDFs. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Forecast
Amazon Translate
Amazon Textract
Amazon Polly
explain: Amazon Textract goes beyond simple OCR: it extracts text, handwriting, tables, and form data from scanned documents automatically.

q: An online retailer wants personalized product recommendations for each shopper. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Personalize
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Transcribe
explain: Amazon Personalize delivers real-time personalized recommendations using the same machine learning technology that powers Amazon.com - with no ML expertise required.

q: A manufacturer wants to predict future inventory needs from historical time-series data. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Lex
Amazon Polly
Amazon Translate
Amazon Forecast
explain: Amazon Forecast uses machine learning on historical time-series data to produce accurate forecasts for demand, inventory, staffing, and more.

q: A payment processor wants to identify potentially fraudulent transactions in real time. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Fraud Detector
Amazon Polly
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Translate
explain: Amazon Fraud Detector builds real-time fraud detection models using your own historical fraud data, with no ML expertise required.

q: Amazon SageMaker AI is best described as:
options: A speech synthesis tool only
A chatbot product
A data warehouse
A fully managed service to build, train, and deploy machine learning models at scale
explain: Amazon SageMaker AI is a fully managed ML platform covering the whole workflow: data preparation, training, tuning, deployment, and MLOps for models at scale.

q: A developer wants a model to output its answer in strict JSON format. Which prompt engineering approach helps most?
options: Removing all instructions from the prompt
Raising the temperature to its maximum value
Using the longest possible context
Providing clear instructions plus an example of the desired JSON format
explain: Clear instructions combined with a formatted example (few-shot prompting) strongly guide the model to match a desired output structure such as JSON. High temperature would make formatting less reliable.

q: A team is comparing foundation models on Bedrock from different providers for a summarization task. Which is a valid evaluation approach?
options: Run model evaluation with automatic metrics and human review on representative prompts
Skip evaluation entirely
Pick the model with the most parameters without testing
Choose based on the provider's logo
explain: The responsible approach is to evaluate candidate models on your own representative prompts using automatic metrics plus human judgment - parameter count alone does not predict task performance.

q: An AI agent books a flight by checking calendars, searching options, and confirming payment across multiple APIs. This demonstrates:
options: A database backup
A simple single-prompt text completion
A diffusion image model
An agentic workflow - reasoning, planning multi-step tasks, and invoking tools and APIs
explain: AI agents go beyond single responses: they plan, use tools and APIs, and execute multi-step workflows to accomplish a goal - as with Agents for Amazon Bedrock.

q: In a RAG system, what is the role of a vector database?
options: Storing user passwords
Hosting the foundation model weights
Caching billing records
Storing embeddings so the retriever can quickly find the documents most semantically similar to a query
explain: A vector database stores document embeddings and enables fast similarity search - the retrieval step of RAG that finds the most relevant context for the model's prompt.

q: A company must choose between a pre-built AWS AI service and building on Amazon Bedrock. When is a pre-built AI service (such as Comprehend or Rekognition) typically the better fit?
options: When the task matches the service's purpose and the team wants minimal ML expertise and setup
When they want to train a foundation model from scratch DOMAIN 4 - GUIDELINES FOR RESPONSIBLE AI
When they need full control over model weights
When they need a custom multimodal architecture
explain: Pre-built AI services are purpose-built, require no ML expertise, and deploy quickly - ideal when the task matches the service. Bedrock or custom approaches fit when you need flexible generative capabilities or deep customization.

q: A startup wants to build a generative AI chat application using leading foundation models through a single API, without managing any ML infrastructure. Which AWS service is the best fit?
options: AWS Lambda
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon EC2
explain: Amazon Bedrock is the fully managed service for using foundation models from multiple providers through one API, with no infrastructure to manage.

q: A prompt asks a model to translate a sentence and includes no examples - only instructions. This is:
options: Prompt chaining
Zero-shot prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
Few-shot prompting
explain: Zero-shot prompting gives instructions with no examples. Adding examples would make it one-shot or few-shot.

q: A prompt includes three example customer-review summaries, then asks the model to summarize a fourth review in the same style. This is:
options: Model distillation
Zero-shot prompting
Negative prompting
Few-shot prompting
explain: Including several examples to demonstrate the desired pattern is few-shot prompting.

q: To improve a model's accuracy on multi-step math word problems, a developer adds 'Let's think step by step' to the prompt. This technique is:
options: Temperature scaling
One-shot prompting
Chain-of-thought prompting
Stop-sequence tuning
explain: Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before answering, which improves performance on complex reasoning tasks.

q: A company wants its chatbot to answer questions using only its internal policy documents, with citations, and without retraining a model. The best approach is:
options: RAG with a knowledge base
Increasing the temperature
Fine-tuning on the policies
Pre-training from scratch
explain: Retrieval-Augmented Generation retrieves relevant policy passages at query time and grounds the answer in them - no retraining needed, and it reduces hallucinations. On AWS this is Knowledge Bases for Bedrock.

q: A data science team needs full control over training pipelines and hyperparameter tuning for a custom model. Which AWS offering fits best?
options: Amazon Kendra
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Polly
Amazon SageMaker AI
explain: SageMaker AI is the platform for building, training, tuning, and deploying custom ML models with full control. Bedrock is for consuming foundation models via API.

q: Which AWS AI service converts written text into lifelike spoken audio?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Lex
Amazon Transcribe
explain: Amazon Polly is text-to-speech. Transcribe does the reverse (speech-to-text), Lex builds chatbots, and Comprehend does NLP analysis.

q: A bank needs to extract text, tables, and form fields from thousands of scanned loan applications. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Translate
Amazon Personalize
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Amazon Textract is the OCR/document-analysis service that extracts text, tables, and forms from scanned documents.

q: A company wants to automatically block hate speech and redact credit card numbers in its Bedrock application's prompts and responses. Which Bedrock feature provides this?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Guardrails for Bedrock
Agents for Bedrock
Model evaluation
explain: Guardrails for Bedrock applies safeguards including content filters, denied topics, PII redaction, and word policies.

q: A company needs a Bedrock solution that retrieves answers from its policy library AND files tickets in its helpdesk system. Which fits?
options: An agent with a knowledge base and action groups
Guardrails only
Prompt chaining
Model distillation
explain: Knowledge bases handle retrieval; action groups let the agent act in external systems - agents combine both.

q: A Bedrock agent must check inventory, place purchase orders, and update the CRM. The component that lets the agent take these actions is:
options: Guardrails
Knowledge bases
Prompt templates
Action groups
explain: Action groups define the APIs and functions an agent can call - they turn a question-answering model into one that can act in your systems.

q: A team wants Bedrock to verify that generated answers are grounded in the retrieved source documents. Which Guardrails feature does this?
options: Action groups
Contextual grounding check
Model distillation
Knowledge Bases
explain: Guardrails for Bedrock include contextual grounding checks that detect when responses drift from the source material, reducing hallucinations.

q: A team compares candidate Bedrock models using automatic metrics like ROUGE plus human review of sample outputs. This process is:
options: Continued pre-training
Fine-tuning
Model evaluation
Prompt chaining
explain: Bedrock model evaluation combines automatic metrics with human evaluation so teams can compare foundation models on their own use case.

q: A media company turns written video scripts into natural-sounding voiceovers. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Comprehend
explain: Polly is text-to-speech: it converts written text into lifelike spoken audio in many voices and languages.

q: A call center wants searchable transcripts of support calls with speaker labels. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Lex
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe
explain: Transcribe is speech-to-text: it converts audio into text with speaker identification, timestamps, and call-analytics features.

q: A company needs live chat messages translated between customers and agents in real time. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Transcribe
Amazon Polly
explain: Amazon Translate provides fast, real-time language translation - the right service when the task is translation rather than transcription or speech.

q: A social app must automatically detect and remove violent imagery from user uploads. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Polly
Amazon Forecast
Amazon Textract
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Rekognition analyzes images and video - detecting objects, faces, and unsafe content - making it the content-moderation answer.

q: A hospital wants to find and redact patient names and ID numbers in clinical notes before sharing datasets. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Lex
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Polly
explain: Comprehend is NLP for text: it detects sentiment, entities, key phrases, and PII - including redaction of sensitive identifiers.

q: A company wants natural-language search across its wikis, SharePoint, and S3 documents with direct answers. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Kendra
Amazon Textract
Amazon Lex
Amazon Personalize
explain: Kendra is intelligent enterprise search: it indexes content across data sources and returns answers - not just document links - to natural-language questions.

q: A news app wants to reorder its article feed for each reader based on reading history. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Personalize
Amazon Forecast
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Personalize delivers real-time personalized rankings and recommendations from user behavior including content feeds, not just products.

q: A company needs predictions of future values from historical time-series data - not personalized recommendations. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Personalize
Amazon Forecast
Amazon Lex
Amazon Rekognition
explain: Forecast is the managed time-series forecasting service; Personalize is for recommendations matching the problem type to the service is the exam skill.

q: A lender wants ML-based risk scores for new account applications to catch synthetic identities. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Forecast
Amazon Fraud Detector
Amazon Textract
Amazon Polly
explain: Fraud Detector builds ML models that score events - account openings, transactions, logins - for fraud risk in real time.

q: A team trains a custom model with full control of the pipeline and deploys it to autoscaling GPU endpoints with experiment tracking. Which service fits?
options: Amazon Bedrock
Amazon SageMaker AI
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Q Business
explain: SageMaker AI is the full ML platform - training, tuning, and deploying custom models at scale when you need control beyond Bedrock's managed models.

q: A product manager wants to experiment with foundation models in a browser playground, writing no code. Which option fits?
options: AWS CloudShell
The Bedrock API
SageMaker Studio
PartyRock
explain: PartyRock is Amazon Bedrock's no-code playground for building and trying generative AI apps in the browser.

q: A developer wants one API to call Anthropic Claude, Meta Llama, and Amazon Nova without managing infrastructure. Which service provides this?
options: Amazon EC2
Amazon Bedrock
PartyRock
SageMaker JumpStart
explain: Bedrock offers leading foundation models from multiple providers through a single fully managed API - no infrastructure to run.

q: A team wants a smaller, faster, cheaper model that mimics its fine-tuned Bedrock model's behavior. The Bedrock technique for this is:
options: RAG
Continued pre-training
Prompt chaining
Model distillation
explain: Model distillation trains a compact "student" model to imitate a larger model - trading a little accuracy for much lower cost and latency.

q: A Python developer wants an open-source-style SDK for building agents with tool use and multi-step reasoning. The AWS offering is:
options: PartyRock
Strands Agents
Knowledge Bases for Bedrock
Amazon Q Business
explain: Strands Agents is AWS's open-source SDK for building AI agents with tools and reasoning loops, deployable with Bedrock AgentCore.

q: A developer needs code completions, while a sales rep needs answers from the company's sales playbook. Which Amazon Q offering serves the sales rep?
options: PartyRock
Amazon Q Business
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Q Developer
explain: Q Business is the assistant for business users over company data (respecting permissions); Q Developer is the coding assistant for developers.

q: A RAG solution needs a managed store for document embeddings with fast similarity search. Which AWS service provides vector search?
options: Amazon RDS
Amazon Polly
AWS Budgets
Amazon OpenSearch Service
explain: OpenSearch Service supports k-NN vector search, making it a standard managed vector store behind RAG retrieval.

q: A retail company is choosing a foundation model for a customer chat widget that must reply in under one second during peak sales events while keeping per-request cost low. Which selection criterion should the team prioritize?
options: Support for image generation
The largest available context window
Low latency combined with a small, cost-efficient model size
The highest parameter count available on Amazon Bedrock
explain: For high-volume, real-time chat, response speed and unit cost dominate. A smaller, faster model meets the latency target at lower cost, while a huge context window or parameter count would add latency and expense without helping short chat exchanges.

q: A healthcare provider wants a model to summarize complete patient discharge packets that routinely exceed 150,000 tokens in a single request. Which model attribute is MOST important to verify before selection?
options: The number of languages the model was marketed in
Whether the model supports text-to-speech
The model's context length
Whether the model offers provisioned throughput discounts
explain: Context length is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request. If the discharge packet exceeds that limit, content will be truncated or rejected, so the team must confirm the window fits the full document before any other comparison.

q: A bank is evaluating two models for extracting fields from loan documents. Model X scores higher on a public leaderboard, but Model Y performs better on the bank's own labeled document set in Amazon Bedrock model evaluation. Which model should the bank prefer and why?
options: Model X, because public benchmarks always predict production performance
Model Y, because evaluation on representative task data is the most reliable predictor of real-world performance
Model X, because it avoids the cost of running an evaluation job
Either model, because benchmark differences never matter for extraction tasks
explain: Public benchmarks measure general capability, not performance on a specific task and data distribution. Bedrock model evaluation on the bank's own representative documents directly measures the extraction quality the bank will actually get, so Model Y is the safer choice.

q: An education company needs a model that answers student questions in Spanish, French, and Portuguese with equal quality. When comparing models in Amazon Bedrock, which criterion addresses this requirement directly?
options: Language support and quality for each required language
Whether the model is available in multiple AWS Regions
The model's image resolution
Maximum tokens per response
explain: Models differ in the languages they were trained and evaluated on. The team should verify documented language support and test quality in Spanish, French, and Portuguese specifically, rather than assuming English performance transfers to other languages.

q: A media company plans to use a foundation model's outputs in a commercial streaming product and resell the service to partners. Before selecting the model, the legal team asks about a specific risk. Which criterion are they MOST likely reviewing?
options: Top p default value
Model licensing terms and permitted commercial use
The model's temperature range
Whether the playground supports dark mode
explain: Foundation models carry different license terms governing commercial use, redistribution, and acceptable use. Legal review of licensing is a legitimate selection gate: a technically strong model that cannot be used commercially as intended is not a viable choice.

q: An insurance firm wants to compare how three Bedrock models handle the same claims-summarization prompt side by side before writing any application code. Which approach meets this need with the LEAST effort?
options: Fine-tune all three models first
Deploy each model to a separate SageMaker endpoint
Purchase provisioned throughput for all three models
Use the Amazon Bedrock playgrounds to run the same prompt against each model and compare outputs
explain: Bedrock playgrounds let teams interactively test and compare models with identical prompts in the console without code or infrastructure. That quick qualitative comparison narrows candidates before a formal evaluation job or any fine-tuning investment.

q: A logistics company needs a model evaluation that captures whether summaries are actually helpful and well written, not just whether they overlap with reference text. Which Bedrock evaluation method should the company add?
options: Automatic evaluation only, using word-overlap metrics
Human evaluation using a managed or team-provided workforce
Cost analysis only
Latency measurement only
explain: Automatic metrics such as ROUGE measure surface overlap with references and miss qualities like helpfulness, tone, and readability. Human evaluation workflows in Bedrock let reviewers score those subjective qualities on the team's own data.

q: A manufacturing company processes millions of short sensor-comment classifications per day. A very large model is accurate but costs ten times more per call than a smaller model that is only slightly less accurate. Which trade-off best describes the recommended decision process?
options: Choose based on context window alone
Balance task performance against cost at the expected request volume, favoring the smaller model if it meets the accuracy bar
Ignore cost because inference is billed annually
Always choose the largest model regardless of volume
explain: Model selection is a multi-criteria trade-off among quality, cost, and latency. At millions of daily requests, small per-call cost differences dominate, so a smaller model that clears the required accuracy threshold is usually the better business choice.

q: A government agency will send a model images of scanned forms plus typed instructions and expects a text answer describing the forms. Which capability must the selected foundation model have?
options: Multimodal input support for both image and text
Real-time streaming speech output
Audio transcription
Text-to-image generation
explain: The task provides two input modalities, image and text, and needs a text response. Only a multimodal model that accepts image plus text input can perform it; unimodal text models cannot see the scanned forms at all.

q: Which factors should a team weigh when selecting a foundation model for a new application? (Choose two.)
options: Whether the model supports the required task and input modality
The number of offices the provider has
The model's cost and latency at the expected request volume
The color scheme of the provider's website
explain: Sound model selection weighs task and modality fit, benchmark and evaluation performance on representative data, cost, latency, context length, language support, and licensing. Cosmetic factors such as branding or office count have no bearing on application outcomes.

q: A real estate platform generates property descriptions and wants the same input to produce nearly identical wording every time for compliance review. Which inference setting best supports this requirement?
options: Top k set to the largest possible value
Temperature set to a low value for more deterministic output
Max tokens set to 1
Temperature set near its maximum
explain: Low temperature makes the model favor its most probable tokens, producing focused, repeatable, near-deterministic output suited to compliance-reviewed text. High temperature or a very large top k would increase randomness and variation between runs.

q: A hospitality company's creative assistant produces bland, nearly identical marketing taglines on every run, and the team wants more varied and imaginative options. Which parameter change should the team make first?
options: Decrease max tokens to 5
Decrease temperature
Add a stop sequence after the first word
Increase temperature
explain: Temperature controls randomness and creativity. Raising it lets the model sample less predictable tokens, yielding more diverse and imaginative taglines, while lowering it would make the already bland output even more repetitive.

q: A legal team's contract summarizer keeps stopping mid-sentence, and every summary ends abruptly at roughly the same length. What is the MOST likely cause and fix?
options: Temperature is too high; lower it
The system prompt is too short; lengthen it
Top p is too low; raise it to 1.0
The max tokens limit is too small; increase the maximum output length
explain: Consistent truncation at about the same length is the classic signature of the max tokens (maximum output length) limit being reached. Raising that limit lets the model finish its sentences; sampling parameters affect word choice, not output length.

q: An energy company's assistant must return exactly one classification label and then stop, but it keeps continuing with an invented second example after the label. Which inference feature directly solves this?
options: Removing the instruction from the prompt
A stop sequence set to the delimiter that follows the label
Increasing top k
Increasing temperature
explain: A stop sequence tells the model to halt generation as soon as it produces a specified string, such as the newline or delimiter after the label. That cleanly ends output at the intended boundary instead of letting the model ramble into fabricated extra examples.

q: A sports media app uses top p set to 0.9 for headline generation. What does this setting do?
options: It guarantees 90 percent factual accuracy
It samples each next token from the smallest set of candidates whose cumulative probability reaches 0.9
It caps the response at 90 tokens
It limits generation to 0.9 tokens per second
explain: Top p, or nucleus sampling, restricts each token choice to the most likely candidates whose probabilities sum to p, here 0.9. It balances coherence and diversity but says nothing about accuracy, speed, or response length.

q: A banking chatbot gives different account-policy answers to the same question across sessions, and auditors require consistent factual replies. Which combination of settings best addresses this? (Choose two.)
options: Lower the temperature toward 0
Set max tokens to the smallest possible value
Lower top p to narrow the candidate token pool
Raise the temperature toward its maximum
