q: An agriculture cooperative stores equipment repair guides in S3 and sensor manuals in a web crawl source. It wants both collections searchable by one RAG application. How should the cooperative configure its Bedrock Knowledge Base?
options: Create a data source for each collection within the knowledge base and sync both
Store the manuals as prompt templates instead
Fine-tune two separate models, one per collection
Merge the files manually into one PDF before uploading
explain: A Bedrock Knowledge Base can hold multiple data sources, such as S3 buckets and web crawlers, and syncs each into the same vector index so one application can retrieve across all collections.

q: A bank's RAG pilot retrieves relevant passages reliably, but the final answers are long, rambling, and written in an inconsistent tone. Retrieval quality tests are strong. Where should the team focus first?
options: Increase the chunk size
Improve the generation prompt with clear instructions on length, structure, and tone
Re-embed the entire corpus with a different model
Replace the vector store
explain: When retrieval is demonstrably good, rambling output is a generation-side problem. Prompt instructions on format, length, and tone, plus generation parameters, fix presentation without rebuilding the index.

q: A company already operates Redis Enterprise Cloud for caching and wants to reuse it to store embeddings for a Bedrock Knowledge Base rather than adopting a new database. Is this supported, and what must the data be stored as?
options: No, Redis can only store the source documents, not vectors
No, Bedrock Knowledge Bases only support Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
Yes, Redis Enterprise Cloud is a supported vector store when configured for vector search
Yes, but only if the embeddings are stored as plain text strings
explain: Redis Enterprise Cloud is one of the supported third-party vector stores for Bedrock Knowledge Bases, alongside Pinecone and MongoDB Atlas, provided it is configured as a vector index. Embeddings must be stored as vectors, not plain text.

q: A healthcare startup's RAG system must not expose one clinic's patient education documents to another clinic's staff, even though both use the same application. Which design provides this separation at retrieval time?
options: A higher max token setting so the model can explain its sources
A single shared index with no attributes, relying on the model to be careful
Separate prompts written in different tones per clinic
Tenant identifiers stored as chunk metadata with a mandatory filter for the signed-in clinic
explain: Attaching a tenant or clinic identifier as metadata and always filtering retrieval by the caller's clinic enforces separation in the data layer, before generation. Relying on the model's care or on prompt wording does not enforce access boundaries.

q: In a RAG system, what does the term augmented refer to in augmented generation?
options: The model's parameters are enlarged after each query
The vector store is augmented with extra replicas
The training dataset is augmented with synthetic examples
The prompt is augmented with retrieved context before the model generates its response
explain: Augmentation in RAG means enriching the user's prompt with the retrieved passages, so generation is conditioned on external evidence. It does not change model parameters or the training dataset.

q: A retailer wants its RAG assistant to quote the exact return window from the current policy and link shoppers to that policy. The legal team requires that every factual claim in an answer be traceable to a source document. Which RAG property most directly satisfies the legal team?
options: The embedding model guarantees legal accuracy
A lower temperature produces traceable claims
Retrieved passages can be returned as citations alongside the generated answer
Fine-tuned models always cite their training data
explain: Because answers are generated from specific retrieved chunks, a Knowledge Base response can include citations to the source documents and locations, giving traceability. Neither embeddings nor temperature settings create source attribution.

q: An insurance adjuster tool retrieves the top matching chunks for a claim question, but the single most relevant chunk is often ranked just below the cutoff. The team wants a second pass that re-scores the retrieved candidates against the question before generation. Which technique is this?
options: Increasing the overlap between chunks
Reranking the retrieved results
Re-embedding the corpus nightly
Lowering the model's top p value
explain: Reranking applies a more precise scoring pass over the initially retrieved candidates so the most relevant chunks are promoted into the prompt. Chunk overlap and generation parameters do not re-score retrieval results.

q: Which of the following are stages of a typical RAG request flow after a user submits a question? (Choose two.)
options: The vector store rewrites the user's question into SQL
The foundation model is fine-tuned on the retrieved passages
The question is converted into an embedding and used to search the vector store
The retrieved passages are placed into the prompt context for the foundation model
explain: At query time the question is embedded for similarity search, and the retrieved passages are inserted into the prompt as context for generation. Retrieval results never trigger fine-tuning, and the vector store performs similarity search, not SQL rewriting.

q: A logistics firm indexes 2 million shipment documents. After launch, answers are accurate but slow, and analysis shows the application retrieves and sends 40 chunks per question to the model. Which change reduces latency and cost while likely preserving accuracy?
options: Reduce the maximum number of retrieved results to a smaller set of the most relevant chunks
Send every chunk in the index with each question
Disable metadata so more chunks qualify
Switch the embedding model to generate the answers
explain: Sending dozens of chunks inflates prompt tokens, which drives both latency and cost. Returning a smaller number of top-ranked chunks keeps the relevant evidence while shrinking the prompt the model must process.

q: A university wants a study assistant that answers from its own lecture notes and textbooks, which it updates each semester. Professors will not label training examples. Which combination best fits these constraints?
options: Continued pretraining on unlabeled web text
RAG over the course materials, re-synced each semester
Instruction fine-tuning with professor-written examples
RLHF with a reward model trained on student rankings
explain: The content is private, changes each term, and no labeled examples exist, which is the classic RAG case: index the materials and re-sync when they change. Fine-tuning and RLHF both require labeled or ranked data the professors will not produce.

q: What happens to the source documents and embeddings when a Bedrock Knowledge Base data source sync completes?
options: Documents are chunked, embedded, and written to the configured vector store, replacing stale chunks for changed files
Documents are deleted from S3 after indexing
Documents are converted into a fine-tuning dataset automatically
The foundation model weights are updated with the document content
explain: A sync job processes source content into chunks and embeddings stored in the vector store, updating entries for changed documents. Source files remain in place, and no model weights or fine-tuning datasets are created.

q: A streaming service's RAG assistant for creator documentation performs well on common questions but fails on questions whose wording differs greatly from the documents, even though the documents contain the answers. Which component should the team evaluate first?
options: The embedding model, because mismatched wording is a semantic matching problem
The text-to-speech voice
The provisioned throughput level
The model's stop sequences
explain: When the answer exists in the corpus but differently worded questions miss it, the weakness is semantic matching between query and document embeddings. A different or better-suited embedding model, or query reformulation, addresses retrieval recall.

q: A retailer's chatbot gives correct product facts but its replies vary wildly in format, breaking the downstream system that parses them. The team first adds a strict output template and two examples to the prompt, which fixes most replies at almost no cost. Which principle guided this choice?
options: Always fine-tune before trying prompt changes
Distillation is the only way to control output format
Continued pretraining is required for any format change
Try prompt engineering first because it is the fastest and cheapest way to change model behavior
explain: Prompt engineering is the first lever to try: instructions, templates, and few-shot examples often fix format and tone with no training cost or delay. Fine-tuning is justified when prompting cannot consistently achieve the required behavior.

q: A bank's model must consistently classify transaction memos into a fixed set of internal categories using the bank's own labeling conventions, which prompting cannot achieve reliably despite many attempts. The bank has 40,000 memos already labeled by analysts. Which approach is the best fit?
options: RAG over the labeled memos
Fine-tuning on the labeled examples so the model learns the category conventions
Zero-shot prompting with a longer system prompt
Continued pretraining on unlabeled memos
explain: Abundant labeled examples plus a persistent behavior that prompting cannot deliver is the classic fine-tuning case: training on the examples teaches the model the task and the organization's conventions. RAG supplies facts at query time but does not teach classification behavior.

q: A healthcare company wants a model that deeply understands clinical terminology and the style of medical literature so it performs better across many downstream clinical text tasks. It has a large corpus of unlabeled medical journals and notes. Which approach fits?
options: Continued pretraining on the unlabeled domain corpus
Few-shot prompting with three examples
RAG over a small FAQ page
Raising the temperature during inference
explain: Continued pretraining adapts a foundation model to a domain by training further on large amounts of unlabeled domain text, improving its grasp of terminology and style. Prompting and RAG do not change the model's underlying domain knowledge.

q: An insurer fine-tuned a model to draft claim summaries in its house style. Six months later, regulations change and the summaries must reflect new disclosure rules published in official bulletins. Which limitation of fine-tuning does this situation expose?
options: Fine-tuning removes the model's ability to follow prompts
Fine-tuned models cannot produce summaries
Fine-tuned models require a vector store to run
Knowledge baked in during fine-tuning goes stale and does not update when source facts change
explain: Fine-tuning captures behavior and knowledge as of training time; when facts change, the model does not learn the update on its own and must be retrained or paired with retrieval. This staleness is a core reason changing facts are usually handled with RAG instead.

q: What data does instruction fine-tuning use to teach a model to follow directions for a specific task?
options: Embeddings stored in a vector database
Only the model's own unfiltered outputs
Unlabeled raw text from the open web
Pairs of prompts and the desired completions, formatted as labeled examples
explain: Instruction fine-tuning trains on labeled prompt-and-completion pairs that demonstrate the desired response to each instruction, which teaches task behavior and output format. Unlabeled text is used for pretraining or continued pretraining, not instruction tuning.

q: A media company fine-tuned a Bedrock model and now wants to deploy the customized model for production traffic with predictable performance. What must the company arrange to serve the fine-tuned model?
options: A second knowledge base containing the training data
A SageMaker training cluster left running permanently
Provisioned throughput for the customized model
Nothing, customized models run on shared on-demand capacity automatically
explain: Customized Bedrock models, whether fine-tuned or distilled, are served through provisioned throughput, which reserves model units for predictable performance. Base models can be used on demand, but custom models require this step.

q: A logistics company fine-tuned a general model heavily on routing documents. Afterwards the model writes excellent routing summaries but its previously strong general question-answering and math abilities noticeably declined. Which phenomenon does this describe?
options: Token overflow
Data drift
Catastrophic forgetting
Prompt injection
explain: Catastrophic forgetting occurs when training on a narrow dataset degrades capabilities the model previously had, because its weights shift toward the new task. Mitigations include mixing in general data and using careful training settings.

q: A startup's fine-tuned model performs well, but inference with the large teacher model it was based on is too expensive at scale. The team trains a smaller model on the larger model's outputs so the small model imitates its behavior on their task. What is this technique called?
options: Chunking
Continued pretraining
Reranking
Distillation
explain: Distillation trains a smaller student model on a larger teacher model's outputs so the student approximates the teacher's behavior at lower cost and latency. Amazon Bedrock supports distillation for models such as Nova and Llama families.

q: In model distillation, what are the roles of the teacher and the student?
options: The teacher is the smaller model and the student is the larger model
Both models are the same size and train each other
The student labels data that the teacher uses for pretraining
The larger teacher generates outputs or behavior that the smaller student learns to imitate
explain: The teacher is the larger, capable model whose outputs become training signal; the student is the smaller model trained to reproduce that behavior more cheaply. Reversing the roles would defeat the purpose of compression.

q: A government agency wants its assistant to adopt a formal, consistent tone and always structure answers with a summary followed by supporting details. Facts will come from retrieved documents. After prompt changes alone prove inconsistent across thousands of daily queries, which addition best addresses the tone and structure requirement?
options: More metadata filters
A higher temperature setting
Fine-tuning on examples written in the required tone and structure
A larger vector store
explain: Persistent tone and format behavior across high volume is a fine-tuning strength: labeled examples in the target style teach the model to produce that structure by default, while RAG continues to supply the facts. Retrieval settings do not change writing style.

q: Which factors should drive a team to choose RAG over fine-tuning for a knowledge assistant? (Choose two.)
options: Answers must cite specific proprietary source documents
The team has millions of labeled examples and a fixed task
The underlying facts change frequently and must stay current
The model must permanently change its personality
explain: Frequently changing facts and a need for citations to proprietary sources are the strongest signals for RAG, since retrieval always reflects the current indexed documents. Permanent behavior change and large labeled datasets point toward fine-tuning instead.

q: An education platform fine-tunes a model using examples in JSONL format, where each record contains a prompt and the ideal completion. Midway through preparation, the team realizes half its examples have completions that contradict its style guide. What is the MOST important action before starting the training job?
options: Increase the number of training epochs to compensate
Lower the inference temperature after training
Move the dataset into a vector store
Fix or remove the contradictory examples, because the model will learn whatever patterns the data demonstrates
explain: Fine-tuning teaches the model to imitate its training data, so contradictory or low-quality examples directly become learned behavior. Data quality review matters more than hyperparameters; no epoch count fixes examples that teach the wrong style.

q: A manufacturer wants a model to better understand its proprietary engineering vocabulary across all its text applications, and it has millions of unlabeled internal documents but almost no labeled examples. Which approach should it choose?
options: Instruction fine-tuning
Continued pretraining on the unlabeled internal corpus
Few-shot prompting
RLHF
explain: Continued pretraining is designed for domain adaptation from large unlabeled corpora, teaching vocabulary and domain patterns. Instruction fine-tuning and RLHF both require labeled or preference data the manufacturer does not have.

q: A company used human reviewers to rank pairs of model responses, trained a reward model on those rankings, and then optimized the language model against that reward model so its answers better match human preferences. Which technique is the company using?
options: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
Semantic chunking
Knowledge distillation
Retrieval Augmented Generation
explain: RLHF uses human preference rankings to train a reward model, then uses reinforcement learning to steer the language model toward higher-reward responses. It aligns behavior with human preferences rather than adding facts or compressing the model.

q: A hospitality chain compares three options for its FAQ assistant: the answers already exist in policy documents that change quarterly, query volume is high, and the budget is limited. Which option offers the best balance of currency and cost?
options: RAG, updating the index when policies change instead of retraining
Continued pretraining on hospitality text
Quarterly fine-tuning runs on the policy documents
A distilled model retrained monthly
explain: With changing documents and limited budget, RAG wins: a re-sync updates answers at a fraction of retraining cost, and no training jobs are needed at all. Every training-based option pays repeatedly to chase facts that retrieval handles directly.

q: What is a key cost consideration when a company fine-tunes a Bedrock model instead of using the base model on demand?
options: The company pays for the training job and for provisioned throughput to host the customized model
Fine-tuning eliminates all inference costs
There are no additional costs beyond the base model price
Fine-tuned models are billed only per document indexed
explain: Customization adds a training job cost, and serving a customized Bedrock model requires provisioned throughput, an ongoing capacity cost on top of usage. This is why fine-tuning is justified by durable behavior needs, not one-off questions.

q: A legal tech team wants a smaller model that handles contract clause extraction almost as well as the large model it currently calls, to cut per-document cost. The large model can generate extraction outputs for tens of thousands of sample clauses. Which plan fits distillation?
options: Ask the large model to write a longer system prompt
Use the large model's extraction outputs as training data for a smaller model, then evaluate the smaller model against the large one
Embed the contracts and let the vector store extract clauses
Fine-tune the large model further on the same contracts
explain: Distillation uses teacher outputs on representative inputs as the student's training signal, then validates that the student retains acceptable quality. The goal is a cheaper model that mimics the teacher on this task.

q: A retail team is deciding how to make its assistant answer sizing questions from a size-guide document that the merchandising team edits weekly. An engineer suggests fine-tuning weekly; the architect suggests retrieval. Which reasoning supports the architect?
options: Retrieval changes the model's tone automatically
Fine-tuning cannot read documents at all
Fine-tuning requires human preference rankings
Retrieval reflects the edited document after a re-sync, while weekly fine-tuning is slower, costlier, and still stale between runs
explain: For facts that live in an editable document, retrieval is updated by re-indexing, which is fast and cheap compared with repeated training jobs that freeze knowledge between runs. The deciding factor is data freshness, not reading ability.

q: Which scenario is the clearest case for fine-tuning rather than prompt engineering or RAG?
options: The knowledge base adds new documents every hour
The model must reliably produce a specialized output format it keeps getting wrong despite detailed prompts and examples, and thousands of labeled demonstrations exist
Answers must reflect today's inventory levels
Users need citations to policy documents
explain: A stubborn, specialized behavior plus abundant labeled demonstrations is exactly what fine-tuning is for. Fresh inventory, citations, and hourly document changes are retrieval problems that training cannot solve economically.

q: A team plans to fine-tune a model and wants to verify the customized model actually improved on its target task before paying for production provisioned throughput. What should the team do?
options: Evaluate the customized model against the base model on a held-out test set for the target task
Only test the model on its training examples
Compare the models on unrelated general knowledge questions only
Skip evaluation because training loss decreased
explain: A held-out test set the model never trained on shows whether fine-tuning genuinely improved the target task versus the base model. Testing on training examples measures memorization, and falling training loss alone does not prove task quality.

q: An energy company wants consistent, terse field-technician summaries. It has no labeled dataset yet, a small budget, and the requirement is about writing style rather than new facts. What is the MOST sensible first step?
options: Craft a system prompt with style rules and a few example summaries, and measure whether it meets the bar
Train a reward model from scratch
Build a vector store of technician manuals
Immediately commission continued pretraining
explain: Style requirements should first be tested with prompt engineering, including few-shot examples, because it is nearly free and may fully satisfy the need. Training approaches are escalations if prompting measurably falls short.

q: A bank fine-tunes a model on internal credit-policy examples. A risk officer asks what could go wrong if the training set accidentally includes outdated policy examples mixed with current ones. Which risk is MOST accurate?
options: The model can learn and reproduce the outdated behavior, because fine-tuning absorbs the patterns present in the data
The model will refuse to answer policy questions
The base model will be permanently changed for all AWS customers
The vector store will reject the files
explain: Fine-tuning internalizes the patterns in its training data, including outdated ones, so data curation is a governance control. Customization affects only the customer's own model copy, never the shared base model.

q: Which statements correctly contrast fine-tuning with RAG? (Choose two.)
options: RAG permanently modifies the foundation model's weights
Fine-tuning is well suited to teaching a consistent tone or format
Fine-tuning changes model behavior by training on examples, while RAG supplies external context at inference time
RAG requires retraining the model whenever documents change
explain: Fine-tuning trains weights on examples and is strong for durable behavior such as tone and format; RAG leaves weights untouched and injects retrieved context per query. Neither RAG statement about retraining or weight changes is true.

q: A streaming company distilled a large model into a smaller one for subtitle classification. After distillation, the smaller model is much cheaper but slightly less accurate on rare categories. How should the team decide whether the distilled model is acceptable?
options: Compare its quality on a representative evaluation set against the business's minimum acceptable accuracy and cost targets
Judge it only by its parameter count
Test it only on the categories where it performs best
Accept it automatically because smaller is always better
explain: Distillation is a trade-off decision: the student is acceptable when measured quality on representative data stays above the business threshold while cost and latency savings are realized. Cherry-picked categories would hide the rare-category weakness.

q: A company wants its Bedrock application to answer questions about internal procedures and to adopt the company's concise writing voice. Procedures change monthly; the voice never changes. Which combination best matches each requirement to the right technique?
options: Continued pretraining for both requirements
Fine-tune for the procedures and use RAG for the voice
RAG for the changing procedures and fine-tuning for the stable voice and format
Prompt engineering alone for both, with no evaluation
explain: Changing facts belong in retrieval, which updates by re-indexing, while a stable voice and format are durable behavior that fine-tuning teaches once. Swapping the two would bake monthly facts into weights and leave style to per-query context.

q: What does Amazon Bedrock model distillation use as the primary training signal for the student model?
options: The teacher model's responses to training prompts
Raw web text unrelated to the task
The student's own previous mistakes, unlabeled
Human preference rankings only
explain: In Bedrock distillation, the selected teacher model generates responses to the provided prompts, and those responses become the examples the smaller student model is trained on. Human rankings are the signal for RLHF, not distillation.

q: An agriculture firm fine-tuned a model to format soil reports. It now needs the same model to also answer questions from a frequently updated pesticide regulation database with citations. What should the firm add?
options: A second embedding of the training data
A higher temperature so the model guesses regulations more creatively
A RAG layer over the regulation database, keeping the fine-tuned model for formatting
Another fine-tuning run every time regulations change
explain: The fine-tuned formatting behavior remains valuable, while changing, citable facts are a retrieval job. Adding RAG over the regulation database supplies current, attributable content without disturbing the learned format.

q: A team with a limited budget must improve a support assistant. Usage data shows 80 percent of failures are the model lacking the company's latest troubleshooting facts, and 20 percent are formatting slips. Which investment should come first?
options: Fine-tuning, because it addresses both problems equally
A knowledge base with RAG, because the dominant failure is missing current facts
Continued pretraining on general web text
Distillation, because smaller models hallucinate less
explain: Prioritize the dominant failure mode: missing current facts is a retrieval problem, so a knowledge base delivers the largest improvement per dollar. Formatting slips can then be handled with prompt refinements.

q: A travel company builds a Bedrock agent that plans trips: it checks a calendar API, searches flights, holds a booking, and emails the itinerary, deciding each next step from the results of the previous one. Which property makes this an agent rather than a single model call?
options: It stores its answers in a vector database
It reasons over multiple steps and invokes tools to complete a task, adapting as results come back
It was fine-tuned on travel data
It uses a larger context window than a chatbot
explain: An agent orchestrates multi-step work: it interprets the goal, plans actions, calls tools or APIs, observes results, and continues until the task is done. A single prompt-response exchange, however large the context, is not agentic behavior.

q: In Amazon Bedrock Agents, what is an action group?
options: A cluster of provisioned throughput units
A bundle of guardrail policies
A set of API operations, backed by a Lambda function, that the agent can invoke to perform tasks in external systems
A group of users who share access to an agent
explain: An action group defines the actions an agent can take, described by an API schema and executed by a Lambda function that calls the real systems, such as a booking or inventory service. It is how an agent affects the world beyond generating text.

q: A retailer wants its Bedrock agent to check live stock levels before promising a delivery date. The stock data lives in an internal inventory service. Which components connect the agent to that service? (Choose two.)
options: A larger embedding model
An AWS Lambda function that implements the call to the inventory service
A fine-tuning job run before every query
An action group whose API schema describes the stock-check operation
explain: Agents act through action groups: the OpenAPI schema declares the operation and a Lambda function executes it against the backing system. Neither fine-tuning nor embeddings give an agent live access to an internal service.

q: A bank's Bedrock agent helps staff process loan applications: it retrieves the applicant's documents from a knowledge base, runs a credit-check API, and drafts a summary for a human approver. Which statement about the agent's orchestration is correct?
options: The Lambda functions decide the overall plan and the model only formats text
The knowledge base executes the credit-check API
The agent uses the foundation model to interpret the request, sequence the tool calls and knowledge base lookups, and compose the result
Orchestration requires retraining the model for each new task
explain: In Bedrock Agents the foundation model drives orchestration: it reasons about what to do next, invokes action groups and knowledge base queries in sequence, and assembles the outcome. Lambda functions execute individual actions; they do not plan the workflow.

q: An insurance company wants its agent to answer adjuster questions using the same claims knowledge base the company already built for its RAG chatbot, rather than duplicating the documents. How should the company configure the agent?
options: Associate the existing knowledge base with the agent so it can query it during task execution
Export the knowledge base into a CSV file for the Lambda function
Copy the documents into the agent's system prompt
Fine-tune the agent's model on the claims documents
explain: Bedrock Agents can be associated with one or more knowledge bases, letting the agent retrieve grounded information as part of completing a task. This reuses the existing indexed content instead of duplicating or training on it.

q: A logistics agent that books freight sometimes needs a dispatcher to approve shipments over a cost threshold before it proceeds. Which agent capability supports pausing for that approval and then continuing the same task?
options: Automatic model evaluation
Semantic chunking of the shipment documents
Returning control to the application so a human can review and the session can resume
Increasing provisioned throughput
explain: Bedrock Agents support return of control, which hands execution back to the calling application mid-task so a human approval or custom logic can occur before the agent continues. Throughput and chunking do not provide human-in-the-loop pauses.

q: A healthcare provider is piloting an agent that schedules appointments. During a multi-turn conversation, the patient changes the preferred day twice, and the agent must remember the latest preference and the already-confirmed location. Which concept does this requirement exercise?
options: Data augmentation
Model quantization
Session state and conversational memory across the agent's steps and turns
Batch inference
explain: Multi-step agents maintain session state so facts gathered earlier, and corrections made later, carry through the task. Remembering the current preference across turns is memory in the orchestration sense, not a training technique.

q: A development team wants to build production agents on Bedrock with managed infrastructure for running agent code securely at scale, persistent memory across sessions, and built-in tools such as a code interpreter and a browser. Which offering is designed for this?
options: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
AWS CloudFormation
Amazon PartyRock
explain: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides a managed runtime for deploying agents, plus services such as memory, identity, a gateway to tools, and built-in code interpreter and browser tools. PartyRock is a no-code playground, and Canvas is no-code ML model building.

q: A media company's agent must research a topic by opening several web pages, extracting figures, and running a small script to total them before writing a briefing. Which AgentCore capabilities map to these needs? (Choose two.)
options: A managed browser tool for interacting with web pages
A code interpreter tool for executing the calculation script
A text-to-speech voice for reading the briefing
A Rekognition label detection job
explain: AgentCore offers a managed browser tool for web interaction and a code interpreter for safely executing code such as calculations, both designed for agent workflows. Speech synthesis and image labeling are unrelated AI services, not agent tools here.

q: A government benefits agent answers eligibility questions and then submits applications through an API. Auditors require a record showing which sources the agent consulted and which actions it took, in order. Which practice best satisfies the auditors?
options: Raise the agent's temperature for more detailed answers
Store the audit record only in the model's context window
Enable tracing and logging of the agent's reasoning steps, retrievals, and action invocations
Fine-tune the model on past audit reports
explain: Agent traces expose the sequence of reasoning, knowledge base queries, and action group calls for each session, giving auditors a reviewable record. Context windows are transient and cannot serve as an audit trail.

q: Which task is the BEST fit for a Bedrock agent rather than a plain RAG chatbot?
options: Summarizing a single uploaded document
Looking up a product's warranty period
Rebooking a customer's delivery: checking inventory, reserving a new slot, charging the difference, and sending confirmation
Answering what the return policy says
explain: Rebooking spans several dependent actions across external systems, which is exactly the multi-step, tool-using work agents are built for. The other tasks are single lookups or single-document generation that RAG or a plain prompt handles well.

q: A real estate agency's agent drafts listing descriptions and must call an external pricing API. The API occasionally returns an error, and the agent currently stops and reports total failure even when a retry would succeed. Which design improvement addresses this?
options: Lower the model's maximum token count to zero
Give the agent instructions and error handling so it can observe the failure, retry or choose an alternate step, and continue the task
Remove the pricing API and let the model invent prices
Increase the knowledge base chunk size
explain: Agents are expected to reason about tool results, including failures, and adapt by retrying or replanning within the task. Removing the API would replace live data with invented figures, which is worse than the original problem.

q: What role does the OpenAPI schema play in a Bedrock agent's action group?
options: It describes each action's purpose, parameters, and responses so the agent knows how and when to call it
It defines the agent's guardrail word filters
It sets the price of provisioned throughput
It stores the embeddings for the knowledge base
explain: The action group's API schema, in OpenAPI format, tells the agent what operations exist, what inputs they need, and what they return, which the model uses to plan correct calls. It is a contract for tool use, not a data store or policy file.

q: A hospitality group wants one agent to handle the full guest request flow: find available rooms, apply a loyalty discount, charge the card on file, and add a late checkout note to the reservation. Why is an agent architecture appropriate here?
options: Because agents guarantee lower cost than a single model call for every task
Because the flow requires training a new foundation model
Because the flow is a sequence of dependent actions across multiple systems that must be coordinated toward one goal
Because agents eliminate the need for any APIs
explain: The request chains dependent steps across booking, loyalty, payment, and reservation systems, which requires planning and tool orchestration rather than one text generation. Agents still depend on APIs; they coordinate them.

q: A team is preparing to evaluate two candidate foundation models for a document summarization workload on Bedrock. Which Bedrock feature runs structured comparisons of models on their task data?
options: Model evaluation jobs
Knowledge Base sync jobs
Prompt Management versioning alone
Provisioned throughput
explain: Amazon Bedrock model evaluation jobs run candidate models against datasets and score the outputs with automatic metrics or human reviewers, producing a comparison for selection. Sync jobs index documents and throughput reserves capacity; neither evaluates models.

q: An education company runs a Bedrock model evaluation job for its tutoring summaries. Because summary quality is subjective, the company wants people to rate accuracy, completeness, and tone for a sample of outputs instead of relying only on computed scores. Which evaluation type should the company add to the job?
options: Latency benchmarking
A/B testing in production without labels
Human evaluation with a managed or company-provided review team
Automatic evaluation with built-in metrics only
explain: Bedrock evaluation jobs support human evaluation workflows where reviewers score outputs on custom criteria such as accuracy and tone, which suits subjective quality that automatic metrics capture poorly. Production A/B testing measures user behavior, not judged quality.

q: A streaming service wants an evaluation in which a strong foundation model scores candidate models' answers against a rubric for helpfulness and correctness, so thousands of test cases can be graded without a human reading each one. Which approach is this?
options: Manual spot checks
Keyword matching
LLM-as-a-judge evaluation
Perplexity-only scoring
explain: LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable model to grade outputs against defined criteria at scale, a pattern supported in Bedrock evaluation workflows. It trades some human nuance for coverage and speed across large test sets.

q: A translation team evaluates candidate models by comparing their output against professional reference translations, counting overlapping word sequences between the machine output and the references. Which metric are they using?
options: F1 score
BLEU
Perplexity
ROUGE
explain: BLEU measures n-gram overlap between machine translation and reference translations and is the standard automatic metric for translation quality. ROUGE is oriented to summarization recall against references, and perplexity measures prediction confidence, not overlap.

q: A news company evaluates summarization models by measuring how much of the reference summary's key content appears in each generated summary. Which metric is designed for this summarization comparison?
options: ROUGE
BLEU
AUC
RMSE
explain: ROUGE compares generated summaries with reference summaries, emphasizing recall of reference n-grams and sequences, which fits summarization evaluation. RMSE and AUC are for regression and classification, and BLEU is primarily a translation metric.

q: A research team reports that one language model has lower perplexity on its domain test set than another. What does lower perplexity indicate?
options: The model predicts the text more accurately and confidently, on average
The model generates text faster
The model has more parameters
The model is less confident and more surprised by the text
explain: Perplexity measures how surprised a model is by a sequence; lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the actual next tokens, indicating a better fit to that text distribution. It says nothing directly about speed or size.

q: Which metrics would a team MOST appropriately pair with a summarization use case and a translation use case respectively? (Choose two.)
options: Precision-recall AUC for translation
RMSE for summarization
BLEU for translation
ROUGE for summarization
explain: ROUGE is the standard reference-based metric family for summarization, and BLEU is the standard for machine translation. RMSE evaluates numeric regression error, which does not apply to generated text comparisons.

q: A manufacturer evaluates a Bedrock model for generating equipment manuals summaries. Automatic scores look strong, but plant engineers say the summaries omit safety warnings that appear in the source manuals. What is the BEST next evaluation step?
options: Increase the chunk overlap in the knowledge base
Compare perplexity across more models
Ship the model because automatic metrics are decisive
Add human evaluation with criteria that specifically check completeness on safety-critical content
explain: Automatic overlap metrics reward surface similarity and can miss whether critical content survived summarization. Targeted human evaluation on the safety criterion measures the failure that actually matters before deployment.

q: A company built a custom evaluation dataset of 800 real support questions with approved reference answers, drawn from its own tickets rather than a public benchmark. Why does this matter for model selection?
options: Public benchmarks are always fabricated
It removes the need for any human review ever
It guarantees the chosen model will never hallucinate
Scores on data that mirrors the company's actual workload predict production performance better than generic benchmarks
explain: Evaluation is only as useful as its resemblance to the real task distribution; a dataset built from actual tickets tests the phrasing, topics, and difficulty the model will face in production. It improves selection confidence but cannot guarantee perfection.

q: An agriculture platform compares two models for a crop-advice assistant. Model X scores slightly higher on automatic metrics, but costs three times more per request and is twice as slow. Which additional evaluation dimensions should inform the final choice? (Choose two.)
options: Latency under expected production load
The color of the provider's logo
Cost per request at projected volume
The number of letters in the model name
explain: Model selection is multi-dimensional: quality scores must be weighed against latency and cost at the expected scale, which is why evaluation reports quality alongside operational measures. The remaining options are irrelevant to fitness for the workload.

q: A bank is about to switch its production assistant to a newer model version. Before the switch, the team replays a fixed set of representative questions through both versions and compares answers for dropped facts and new errors. What is this practice called?
options: Distillation
Continued pretraining
Regression testing against a golden dataset
Load shedding
explain: Regression testing re-runs a stable, representative test set after any change, such as a model swap, to catch quality drops before users do. A curated set with expected answers is often called a golden dataset.

q: What is the primary purpose of evaluating a foundation model before deploying it in an application?
options: To satisfy the vector store's indexing requirements
To increase the model's parameter count
To convert the model into an embedding model
To verify the model performs acceptably on the application's actual tasks so the team can choose and configure it with evidence
explain: Evaluation provides evidence that a model meets quality requirements on the real workload, informing model choice and configuration before users are exposed. It does not change the model's architecture or satisfy storage requirements.

q: A sports media team uses LLM-as-a-judge to grade match-report drafts. Reviewers later find the judge consistently favors longer reports even when they contain errors, while concise accurate reports score lower. Which risk of automated judging does this illustrate?
options: The judge model can carry biases, such as preferring length, that distort scores unless the rubric and calibration address them
Automatic evaluation always requires provisioned throughput
LLM judges cannot read more than one report per day
Human evaluation has the identical bias in all cases
explain: A judge model inherits preferences and blind spots, including length bias, so teams must design rubrics carefully and calibrate judge scores against human judgments. The bias is a real limitation, not a throughput or capacity constraint.

q: An energy utility wants to compare a base model and a fine-tuned version for outage-report drafting. Which evaluation design gives the fairest comparison?
options: Run both models on the same held-out dataset with the same metrics and review criteria
Compare the models on different days with different reviewers and no shared rubric
Test the base model on easy questions and the fine-tuned model on hard ones
Judge the fine-tuned model only on its training examples
explain: A fair comparison holds the dataset, metrics, and criteria constant across candidates, and uses held-out data so neither model benefits from memorized examples. Varying difficulty or rubric between models makes the results uninterpretable.

q: A retailer's GenAI shopping assistant scores well on offline text metrics, but executives ask whether it actually helps the business. Which set of measures best answers the executives' question?
options: The size of the vector index
Conversion rate, average order value, and support-ticket deflection for users of the assistant
Perplexity and BLEU scores only
The number of parameters in the model
explain: Business metrics connect the application to outcomes the company values, such as conversion, basket size, and deflected support contacts. Offline text metrics measure output similarity, which does not by itself prove business value.

q: An insurer rolls out a new claims assistant to 10 percent of users while the remaining users keep the current version, then compares claim completion rates and error reports between the groups. What is this deployment evaluation method called?
options: Semantic chunking
A/B testing
Continued pretraining
Prompt caching
explain: A/B testing splits live traffic between two versions and compares measured outcomes, giving causal evidence about the new version's effect in production. It is an evaluation method, not a training or indexing technique.

q: Before launching a RAG assistant, a healthcare team assembles questions whose correct answers are known, including questions the documents cannot answer. For the unanswerable ones, the expected behavior is to decline rather than invent an answer. Which failure is this test designed to catch?
options: Hallucination, where the model fabricates an answer instead of grounding or abstaining
Slow embedding generation
High provisioned throughput cost
Excessive chunk overlap
explain: Including unanswerable questions exposes whether the system abstains or fabricates; fabrication under missing evidence is hallucination. Testing for it before launch is a core part of evaluating grounded applications.

q: A bank's evaluation shows its assistant sometimes states interest rates that appear in none of the retrieved documents. Which evaluation approach directly measures whether answers are supported by the retrieved sources?
options: Counting the tokens in each prompt
Measuring only response latency
Checking each answer's claims against the retrieved passages for groundedness
Comparing the model's parameter count to a competitor's
explain: Groundedness checking compares generated claims with the retrieved evidence, which is precisely the failure shown when stated rates appear in no source passage. Bedrock Guardrails also offers contextual grounding checks for this purpose at runtime.

q: A logistics company A/B tests two versions of its tracking assistant. Version B gets slightly lower text-quality scores but resolves 25 percent more customer chats without a human handoff. Which conclusion is MOST justified?
options: Version B must be rejected because text scores are the only valid measure
The A/B test was invalid because the versions differed
Resolution rate is unrelated to assistant quality
Version B may be the better production choice because the business outcome improved, provided error and safety measures did not degrade
explain: Model selection weighs business outcomes alongside quality and safety measures; a version that resolves more chats without worse errors can be the right choice despite marginally lower similarity scores. A/B tests exist precisely to surface such trade-offs.

q: Which of the following are appropriate business metrics for a GenAI support assistant? (Choose two.)
options: The model's vocabulary size
Average resolution time for support cases
Customer satisfaction scores for assisted conversations
The number of GPUs used in pretraining
explain: Satisfaction and resolution time measure the assistant's effect on the support operation and its customers. Vocabulary size and pretraining hardware are model internals that do not demonstrate business impact.

q: A media company plans to replace its summarization model. The team defines success in advance: ROUGE scores no worse than the current model, human reviewers rate at least 90 percent of summaries acceptable, and cost per article must fall. Why define these criteria before testing?
options: So the decision rests on pre-agreed thresholds across quality and cost rather than cherry-picked results
To avoid running any human evaluation
Because Bedrock requires criteria before any evaluation job
So the team can pick whichever metric looks best after seeing results
explain: Pre-defined acceptance criteria prevent post-hoc cherry-picking and force a balanced decision across automatic quality, human judgment, and cost. They do not remove the need for human review; they specify how much of it must pass.

q: An education provider evaluates its quiz-generation application by having teachers grade generated questions for correctness and curriculum fit, in addition to automatic checks. Which evaluation gap do the teachers fill?
options: Automatic metrics cannot judge factual correctness and pedagogical fit as reliably as domain experts
Human graders reduce inference latency
Teachers are needed to operate the vector store
Automatic checks cannot count questions
explain: Domain experts catch wrong facts and poor curriculum alignment that surface-level automatic metrics miss, which is why human evaluation complements computed scores for high-stakes content. Teachers do not affect latency or indexing.

q: A government agency's RAG system passes its accuracy tests, but testers discover it answers questions about a repealed regulation because an old PDF remains in the source bucket. Which part of the system failed, and what is the fix?
options: The embedding model failed; switch to a larger model
The temperature failed; set it to zero
The data pipeline failed; remove the outdated document and re-sync the knowledge base
The foundation model failed; fine-tune it to forget the regulation
explain: The system faithfully retrieved what it was given; the stale source document is a data curation failure. Removing the repealed PDF and re-syncing updates the index, while model-side changes cannot fix incorrect source content.

q: What does an evaluation of a RAG application typically need to assess separately? (Choose two.)
options: Retrieval quality: whether the right passages are found for a question
The font used in the source documents
The office lighting where the servers are installed
Generation quality: whether the answer uses the retrieved passages correctly and completely
explain: RAG failures can originate in retrieval or in generation, so evaluations measure both: did search surface the right evidence, and did the model answer faithfully from it. Conflating the two hides which component needs fixing.

q: A hospitality chain tests a new prompt for its booking assistant on a small share of traffic before full rollout, comparing booking completion against the current prompt. A defect would affect only the small group. Which practice is the chain following?
options: Canary-style A/B rollout with measured comparison before full deployment
Skipping staging environments
Deleting the evaluation dataset
Training a model on live traffic
explain: Releasing a change to a small traffic slice and comparing outcomes before a full rollout limits blast radius while producing real evidence. The comparison group and gradual exposure are the defining features.

q: A manufacturer evaluates an agent that orders parts. In a sandbox connected to test systems, the agent completes 92 of 100 scripted ordering scenarios correctly, including two where a supplier API is deliberately made to fail. Why run the evaluation in a sandbox with failure cases?
options: Agents should never be tested before production
Failure cases make the evaluation invalid
Sandbox results are legally binding on suppliers
Task-completion testing, including recovery from tool failures, must happen where mistakes cannot place real orders
explain: Agent evaluation measures end-to-end task success, and agents act on real systems, so testing belongs in a sandbox where errors are harmless. Injecting tool failures verifies the agent's recovery behavior, which happy-path tests cannot show.

q: Which measure best captures whether a Bedrock agent is succeeding at its job?
options: Its perplexity on general text
The number of action groups it has, regardless of use
Its end-to-end task completion rate on representative scenarios
The average length of its responses
explain: An agent exists to complete tasks, so the completion rate on realistic scenarios is the headline success measure, supplemented by correctness and safety checks. Response length and raw perplexity do not show whether the work got done.

q: A real estate platform's assistant passes offline evaluation, but after launch, user thumbs-down ratings spike on questions about new developments. The likely evaluation gap is that the offline test set did not include recent listings topics. What should the team do?
options: Remove the thumbs-down button
Lower the model's temperature and stop evaluating
Fine-tune the model on the negative ratings immediately
Expand the evaluation dataset with current, representative questions and re-test before and after fixes
explain: When production failures cluster in topics missing from the test set, the fix is a more representative evaluation dataset that covers them, so regressions become visible before release. Removing feedback hides the problem instead of measuring it.

q: A team wants a quick, repeatable signal during development for whether prompt changes help or hurt its RAG assistant, without waiting for production traffic. Which approach provides this?
options: Run the fixed evaluation question set against each prompt version and compare groundedness and correctness scores
Check only the application's uptime
Ask one employee to try the assistant once
Compare the prompts' word counts
explain: A fixed benchmark set run against every version turns prompt iteration into a measured experiment with comparable scores for correctness and grounding. Anecdotes and uptime do not measure answer quality.

q: Which statements about evaluating generative AI applications are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Once deployed, an application never needs re-evaluation
Automatic metrics are useful but often need to be complemented by human judgment for subjective or high-stakes quality
A model that wins on a public benchmark is guaranteed to be best for a company's specific workload
Evaluation should use data representative of the application's real inputs
explain: Automatic metrics are partial measures, so human review complements them, and representative test data is what makes any metric meaningful for a specific workload. Benchmark wins do not transfer automatically, and models, data, and prompts change, so evaluation is ongoing.

q: A sports league assistant must not invent player statistics. The team builds a test that asks about players who do not exist and about games that have not been played yet. What behavior should a passing system show?
options: It should state that it cannot find that information rather than fabricating it
It should answer with statistics from a different player
It should invent plausible statistics to stay helpful
It should refuse all statistics questions, including legitimate ones
explain: Probing with nonexistent entities is a standard hallucination test: a grounded system abstains when evidence is absent, while still answering legitimate questions. Substituting another player's stats is a subtler form of fabrication.

q: An energy company compares two candidate models with an A/B test. After one day, Version B leads on user satisfaction, and the product manager wants to declare victory and stop the test. What is the sound evaluation response?
options: Stop immediately, since one day of data settles the question
Only count satisfaction from the first hour
Let the test run long enough to cover varied usage and reach a reliable sample before deciding
Average the two versions' code together
explain: Short tests over-represent early, unrepresentative traffic and random noise; A/B tests need adequate duration and sample size across normal usage patterns before differences are trustworthy. Declaring victory on one day risks shipping a false winner.

q: A legal firm evaluates a contract-review assistant. Lawyers grade a sample of outputs, but their grades disagree sharply with each other on the same documents. What should the firm fix first?
options: The model's context window
The firm's document retention policy
The evaluation rubric, by defining criteria and examples clearly so reviewers apply a shared standard
The vector store's index settings
explain: Inconsistent human grades usually signal an ambiguous rubric rather than a bad model; clear criteria, anchored examples, and reviewer calibration make human evaluation reliable enough to act on. Infrastructure settings do not affect reviewer agreement.

q: Which of the following describes a business metric rather than a model metric?
options: Revenue per customer conversation handled by the assistant
ROUGE score on a summarization test set
Perplexity on a validation corpus
BLEU score against reference translations
explain: Revenue per conversation ties the application to a financial outcome, which is a business metric. ROUGE, BLEU, and perplexity are model-output metrics that describe text quality or fit, not business impact.

q: A bank wants ongoing assurance that a model update, prompt change, or knowledge base refresh has not quietly degraded its assistant. Which standing practice provides this? (Choose two.)
options: Monitoring production quality signals such as user feedback and groundedness checks
Re-running a fixed regression test set after every change and comparing results to the previous baseline
Assuming quality is unchanged if the application still starts
Deleting older evaluation results so they cannot contradict new ones
explain: Continuous assurance combines offline regression runs against a stable baseline with live production signals, catching degradation from any kind of change. Assuming stability and destroying history both eliminate the evidence needed to detect a decline.

q: A company must choose between two equally accurate models for a high-volume assistant. Evaluation shows one answers in half the time and at 40 percent lower cost per thousand requests. Which decision framework is the team applying?
options: Balancing quality with latency and cost, since all three determine production viability
Preferring whichever model was released first
Choosing the model with the longer name
Selecting on quality alone and ignoring operations
explain: Production model selection is a trade-off among quality, latency, and cost; when quality ties, the faster and cheaper model is the rational choice. Ignoring operational measures leads to systems that are accurate but unaffordable or too slow.

q: What is the main advantage of automatic evaluation metrics in a Bedrock model evaluation workflow?
options: They completely replace the need for any human judgment in all cases
They guarantee the model will behave safely in production
They score large test sets quickly and consistently, making broad comparisons practical
They reduce the cost of provisioned throughput
explain: Automatic metrics scale: thousands of outputs can be scored the same way in minutes, enabling broad model comparisons that human review alone could not cover. They complement rather than fully replace judgment, especially for subjective quality.

q: An agriculture assistant's evaluation dataset contains only questions about corn, although the product also covers wheat, soy, and livestock. The model chosen from this evaluation later underperforms on livestock questions. Which evaluation principle was violated?
options: Models must be evaluated only on their strongest topic
The test data must represent the full range of inputs the application will face in production
Evaluation datasets should be as small as possible
Livestock questions should be excluded from the product
explain: Unrepresentative test data produces misleading selection results: the winning model was only proven on corn. Evaluation sets must span the real input distribution, including every major topic the product serves.

q: A streaming service's fine-tuned model for content tagging must be re-evaluated after the company adds a new content category. Why is re-evaluation necessary even though the model itself did not change?
options: Because new categories delete the old test set
Because evaluation results only hold for the task distribution they measured; a new category is untested territory
Because fine-tuned models retrain themselves nightly
Because models lose accuracy simply as time passes
explain: Prior scores certify performance only on what was tested; a new category changes the task distribution, so the model needs fresh evaluation on examples of that category before its tags can be trusted. Nothing about the model changed on its own.

q: A team testing for hallucinations finds its assistant confidently answers questions about a product feature that was announced but never shipped, because a marketing draft sits in the knowledge base. Which fixes address the root cause? (Choose two.)
options: Add grounding instructions and checks so answers cite shipped documentation only
Raise the temperature so answers vary more
Increase the number of chunks retrieved per query
Remove or clearly exclude pre-release drafts from the indexed sources
explain: The hallucination is grounded in bad source content, so curating the corpus to exclude unreleased drafts and enforcing grounding to authoritative documents addresses the cause. More retrieval or randomness would surface the draft more often, not less.

q: A company submits a fine-tuning job for a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock using its prepared training dataset. What does the completed job produce?
options: A customized version of the model that reflects the patterns in the training data
A guardrail that blocks off-topic prompts
A report comparing the model against its competitors
A new vector store containing the training data
explain: A Bedrock fine-tuning job produces a customized model whose behavior reflects the training examples, which the company can then evaluate and deploy through provisioned throughput. It does not create a vector store, a guardrail, or a competitive evaluation report.

q: Which responsible AI principle focuses on ensuring AI systems treat all individuals and groups equitably and do not produce discriminatory outcomes?
options: Explainability
Transparency
Fairness
Robustness
explain: Fairness means AI systems should avoid bias and treat people equitably - for example, by testing models for disparate impact across demographic groups and correcting skewed training data.

q: Explainability in responsible AI refers to:
options: Reducing model size
Encrypting model outputs
Making models run faster
The ability to understand and communicate how and why an AI system made a particular decision
explain: Explainability is about making AI decisions interpretable - understanding which factors drove an outcome. It builds trust, aids debugging, and is especially important for high-stakes decisions.

q: Which practice best supports privacy in a generative AI application?
options: Storing prompts without access controls
Logging all user prompts in plaintext permanently
Sharing prompts publicly for debugging
Avoiding sending sensitive personal data to the model unnecessarily and redacting PII
explain: Privacy best practices include data minimization (only send what the model needs), PII redaction (for example with guardrails), proper access controls, and sensible data retention policies.

q: In responsible AI, "safety" primarily means:
options: Preventing physical server damage
Designing systems to prevent harmful outputs and operate reliably without causing harm
Making models open source
Increasing inference speed
explain: Safety means AI systems should avoid generating harmful content and behave reliably. It is achieved through safety testing, guardrails, content filters, and production monitoring.

q: "Controllability" in responsible AI means:
options: The model controls the user
The model trains itself without supervision
Outputs cannot be modified
Humans can oversee, direct, and intervene in AI system behavior
explain: Controllability ensures humans remain in control of AI systems - able to guide, override, or shut them down. Human-in-the-loop review for high-stakes decisions is a key example.

q: Veracity and robustness in generative AI refer to:
options: The model's ability to produce truthful, accurate outputs and perform reliably under varied or adversarial inputs
The cost efficiency of inference
The number of languages supported
The model's training speed
explain: Veracity is about truthfulness and accuracy of outputs; robustness is about reliable performance even with unexpected, noisy, or adversarial inputs. RAG, evaluation, and adversarial testing support both.

q: AI governance primarily involves:
options: Designing user interfaces
The policies, processes, and oversight structures that ensure AI is developed and used responsibly and in compliance with regulations
Choosing GPU hardware
Writing marketing copy for AI products
explain: Governance is the framework of policies, roles, risk assessments, and compliance processes that guides responsible AI development and deployment across an organization.

q: Transparency in AI systems means:
options: Hiding how the system works from users
Making all model weights public
Being open about when AI is used, its capabilities, limitations, and how decisions are made
Removing all documentation
explain: Transparency includes disclosing AI use to users, documenting capabilities and limitations (for example in model cards), and explaining how decisions are reached.

q: Which of the following reflects AWS's approach to responsible AI?
options: Bias testing is unnecessary
AI safety is solely the customer's problem
A shared commitment: AWS builds responsible AI tools and guardrails while customers implement best practices in their applications
Responsible AI requires no testing
explain: AWS embeds responsible AI into its services - for example Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock and model evaluation tools - and publishes best practices, while customers apply them through fairness testing, human oversight, and governance in their own use cases.

q: For high-stakes AI decisions (such as loan approvals), which best practice is most important?
options: Hiding the AI's involvement from applicants
Keeping a human in the loop to review and oversee AI-influenced decisions
Using the largest model regardless of evaluation
Fully automating with no human review to save time
explain: Human oversight - human-in-the-loop review - is critical for high-stakes decisions. It catches model errors and bias, ensures accountability, and supports regulatory compliance.

q: Why do responsible AI best practices recommend involving diverse perspectives in AI development?
options: To increase marketing reach
To reduce cloud costs
It is not recommended
Because diverse teams are more likely to identify biases and blind spots in data and models
explain: Diverse perspectives help surface biases in data, design choices, and evaluation that homogeneous teams might miss - directly improving fairness and safety.

q: Which prompt design practice supports responsible AI?
options: Asking the model to bypass its safety guidelines
Including sensitive customer data verbatim in prompts
Using vague, open-ended prompts for critical tasks
Giving clear, specific instructions and constraints to reduce the chance of harmful or off-topic outputs
explain: Clear, constrained prompts - specifying scope, format, and boundaries - reduce hallucinations and harmful outputs. This is a core responsible-prompting practice.

q: A team discovers their chatbot sometimes produces toxic language. Which is the most appropriate mitigation?
options: Apply content filters and guardrails, refine prompts, evaluate outputs, and monitor in production
Ignore it; users expect some toxicity
Delete all logs
Increase the temperature
explain: Harmful outputs require layered defenses: guardrails and content filters, improved prompts, safety evaluation, and ongoing production monitoring - not ignoring the problem.

q: Which data practice best supports responsible AI?
options: Using representative, high-quality data; checking for bias; and respecting data privacy and usage rights
Training on data without checking for bias or consent considerations DOMAIN 5 - SECURITY, COMPLIANCE, AND GOVERNANCE FOR AI SOLUTIONS
Never documenting data sources
Collecting as much personal data as possible without purpose
explain: Responsible data stewardship means using representative, high-quality data, checking for bias, respecting privacy and usage rights, and documenting data provenance.

q: Before launching a loan-approval model, a team wants to measure whether it treats demographic groups unfairly and understand which features drive its decisions. Which AWS tool helps with both?
options: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
AWS Artifact
explain: SageMaker Clarify detects bias in data and models and explains predictions (e.g., with SHAP values) - covering fairness and explainability.

q: Which of the following is one of AWS's eight dimensions of responsible AI?
options: Minimizing inference cost
Maximizing training speed
Vendor lock-in avoidance
Fairness
explain: Fairness - avoiding biased outcomes across groups - is one of the eight dimensions, alongside explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance, and transparency.

q: A solutions architect wants official AWS documentation describing an AI service's intended use cases and limitations before recommending it. Where should they look?
options: AWS AI Service Cards
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
Service Quotas console
AWS Pricing Calculator
explain: AWS AI Service Cards document each AI service's intended uses, limitations, and design choices - the transparency practice for responsible AI.

q: A hospital uses AI to triage patient cases but requires a clinician to review every high-risk recommendation before action is taken. This is an example of:
options: Red teaming
Data minimization
Continued pre-training
Human-in-the-loop
explain: Keeping a person reviewing AI decisions in high-stakes scenarios is human-in-the-loop - the controllability dimension of responsible AI.

q: A hiring model rejects qualified candidates from certain ZIP codes at far higher rates. The responsible-AI dimension at issue is:
options: Veracity
Fairness
Controllability
Transparency
explain: Fairness means avoiding biased outcomes across groups. ZIP codes can act as proxies for demographics, so the disparity must be measured and fixed.

q: Regulators ask a bank to show which factors drove each AI loan denial. The dimension this satisfies is:
options: Privacy
Robustness
Explainability
Safety
explain: Explainability is understanding - and being able to communicate - why a model made a specific decision, critical for regulated high-stakes use.

q: A team collects only the data fields it needs and deletes raw voice recordings after transcription. This practice is:
options: Prompt chaining
Data minimization
Red teaming
Fine-tuning
explain: Data minimization - collecting and keeping only what's necessary - reduces privacy risk and is a core responsible-AI data practice.

q: Before launch, a team deliberately tries to trick its chatbot into giving dangerous instructions, to find weaknesses. This is:
options: Data labeling
Red teaming
A/B testing
Fine-tuning
explain: Red teaming is adversarial testing: deliberately probing a model for harmful behaviors before attackers - or users - find them.

q: A company labels generated images with "Created with AI." This supports:
options: Privacy
Fairness
Transparency
Controllability
explain: Transparency means being open about when and how AI is used - disclosing AI-generated content lets people judge it appropriately.

q: A medical chatbot refuses to diagnose symptoms and instead urges the user to see a doctor. This reflects:
options: Governance
Explainability
Veracity
Safety
explain: Safety means preventing harmful outputs and misuse - refusing out-of-scope medical advice keeps the system within its safe operating bounds.

q: A team publishes a model card describing its custom model's intended uses, limitations, and evaluation results. This primarily supports:
options: Controllability
Safety
Fairness
Transparency
explain: Documenting what a model is for, its limits, and how it was evaluated is transparency - users and stakeholders can judge it appropriately.

q: A team discovers its loan model performs worse for one demographic group. The best next step is to:
options: Raise the temperature
Investigate the training data for bias, rebalance it, and re-evaluate across groups
Ignore the gap as noise
Ship it anyway
explain: Fairness is operational: measure disparities, find the data root cause, remediate, and re-evaluate not ship and hope.

q: Clever prompting gets a chatbot to reveal private customer data that was in its training set. The failing dimension is:
options: Privacy and security
Controllability
Veracity
Fairness
explain: Privacy and security means protecting training and inference data. Models must not leak private training data, and sensitive data should be minimized or filtered.

q: An AI coding assistant can suggest code changes but cannot merge them without a developer's approval. This is:
options: Red teaming
Full autonomy
Human-in-the-loop
Batch inference
explain: Human-in-the-loop keeps a person approving high-stakes AI actions - controllability in practice.

q: A bank is preparing to launch an AI credit-scoring system and wants to reduce the risk of unfair outcomes before launch. Which actions should the team take? (Choose two.)
options: Test the model on a balanced dataset that represents all applicant groups
Audit the model for bias across demographic groups before deployment
Train the model only on the bank's most profitable past customers
Remove all performance metrics so results cannot be questioned
explain: Pre-deployment bias audits reveal whether a model disadvantages any group, and testing on balanced, representative data makes those disparities visible instead of hiding them. Training only on profitable past customers narrows the data and can entrench past inequities.

q: A lender trains a model on 30 years of past lending decisions. During that period, human loan officers systematically denied applicants from certain neighborhoods. The model now reproduces those denials even though the applicants are creditworthy. Which type of bias is this?
options: Historical bias
Measurement bias
Labeling bias from annotator disagreement
Aggregation bias
explain: Historical bias exists when past societal inequities are embedded in the data itself. The training records faithfully captured discriminatory human decisions, so the model learned and reproduced them. The problem is the history in the data, not a faulty measuring instrument.

q: A retailer builds a demand-forecasting model using survey responses collected only from customers who use its mobile app. The model performs poorly for in-store shoppers, who make up most of its revenue. Which type of bias most likely caused this?
options: Selection bias
Aggregation bias
Measurement bias
Historical bias
explain: Selection bias occurs when the data collected does not represent the population the model will serve. App users were the only group sampled, so the model's view of demand reflects them and misses the in-store majority.

q: A hospital network trains a deterioration-prediction model using readings from a wearable sensor. The sensor systematically under-reads for patients with certain skin tones, so the training values for those patients are consistently wrong. Which type of bias is this?
options: Measurement bias
Survivorship bias
Selection bias
Aggregation bias
explain: Measurement bias arises when the tool or process used to collect data introduces systematic errors for some groups. Here the sensor itself records inaccurate values for a subset of patients, corrupting the data before any modeling begins.

q: A media company trains a speech-to-text model almost entirely on recordings of one regional accent. Users with other accents and non-native speakers experience far more transcription errors. Which concept best explains the performance gap?
options: Concept drift after deployment
Overfitting to the test set
Representation bias in the training data
High variance from too little training data
explain: Representation bias occurs when some groups are underrepresented in training data, so the model learns their patterns poorly. Accents that barely appear in the corpus get worse service, even though the model works well for the dominant group.

q: An agriculture company trains one crop-disease model for all its farms worldwide and applies the same thresholds everywhere. The model works in temperate regions but fails in tropical regions, where disease patterns differ. Which type of bias is this?
options: Historical bias
Selection bias
Aggregation bias
