Measurement bias
explain: Aggregation bias happens when a single model is applied to groups whose underlying patterns differ, so conclusions that hold for the combined population fail for subgroups. One global threshold ignores that tropical and temperate disease behavior is not the same.

q: A social platform hires annotators to label comments as toxic or acceptable. Annotators unfamiliar with a regional dialect repeatedly label its everyday expressions as toxic, and the moderation model learns to suppress that dialect. At which stage was bias introduced?
options: Model compression
Data labeling
Model deployment
Inference parameter tuning
explain: Bias can enter during labeling when annotators' assumptions or unfamiliarity shape the labels. The model simply learned the skewed labels it was given, so the root cause sits in the annotation stage, not in deployment or tuning.

q: An education company validates a tutoring model on students in one country, then deploys it unchanged in another country with a different curriculum and language mix. Accuracy and fairness both degrade. This is an example of bias or harm arising at which stage?
options: Labeling, because annotators disagreed
Data collection, because the original dataset was too large
Deployment to a population different from the one the model was built for
Feature engineering, because too many features were used
explain: A model validated on one population can behave unfairly when deployed to a different population whose characteristics it never encountered. Responsible practice requires re-validating performance and fairness for the new deployment context before and after launch.

q: A school district can see a vendor model's overall accuracy and its published intended uses, but teachers cannot understand why the model flagged a particular student's essay. Which capability is missing?
options: Transparency, because the vendor published documentation
Explainability, because the reasons for a specific decision are not available
Robustness, because the model fails on new inputs
Controllability, because teachers cannot shut the system down
explain: Transparency concerns openness about a system - its purpose, data, and limitations - which the vendor provided. Explainability is about the reasons behind an individual output, and that per-decision reasoning is what the teachers are missing.

q: A hospitality company adds a clear notice at the start of every chat: 'You are talking with an AI assistant, not a human agent.' Which responsible AI dimension does this practice most directly support?
options: Robustness
Controllability
Veracity
Transparency
explain: Transparency means being open about how a system works and when AI is involved. Disclosing that users are interacting with an AI, rather than letting them assume a human, is a direct transparency practice.

q: A law firm's research assistant generates court case citations that sound plausible but do not exist, and a junior lawyer nearly files one. Which responsible AI dimension is most directly failing?
options: Fairness
Privacy
Veracity
Governance
explain: Veracity concerns whether a system's outputs are truthful and factually grounded. Fabricated citations are hallucinations - fluent but false - which is a veracity failure, not a problem of equitable treatment or data protection.

q: A manufacturing company requires its visual-inspection model to keep working accurately when factory lighting changes, camera angles shift slightly, and parts arrive dusty. Which dimension is the company prioritizing?
options: Explainability
Robustness
Fairness
Transparency
explain: Robustness is a system's ability to maintain reliable performance under varied, noisy, or changing real-world conditions. Requiring consistent accuracy despite lighting, angle, and contamination changes is a robustness requirement.

q: An energy utility uses AI to recommend grid switching actions, but requires that the system never issue a recommendation that could endanger field crews or the public. Which dimension is the top priority here?
options: Veracity
Explainability
Privacy
Safety
explain: Safety means designing AI so its outputs and actions do not cause physical or other harm to people. When recommendations could endanger crews or the public, preventing harmful outputs outranks other considerations.

q: A logistics company deploys an AI route-optimization system. Dispatchers can pause it at any time, override any route it proposes, and roll it back to manual planning. Which dimension do these capabilities demonstrate?
options: Controllability
Robustness
Veracity
Transparency
explain: Controllability is the ability of humans to monitor, intervene in, override, or shut down an AI system. Pause, override, and rollback controls keep people in command of the system's behavior.

q: A retail company creates an AI review board, assigns a named executive as accountable for each AI system, documents approval criteria, and schedules periodic audits of models in production. Which dimension is the company building?
options: Explainability
Fairness
Robustness
Governance
explain: Governance covers the structures, policies, accountability, and oversight processes that steer AI across its lifecycle. Review boards, named owners, approval criteria, and audits are governance mechanisms, not properties of any single model.

q: A streaming service encrypts viewing histories and restricts which employees can access them, and it also publishes a plain-language notice explaining what viewing data it collects and why. A manager asks which part addresses privacy rather than security. Which answer is correct?
options: Neither, because privacy and security are the same dimension
The access restrictions, because privacy is only about employee permissions
The encryption, because privacy is only about encryption technology
The published notice about what is collected and why, because privacy concerns appropriate collection and use of personal data
explain: Privacy concerns whether personal data is collected, used, and shared appropriately and with proper notice and consent. Security concerns protecting that data from unauthorized access, which is what encryption and access restrictions provide. The notice is the privacy practice.

q: A bank wants to detect whether its hiring model disadvantages any applicant group. Which analysis is the most direct way to detect disparate outcomes?
options: Compare selection rates and error rates for each demographic group separately
Survey hiring managers about whether they trust the model
Measure the model's overall accuracy across all applicants combined
Check that no protected attribute was used as an input feature
explain: Disparate outcomes only become visible when results are disaggregated by group. Comparing selection and error rates per group reveals disparities that a single overall accuracy figure would hide, and excluding a protected attribute alone does not rule out proxy effects.

q: An insurer finds its claims-triage model performs poorly for rural policyholders because rural claims are rare in the training data. Which mitigation most directly addresses this?
options: Remove geographic features from the model entirely
Lower the model's confidence threshold for all claims
Deploy the model anyway and monitor complaints
Collect additional representative data from rural policyholders and rebalance the training set
explain: When a group is underrepresented, gathering more representative data and rebalancing the training set directly improves what the model learns about that group. Threshold tweaks and feature removal do not give the model the missing examples it needs.

q: A government agency plans to use AI to screen benefit applications. Before launch, an independent team reviews the training data, tests outcomes across demographic groups, and documents the findings for leadership. This process is best described as:
options: A load test
A prompt evaluation
A data migration
A bias audit
explain: A bias audit is a structured, often independent review of data, model behavior, and group-level outcomes to find and document unfairness before or after deployment. It produces the evidence leadership needs to decide whether the system is fit to launch.

q: A media company uses AI to flag potentially defamatory articles before publication. Editors review every flagged article and make the final publish decision themselves. This arrangement is an example of:
options: Human-in-the-loop review
Unsupervised learning
Model distillation
Fully automated publishing
explain: Human-in-the-loop design keeps a person in the decision process: the AI surfaces candidates, but a human reviews them and makes the consequential final call. This preserves human judgment where errors carry legal and reputational risk.

q: A recommendation system promotes videos that already have high engagement. Because promoted videos gain even more engagement, the system promotes them further, and niche creators become nearly invisible. Which phenomenon is occurring?
options: A self-reinforcing feedback loop that amplifies initial bias
Label leakage from the target variable
Concept drift from changing user tastes
Overfitting caused by too many features
explain: A feedback loop occurs when a system's outputs influence the future data it learns from. Early popularity is amplified by promotion, which generates more engagement data, which drives more promotion - progressively disadvantaging less-exposed creators.

q: A model memorizes its training data, including its noise, and performs very differently when the training set changes slightly. Its training accuracy is high but production accuracy swings widely. In bias-variance terms, this model has:
options: Low bias and low variance
High bias and low variance
High bias from underfitting
High variance from overfitting
explain: High variance means a model's predictions change substantially with small changes in training data - the signature of overfitting, where the model fits noise as well as signal. High training accuracy paired with unstable production performance fits this pattern.

q: A real estate firm uses a very simple linear model to price homes. It performs consistently but systematically undervalues renovated homes and overvalues homes near new transit lines, missing patterns a richer model would capture. This model most likely suffers from:
options: High variance from overfitting
Data leakage
High bias from underfitting
Selection bias in deployment
explain: High bias means a model's simplifying assumptions prevent it from capturing the true patterns in the data, producing systematic errors - underfitting. Consistent but predictably wrong predictions in identifiable situations are the classic symptom.

q: A language technology company adds training examples covering more dialects, age groups, and speech patterns. Both overall accuracy and accuracy for previously underserved groups improve. This result best illustrates that:
options: Dataset diversity can improve both performance and fairness
Fairness and accuracy can never improve together
Only dataset size matters, not who is represented
More data always reduces fairness
explain: Diverse, representative data teaches the model patterns for all the groups it will serve, raising overall quality while closing group-level gaps. Fairness work and performance work reinforce each other when the root problem is missing representation.

q: A sports analytics team discovers that 15 percent of its player-tracking records were labeled with the wrong positions by a rushed annotation vendor. Model quality drops sharply. Which lesson does this best illustrate?
options: Only the choice of algorithm affects model quality
Label errors only matter for unsupervised models
Poor-quality labeled data degrades the model trained on it, regardless of dataset size
Larger datasets eliminate the need for label quality
explain: Models learn the labels they are given, so systematic labeling errors teach wrong patterns - garbage in, garbage out. Volume cannot compensate for corrupted ground truth, which is why label quality assurance is a core data practice.

q: A bank's customer service voice assistant can only be operated by speaking, with no text, captions, or screen-reader support. Deaf customers cannot use it. Which human-centered design principle is being violated?
options: Veracity
Accessibility and inclusivity
Controllability
Robustness
explain: Accessible, inclusive design means people with different abilities can use the system. A voice-only interface with no alternative modality excludes users who cannot hear or speak, so the design fails the accessibility dimension of human-centered AI.

q: Before finalizing an AI benefits-eligibility assistant, a government team invites people with disabilities, non-native speakers, and elderly residents to test it and revises the design based on their feedback. This practice best reflects:
options: Adversarial testing
Inclusive, human-centered design with affected users involved
Automated hyperparameter tuning
Model compression for cost savings
explain: Human-centered design involves the people affected by a system in its design and evaluation. Testing with the diverse users who must actually use the assistant - and changing the design based on what they find - surfaces barriers that internal testing would miss.

q: A regulated lender must tell rejected applicants the specific reasons for each denial, but its deep learning model cannot produce reasons a compliance officer can explain. This problem is known as:
options: Concept drift in the applicant population
Prompt injection by applicants
The black-box problem, where a model's internal reasoning is not interpretable
A data residency violation
explain: The black-box problem describes models whose decision process cannot be inspected or explained in human terms. In regulated industries that must justify individual decisions, this opacity can make an otherwise accurate model unusable.

q: A hiring team is auditing its resume-screening pipeline for sources of bias. Which factors should the team investigate as potential sources of bias? (Choose two.)
options: Historical hiring decisions that favored certain universities and are reflected in the training data
A training sample drawn mostly from one region, which underrepresents qualified candidates elsewhere
The physical size of the GPU cluster used for training
The font used in the candidate-facing careers page
explain: Bias commonly enters through the data itself: historical decisions can encode past preferences, and a geographically narrow sample underrepresents other qualified candidates. Hardware size and page typography do not shape what the model learns about candidates.

q: An insurance company routes AI claim decisions through human oversight. Which practices provide meaningful human oversight of high-impact decisions? (Choose two.)
options: Allowing adjusters to override the AI recommendation when their investigation disagrees
Requiring the AI to re-run the same claim until it agrees with itself
Sending low-confidence and high-value cases to a human adjuster for a final decision
Hiding the AI recommendation from adjusters so they cannot be influenced
explain: Meaningful oversight means humans can change outcomes: override authority lets adjusters correct the model, and routing uncertain or high-stakes cases to people concentrates human judgment where errors cost most. Concealing recommendations removes the information oversight needs.

q: Different stakeholders are asking a bank about its AI lending system. Which requests are requests for explainability? (Choose two.)
options: A journalist asks how many employees work in the bank's AI division
A loan officer asks which applicant attributes pushed a specific borderline application toward approval
An auditor asks for the bank's data retention schedule
A rejected applicant asks which factors most influenced the decision on their application
explain: Explainability answers why a model produced a particular output - which factors drove an individual decision. Retention schedules and staffing counts are general organizational information, not explanations of model behavior.

q: A healthcare system uses AI to prioritize patients for a preventive screening program. Overall sensitivity looks strong, but the team suspects one ethnic group is being missed more often. Which evaluation approach will reveal whether that is happening?
options: Report a single blended F1 score for the whole population
Compute performance metrics separately for each demographic group and compare them
Remove demographic data from all evaluation reports
Track only the total number of patients screened each month
explain: Fairness problems hide inside population averages. Disaggregating metrics such as sensitivity and false-negative rates by group exposes whether a specific group is systematically missed, which blended scores cannot show.

q: A lender removes applicants' race and gender from its model inputs, yet approval gaps persist because ZIP code and surname act as stand-ins for those attributes. Which lesson does this illustrate?
options: ZIP code should always be the primary lending feature
Removing protected attributes guarantees fairness
Proxy variables can carry protected-attribute information, so fairness requires outcome testing, not just input removal
Fairness problems disappear once a model reaches high accuracy
explain: Features correlated with protected attributes can act as proxies and reproduce disparities even when the protected fields are removed. Detecting this requires measuring outcomes by group and addressing the proxies, not assuming input removal is sufficient.

q: Two logistics hubs use the same fatigue-detection wearables, but one hub's devices were never recalibrated after a firmware update and now over-report fatigue events. A model trained on the combined data treats that hub's workers unfairly. The root cause is:
options: Historical bias, because past managers discriminated
Aggregation bias, because a single model was used worldwide
Selection bias, because workers volunteered for the study
Measurement bias, because one site's instruments systematically recorded different values
explain: When instruments at one site systematically record values differently from instruments elsewhere, the data itself is distorted in a group-specific way - measurement bias. The unfairness traces to inconsistent data generation, not to the model's structure or history.

q: An education platform uses a single reading-level model for all learners. It systematically misjudges reading ability for students learning in a second language, whose error patterns differ from native speakers. Which bias type best fits?
options: Measurement bias from faulty sensors
Labeling bias from annotator fatigue
Aggregation bias from applying one model to groups with different patterns
Historical bias from outdated textbooks
explain: Aggregation bias arises when one model is expected to serve groups whose data patterns genuinely differ, so group-specific behavior is averaged away. Second-language readers are being judged by patterns learned largely from a different population.

q: A team optimizes its fraud model purely for overall accuracy. Because fraudulent patterns differ by customer segment, the model ends up flagging one segment's legitimate purchases at several times the rate of others, while overall accuracy still improves. Where was bias introduced?
options: During labeling, by the annotation guidelines
During model design, by choosing a single overall objective that hides subgroup harm
During deployment, by the cloud region selected
During data collection, by the payment processor
explain: Design choices shape fairness: optimizing only a global metric lets subgroup harm grow invisibly as long as the average improves. Responsible model design evaluates the objective and its effects per segment before deployment.

q: A manufacturer trains a quality-prediction model at its domestic plants, then deploys it at a new overseas plant with different suppliers, materials, and operating conditions without any local validation. Defect predictions become unreliable and unfairly penalize the new plant's shifts. What should the company have done?
options: Removed the new plant's data from all reports
Validated the model on representative local data before relying on it at the new site
Trained the original model for more epochs
Increased the model's temperature setting
explain: Deploying a model into a materially different environment without validation is a deployment-stage failure. Local representative data would have revealed the mismatch and allowed recalibration before the model's outputs affected people's evaluations.

q: An insurer's AI recommends denying a large disability claim. Company policy requires a licensed claims examiner to review the evidence and make the final denial decision personally. This policy best demonstrates:
options: Human oversight of a high-impact decision
Automated decision-making
Data minimization
Model transparency
explain: High-impact decisions - those affecting income, health, housing, or legal standing - warrant human oversight so a qualified person owns the final call and can catch model errors. The examiner's personal review is oversight, not mere disclosure.

q: A streaming service lets viewers rate AI-generated summaries with thumbs up or down, reviews those signals weekly, and uses them to correct recurring summary errors. Which human-centered practice is this?
options: A feedback loop that lets users improve the system over time
Provisioned throughput management
Differential privacy
Adversarial red teaming
explain: Feedback loops collect user signals about system quality and feed them back into improvement. Regular review of viewer ratings turns everyday use into ongoing correction, a hallmark of human-centered operation after launch.

q: A clinician using an AI diagnostic aid asks why the system rated a case as high risk. Which capability would best answer the clinician?
options: A copy of the model's source code
The model's average accuracy on the full test set
A list of the model's total parameter count
Feature attribution showing which patient factors contributed most to this prediction, such as from Amazon SageMaker Clarify
explain: Clinicians need case-level explanations: feature attribution methods, surfaced by tools such as SageMaker Clarify, show which inputs drove a specific prediction. Global accuracy and parameter counts say nothing about why this patient was flagged.

q: A company publishes its AI system's intended uses, training data sources, known limitations, and evaluation results, but cannot say why the system made any one specific recommendation. Which statement is accurate?
options: The system has explainability but not transparency
The system has neither transparency nor explainability
Publishing limitations makes individual decisions explainable
The system has transparency, but its individual decisions still lack explainability
explain: Transparency is openness about the system as a whole - purpose, data, limitations, and evaluations - which the company achieved. Explainability is about the rationale for a particular output, and that remains missing despite the good documentation.

q: A legal research product grounds every AI-generated summary in retrieved source documents and blocks answers that its grounding check cannot support. The primary responsible AI goal is to improve:
options: Privacy
Veracity
Fairness
Controllability
explain: Grounding generation in retrieved sources and rejecting unsupported claims directly targets veracity - the factual truthfulness of outputs. It reduces hallucinated content rather than changing who the system treats fairly or who can access data.

q: A food-delivery platform's address-parsing model must handle typos, abbreviations, missing apartment numbers, and addresses dictated in noisy environments without failing. The team tests it against deliberately messy inputs. Which dimension are they validating?
options: Transparency of the training process
Fairness across demographic groups
Governance of the model lifecycle
Robustness to imperfect, real-world inputs
explain: Robustness is reliable performance despite noisy, incomplete, or perturbed inputs. Testing with messy addresses confirms the model degrades gracefully in real conditions instead of only working on clean textbook data.

q: After launch, a bank's governance process requires quarterly checks of its credit model for performance drift and for widening approval gaps between groups, with retraining triggered when thresholds are crossed. This is an example of:
options: Prompt engineering
Data anonymization
Ongoing governance and monitoring across the AI lifecycle
One-time pre-launch testing
explain: Governance does not end at deployment. Scheduled monitoring for drift and fairness, with defined retraining triggers, keeps a production system accountable as data and populations change over time.

q: A retail app's AI shopping assistant requests the customer's precise location only when the customer asks for nearby store stock, and does not collect it at any other time. Which privacy practice is this?
options: Indefinite data retention
Data minimization - collecting only the personal data needed for the requested purpose
Data replication across regions
Open data publishing
explain: Data minimization limits collection to what a specific purpose requires, in scope and in timing. Requesting precise location only when the feature genuinely needs it respects privacy while still delivering the service.

q: Warehouse robots guided by AI move inventory near human workers. Each robot has a prominent stop button, and supervisors can halt the whole fleet from a console. These features primarily support which dimension?
options: Explainability
Veracity
Controllability
Transparency
explain: Controllability means humans can intervene in or stop an AI-driven system when needed. Physical stop buttons and a fleet-wide halt give workers immediate control, which also supports safety but is fundamentally about human command of the system.

q: A streaming platform's companion chatbot for teenagers is configured with guardrails that refuse self-harm encouragement, redirect users in crisis to support resources, and escalate concerning conversations for human review. Which dimension do these guardrails primarily serve?
options: Safety
Privacy
Fairness
Robustness
explain: Safety is about preventing the system from causing or enabling harm to users. Content guardrails, crisis redirection, and human escalation for a vulnerable audience are safety controls first and foremost.

q: A data science team doubles its training set size and finds the model's predictions become more stable across retraining runs, though a systematic error for one product category remains. What does this illustrate about the bias-variance tradeoff?
options: More data eliminated both bias and variance
More data increases variance in all cases
More data mainly reduces variance; systematic bias errors persist until the model's assumptions or data representation change
Dataset size has no relationship to variance
explain: Larger training sets generally make models more consistent - lower variance - because estimates rely on more evidence. Systematic bias, such as a consistently mis-modeled category, is not fixed by volume alone and needs different features, a richer model, or better representation.

q: A startup expands its training data tenfold by scraping records that all come from the same narrow customer segment. Leadership expects fairness to improve automatically because the dataset is bigger. Why is that expectation wrong?
options: Scraped data is always illegal to use
Fairness depends only on the model's learning rate
Bigger datasets always make fairness worse
Quantity without diversity reinforces the same narrow patterns, so underrepresented groups remain poorly served
explain: Dataset quantity and dataset diversity are different properties. Ten times more of the same segment teaches the same patterns more strongly; groups absent from the data gain nothing. Fairness improves when coverage broadens, not merely when volume grows.

q: A city government designing an AI assistant for public services holds design workshops with residents from the neighborhoods the service will affect, including people who have previously been underserved, before any model is built. This is an example of:
options: Automated bias auditing
Participatory, human-centered design that includes affected communities early
Post-deployment incident response
Model quantization for edge devices
explain: Human-centered design brings affected people into the process early, when their input can still shape goals and requirements. Consulting underserved communities before building prevents designing around assumptions that exclude them.

q: A government AI information portal provides text alternatives for all spoken content, full keyboard navigation, and compatibility with screen readers. Which responsible AI consideration is being addressed?
options: Cost optimization of inference
Accessibility and inclusivity of the AI system
Data residency compliance
Model robustness under load
explain: Accessibility ensures people using assistive technologies or alternative modalities can use the system on equal terms. Text alternatives, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support are concrete accessibility provisions for an AI service.

q: A hospital wants to check whether its screening model misses cancers at different rates for different patient groups. Which metrics should the team compare across groups? (Choose two.)
options: False negative rates for each patient group
The number of GPUs used during training
Recall (sensitivity) computed separately for each patient group
The hospital's total annual IT budget
explain: Missed cancers are false negatives, so comparing false negative rates and recall per group reveals whether the model protects groups equally. Budget and hardware figures have no bearing on group-level clinical performance.

q: An agriculture firm's plant-disease model was trained on images from one region in one season and fails for smallholder farmers elsewhere. Which mitigation best addresses the fairness and performance problem?
options: Restrict the product to the original region permanently
Increase image resolution in the original dataset only
Lower the price for farmers in other regions
Collect training images across regions, seasons, crop varieties, and camera types, then re-evaluate per group
explain: The failure comes from narrow training coverage. Gathering diverse data across the conditions and populations the model must serve - and verifying performance per group afterward - is the mitigation that fixes both accuracy and equity.

q: Which of the following are dimensions of responsible AI as described by AWS? (Choose three.)
options: Privacy and security
Explainability
Maximizing engagement at any cost
Fairness
explain: Fairness, explainability, and privacy and security are among AWS's responsible AI dimensions, alongside transparency, safety, veracity and robustness, controllability, and governance. Maximizing engagement regardless of consequences is a business tactic, not a responsible AI dimension.

q: Which statements about the bias-variance tradeoff are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Reducing variance can involve using more training data or a simpler model
Bias and variance are both eliminated by choosing the largest available model
A model with high bias typically fits the training data too closely, including its noise
Increasing model complexity generally reduces bias but can increase variance
explain: More complex models can capture truer patterns (lower bias) but react more to training-data quirks (higher variance); simpler models and more training data are standard variance reducers. Fitting noise describes high variance, not high bias, and no model size eliminates both error sources.

q: Six months after launch, a bank's routine fairness monitoring shows its small-business loan model has begun denying applicants from one region at sharply higher rates, traced to a proxy feature whose meaning shifted after a data vendor change. What is the MOST responsible course of action?
options: Wait for the annual model review, since the model was fair at launch
Increase marketing spend in the affected region to offset the denials
Escalate through governance: increase human review of affected decisions, investigate and remediate the proxy feature, and re-audit outcomes before returning to normal operation
Quietly raise approval thresholds documentation so the gap is less visible
explain: Fairness at launch does not guarantee fairness later; drift and vendor changes can reintroduce bias through proxies. Responsible governance responds promptly - protecting applicants with human review, fixing the root cause, and verifying with a fresh audit - rather than concealing or deferring the problem.

q: A bank is preparing historical loan application data to train a credit risk model in Amazon SageMaker AI. Before training begins, the team wants to check whether the dataset itself is skewed against a demographic group. Which SageMaker Clarify analysis should the team run?
options: A pre-training bias analysis in SageMaker Clarify on the dataset and label distribution
A SageMaker Data Wrangler data quality report on missing values only
A SageMaker Autopilot candidate exploration job
A post-training model evaluation job in SageMaker Model Monitor
explain: SageMaker Clarify can analyze a dataset before training to measure class imbalance and differences in label distribution across demographic groups, which reveals bias present in the data itself. Model Monitor tracks a deployed model, so it cannot assess the raw training dataset before a model exists.

q: An insurance company uses a SageMaker model to price policies. Underwriters ask which input factors most influence the model's predictions overall so they can sanity-check its behavior. Which Clarify capability answers this question?
options: A drift baseline generated by SageMaker Model Monitor
A confusion matrix from a SageMaker evaluation job
Data labeling consensus scores from SageMaker Ground Truth
Feature importance scores computed with SHAP values
explain: SageMaker Clarify uses SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to compute feature importance, showing how much each feature contributes to predictions both globally and for individual cases. A confusion matrix measures classification correctness, not which features drive the model's decisions.

q: A retail company is planning the lifecycle of a new demand forecasting model built in SageMaker AI. At which points should the team run SageMaker Clarify to support responsible AI?
options: On the training data before training, on the trained model before deployment, and periodically on the deployed model
Only after the model is retired, as part of a final audit
Only when a customer files a complaint about a prediction
Only once, immediately before the first production deployment
explain: Bias and explainability checks are not a one-time gate. Clarify supports pre-training data bias analysis, post-training bias and explainability analysis before deployment, and scheduled bias and feature-attribution drift monitoring after deployment, so problems are caught at each stage.

q: After training, a healthcare provider runs SageMaker Clarify on a readmission prediction model and finds that positive predictions are distributed very unevenly across age groups compared with the actual outcomes. What has Clarify most directly detected?
options: Training data leakage between the training and test sets
Overfitting of the model to the training set
Post-training bias, shown by a disparity in predicted outcomes across demographic groups
Concept drift in the production data feed
explain: Post-training bias metrics in Clarify compare the model's predicted outcomes across groups, for example with measures of disparate impact and differences in positive prediction rates. A large gap between groups signals the trained model itself treats groups unevenly, separate from raw accuracy problems such as overfitting.

q: A manufacturing firm wants to adopt Amazon SageMaker Clarify for a quality inspection model. Which TWO capabilities does Clarify provide? (Choose two.)
options: Automatic generation of synthetic training images
Detection of bias in training data and in model predictions
Explainability reports based on feature attribution
Automatic retraining of models when accuracy drops
explain: SageMaker Clarify provides bias detection for both datasets and trained models, and explainability through feature attribution methods such as SHAP. It does not generate training data, retrain models automatically, or translate outputs; those belong to other services and pipeline steps.

q: A legal firm uses a SageMaker model to prioritize document review. For one specific matter, a partner asks why a single document was scored as high priority. Which Clarify output best answers this per-decision question?
options: The model's overall accuracy on the validation set
Local SHAP values showing how each feature pushed this individual prediction up or down
The global feature importance ranking for the entire model
The bias report comparing outcomes across client industries
explain: Local explanations attribute a single prediction to its input features, and Clarify's SHAP-based local values show exactly how each feature contributed to that one document's score. Global importance describes average behavior across all predictions and cannot explain why this particular document was prioritized.

q: An education platform finds its SageMaker course recommendation model favors students from a few large school districts. Clarify shows the training data heavily over-represents those districts, while the trained model's own metrics look consistent once data composition is accounted for. Where does the primary problem lie?
options: A missing encryption key for the training bucket
Insufficient provisioned throughput for the endpoint
A defective inference endpoint configuration
Bias in the training data rather than in the model's learned behavior alone
explain: Clarify separates pre-training data bias from post-training model bias. When the dataset itself over-represents some groups, the model learns from a skewed picture of the population, so the fix starts with the data: collect or rebalance representative examples rather than only tuning the algorithm.

q: A bank's ML team wants bias and explainability checks to run automatically every time its SageMaker pipeline retrains the fraud model, and wants an alert if bias metrics drift after deployment. Which combination meets these requirements?
options: Manual Clarify jobs run from a notebook whenever an engineer remembers
Amazon Macie scans of the training bucket combined with AWS Config rules
SageMaker Canvas data quality checks combined with Amazon CloudWatch alarms on CPU use
Clarify processing steps in SageMaker Pipelines for retraining runs, plus Clarify bias and feature-attribution drift monitoring through SageMaker Model Monitor
explain: Clarify integrates with SageMaker Pipelines so bias and explainability jobs run as governed steps on every retraining, and Model Monitor can schedule Clarify bias drift and feature attribution drift checks on a live endpoint. Manual notebook runs are inconsistent, and Macie or CPU alarms do not measure bias at all.

q: What is the primary purpose of Amazon SageMaker Clarify?
options: To label training data using human workforces
To detect bias and explain model predictions throughout the ML lifecycle
To host models on serverless inference endpoints
To convert tabular data into images for training
explain: SageMaker Clarify exists to improve model quality through bias detection and explainability, from dataset analysis before training through monitoring after deployment. Data labeling is SageMaker Ground Truth, and hosting is handled by SageMaker inference options, not Clarify.

q: A media company trains a SageMaker model to moderate user comments. Which TWO Clarify practices help the team keep the model fair after it goes live? (Choose two.)
options: Raising the model's decision threshold until complaints stop
Comparing feature attribution over time to spot shifts in what drives decisions
Scheduling recurring post-training bias checks on production predictions
Deleting all monitoring data so outcomes cannot be reviewed later
explain: Responsible operation means measuring fairness continuously: scheduled Clarify bias checks on live predictions and feature attribution drift analysis show whether group outcomes or decision drivers are shifting. Deleting monitoring data, hiding smaller groups, or blindly moving thresholds removes the evidence needed to manage fairness.

q: A hospitality company launches a customer support chatbot on Amazon Bedrock. The chatbot occasionally echoes insulting language back at guests. Which Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock feature should the team configure to block this category of content in both prompts and responses?
options: Denied topics for the chatbot's subject areas
Provisioned throughput for the underlying model
Content filters for categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, and violence
Prompt templates in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management
explain: Guardrails content filters evaluate user inputs and model responses against harmful categories including hate, insults, sexual content, violence, and misconduct, and can block content above configured thresholds. Denied topics block subject areas, which is a different control from category-based harmful content filtering.

q: A bank's Bedrock-powered assistant answers account questions. Compliance requires that it never provide personalized investment advice, even though the underlying model is capable of it. Which guardrail feature enforces this boundary?
options: Denied topics defined with a name, definition, and sample phrases
Contextual grounding checks
Word filters with a custom word list
Sensitive information filters for PII
explain: Denied topics let you define a topic, describe it in natural language, and supply sample phrases; the guardrail then blocks user inputs and responses that fall into that topic regardless of wording. Word filters only match literal terms, so they cannot reliably stop a whole subject area expressed many different ways.

q: A retailer's Bedrock chatbot must never mention a specific list of competitor brand names or display profanity that customers type into it. Which guardrail feature is the most precise fit for these literal strings?
options: Fine-tuning the model to forget the brand names
Word filters using exact words and phrases to block
Managed content filters set to high strength
Contextual grounding checks with a relevance threshold
explain: Word filters block exact configured words and phrases, which is the precise tool for profanity lists and specific names that must never appear. Content filters judge harmful categories rather than literal strings, and grounding checks compare answers against a source rather than screening vocabulary.

q: A healthcare support assistant built on Amazon Bedrock sometimes includes patients' phone numbers and email addresses from case notes in its replies. The team must prevent this while still answering the question. Which guardrail configuration should they use?
options: Lower the model temperature so responses become more predictable
Add the phone numbers to a denied topics definition
Block the entire response whenever any digit appears in it
Configure sensitive information filters to detect PII and redact or mask it in inputs and outputs
explain: Guardrails sensitive information filters detect PII such as names, email addresses, and phone numbers using built-in types and custom regex, and can mask or redact them while allowing the rest of the answer through. Blocking every response containing a digit would break legitimate answers, and temperature has no effect on PII exposure.

q: An insurance company grounds its Bedrock chatbot in policy documents using a knowledge base, but the chatbot still invents coverage details that are not in the retrieved text. Which guardrail feature directly targets this failure?
options: A denied topic for insurance questions
Word filters listing the invented product names
Higher content filter strength for the violence category
Contextual grounding checks that compare each response against the retrieved source and a relevance threshold
explain: Contextual grounding checks score whether a response is grounded in the provided source material and whether it is relevant to the query, blocking or flagging answers that fall below the configured thresholds. This is the guardrail feature designed to reduce hallucinations in RAG-style applications; vocabulary filters cannot judge factual support.

q: A government agency tests its Bedrock assistant and finds that crafted user prompts can trick it into ignoring its instructions and revealing its system prompt. Which guardrail content category is designed to detect this behavior?
options: Prompt attacks within the misconduct and prompt attack filtering of content filters
Sexual content filtering
PII redaction with custom regex patterns
Denied topics
explain: Guardrails content filters include protection against prompt attacks and jailbreak-style inputs that try to override the application's instructions. This is distinct from PII redaction, which hides sensitive data, and denied topics, which block whole subject areas rather than manipulation attempts.

q: A logistics company is configuring Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock for a driver-facing assistant. Which TWO statements about guardrails are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Guardrails evaluate both user inputs and model outputs against the configured policies
A guardrail works only with one specific foundation model and must be rebuilt for every other model
The same guardrail version can be applied consistently across models, agents, and knowledge bases
Guardrails replace the need to test the application before launch
explain: A guardrail is a reusable, versioned policy layer: it can be attached to model invocation, Amazon Bedrock Agents, and Knowledge Bases, and it screens both what goes into the model and what comes out. It complements rather than replaces application testing, and it is model-agnostic rather than tied to one model.

q: An energy company has three Bedrock applications: a direct model invocation API, an agent that books service visits, and a knowledge base answering safety questions. How can the company apply one consistent safety policy to all three?
options: Fine-tune three separate models with safety examples
Write separate prompt instructions in each application and hope they stay in sync
Attach the same published guardrail version to the model calls, the agent, and the knowledge base
Rely on IAM policies to filter harmful response text
explain: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock are designed for consistent enforcement: a single guardrail version can be associated with model invocation, Agents, and Knowledge Bases so every path applies identical filters. IAM controls who can call services, not the content of responses, and per-app prompt text drifts out of sync.

q: A media streaming company finds its Bedrock guardrail blocks too many harmless movie discussions because a content filter is set aggressively, while a stricter posture is still required for a children's profile. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Lower the model's max tokens so fewer risky words can appear
Remove all content filters so nothing legitimate is blocked
Use one guardrail for every audience and accept the false positives
Tune filter strengths per category and use separate guardrail configurations matched to each audience's risk level
explain: Guardrail content filters have configurable strengths per category, and different applications or audiences can use different guardrail versions. Tuning strengths and separating configurations balances protection against over-blocking, instead of the all-or-nothing choice of removing filters entirely.

q: A bank wants a Bedrock guardrail to stop account numbers from appearing in chatbot output, but a masked form such as a partial account reference is acceptable for confirming identity. Which behavior should the team configure?
options: A word filter containing every possible account number
A denied topic covering all banking conversations
Sensitive information filters set to mask PII in responses rather than block the whole response
Content filters for the misconduct category
explain: Guardrails sensitive information filters can anonymize or mask detected PII in model responses, so the user sees a redacted form while the conversation continues. Blocking the whole response is the alternative action when masking is not acceptable, and enumerating every account number in a word list is impossible in practice.

q: A solutions architect is evaluating an AWS AI service for a government benefits application and needs the vendor's own description of the service's intended use cases, how it performs across different groups, and its limitations. Where should the architect look?
options: AWS AI Service Cards published by AWS
Amazon Bedrock model evaluation reports
The model's SageMaker Model Card in the customer's account
The service's pricing page
explain: AWS AI Service Cards are transparency documentation AWS publishes for its AI services, covering intended use cases, design choices, performance across groups, and known limitations. A SageMaker Model Card documents a customer's own model, not an AWS-managed service.

q: A bank's risk team requires documentation for a custom credit model trained in SageMaker before it can approve deployment. Which artifact should the ML team produce, and what belongs in it?
options: A SageMaker Model Card covering intended uses, risk ratings, training details, and evaluation results
An AWS AI Service Card written by the bank for its own model
A CloudTrail log export showing who trained the model
A Bedrock guardrail configuration describing blocked topics
explain: SageMaker Model Cards document a customer's own model: intended use cases and out-of-scope uses, risk rating, factors affecting performance, training and evaluation details, and ethical considerations. AI Service Cards are published by AWS for AWS services, so a bank cannot issue one for its own model.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes AWS AI Service Cards from SageMaker Model Cards?
options: Both artifacts document the same models and differ only in file format
Model Cards apply only to Amazon Bedrock foundation models
Service Cards are generated automatically for every customer model, while Model Cards are written by AWS
Service Cards document AWS's own AI services and are published by AWS, while Model Cards document a specific customer-built model and are created by the model owner
explain: The two artifacts sit at different layers: AWS publishes AI Service Cards to be transparent about its managed AI services, while SageMaker Model Cards are created by teams to document their own trained models, including intended use, risks, and evaluation results. Model Cards are not limited to Bedrock models.

q: A healthcare company is documenting a SageMaker triage model in a Model Card. Which TWO elements belong in a well-formed Model Card? (Choose two.)
options: The AWS account root user password used to train the model
The model's intended use cases and uses that are out of scope
The personal email addresses of every patient in the training set
Evaluation results, including performance broken down by relevant groups
explain: Model Cards record intended and out-of-scope uses, training information, and evaluation results including performance across groups, plus risks and ethical considerations. They must never contain patient PII or credentials, and honest documentation acknowledges error rather than guaranteeing perfection.

q: A retail company reads in a Model Card that a returns-fraud model was evaluated only on data from one region and carries a medium risk rating with known performance gaps for new product categories. How should the company use this information?
options: Treat the card as marketing material and ignore the limitations section
Use the documented limitations and risk rating to scope deployment, add human review for weak areas, and expand evaluation before wider rollout
Deploy the model nationally without changes because a Model Card exists
Delete the Model Card so auditors do not see the gaps
explain: Transparency artifacts only help if teams act on them: documented limitations and risk ratings should drive deployment scope, compensating controls such as human review, and further evaluation. The card's existence alone does not make a model safe to deploy beyond its validated conditions.

q: What is an AWS AI Service Card?
options: A certification developers earn for responsible AI
A dashboard showing real-time inference latency for a service
A credit product AWS offers to AI startups
A transparency document AWS publishes describing an AI service's intended uses, design, performance characteristics, and limitations
explain: AWS AI Service Cards are part of AWS's responsible AI transparency effort: they explain what an AI service is designed for, how it was built and tested, how it performs for different groups, and where its limitations lie, so customers can decide whether it fits their use case.

q: An agriculture cooperative deploys a SageMaker yield prediction model built by a vendor. Auditors ask for a single shareable record of what the model is for, how it was trained, and how well it performs. Which capability should the cooperative request?
options: A SageMaker Model Card, which can be exported and shared as documentation of the model
A Bedrock guardrail with the cooperative's policies attached
A CloudWatch dashboard of endpoint invocations
A Macie report on the training bucket contents
explain: SageMaker Model Cards consolidate a model's purpose, ownership, training details, and evaluation results into a standard document that can be exported, for example as a PDF, for auditors and stakeholders. Operational dashboards and security scans do not describe the model's intent or performance.

q: A sports analytics team documents in its Model Card that a player injury-risk model's accuracy drops sharply for athletes under 21 because they were scarce in training data. A club wants to use the model mainly for its youth academy. What is the responsible decision?
options: Proceed, because the limitation was at least documented
Hide the limitation from the club to avoid losing the contract
Do not use the model for the youth population until it is retrained and evaluated on representative data for that group
Compensate by lowering the prediction threshold for young athletes
explain: A documented performance gap for a specific group means the model is not validated for that group. Responsible use requires representative data and fresh evaluation for under-21 athletes before deployment; documenting a known weakness does not transfer the risk to the customer or excuse using the model anyway.

q: An education company's tutoring chatbot must refuse to discuss a prohibited subject, but students keep reaching it by rephrasing the request with synonyms and indirect wording. Literal keyword blocking keeps failing. Which guardrail approach handles this?
options: A denied topic, because the guardrail judges the meaning of the request against the topic definition rather than matching exact words
A longer word filter list containing every synonym the team can think of
Raising the content filter strength for the sexual category
Removing the topic from the system prompt so the model forgets it
explain: Denied topics use a natural-language definition and sample phrases, so the guardrail can recognize the subject even when it is phrased indirectly. Word filters match literal strings only, which is why synonym-based evasion defeats them no matter how long the list grows.

q: A hospitality group uses Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock so its assistant can answer questions from guest policy documents. The group wants the same content and PII protections applied to answers generated from retrieved documents. What should the team do?
options: Guardrails cannot be used with knowledge bases, so the team must filter answers in custom code
Associate a guardrail with the knowledge base query so retrieved content and generated responses are evaluated against the configured policies
Disable retrieval for any document that mentions a guest name
Export the documents and manually review every possible answer in advance
explain: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock can be applied to Knowledge Bases, evaluating queries and generated responses so content filters, denied topics, and sensitive information protections also cover RAG answers. Manual pre-review of every possible answer is not feasible for generative responses.

q: A sports media app wants fans to see a polite, consistent explanation such as a standard refusal message whenever its Bedrock guardrail blocks a response, instead of an empty reply. Which guardrail capability provides this?
options: Increasing provisioned throughput for the model
Adding more sample phrases to a denied topic
Enabling model invocation logging in Amazon Bedrock
Configuring the blocked messaging shown to users when the guardrail intervenes
explain: When a guardrail blocks input or output, the application can return a configurable blocked message so users get a clear, consistent explanation rather than silence or a raw error. Logging and throughput affect operations, not what the user sees when content is blocked.

q: An agriculture cooperative trains a SageMaker pest detection model mostly on images from large farms in one climate zone, then deploys it to small farms in different climates where it performs poorly. Which data quality practice would most directly have prevented this failure?
options: Building a representative dataset that reflects the diversity of farms, climates, and conditions where the model will be used
Removing all metadata from the training images
Compressing the training images to reduce storage costs
Labeling the images with a larger annotation team
explain: A model generalizes only to conditions represented in its training data. Collecting representative data across the climates, farm sizes, and conditions of the real deployment population is the practice that prevents this kind of systematic failure; faster labeling or compression does not change what the data covers.

q: A logistics company shares a training dataset with a new ML team. The team cannot tell where the data came from, how it was collected, or what its known limitations are, which slows a fairness review. Which practice should the company adopt for its datasets?
options: Deleting collection records after training completes
Renaming dataset files with random identifiers
Storing datasets without descriptions to keep them neutral
Documenting each dataset's source, collection method, contents, intended use, and known limitations
explain: Data documentation, sometimes captured in datasheets for datasets and reflected in transparency artifacts, records provenance, collection methods, composition, intended use, and limitations. Without it, fairness reviews, audits, and safe reuse are guesswork because nobody can judge whether the data fits a new purpose.

q: A manufacturing company discovers that two labeling teams applied different defect criteria, so thousands of training images carry inconsistent labels. What is the most likely effect on the SageMaker model trained on this data, and what should be fixed first?
options: The model learns contradictory patterns and makes unreliable predictions; the labeling guidelines and label quality must be corrected and the data relabeled or cleaned
The model trains faster because it sees more variety; nothing needs fixing
The only effect is higher training cost; prediction quality is unaffected
The model automatically averages out the disagreement; only the endpoint needs scaling
explain: Labels are the ground truth a supervised model learns from, so inconsistent labels teach contradictory mappings and degrade prediction quality in ways no algorithm change can repair. The responsible fix is at the source: unify labeling instructions, review or relabel the affected data, and add quality checks before retraining.

q: Before training a customer analytics model, a bank finds duplicate records, corrupted fields, and customer Social Security numbers in a free-text column that the model does not need. What is the responsible data preparation step?
options: Share the raw dataset with the whole analytics team for inspection
Encrypt the dataset and leave all fields unchanged
Train on the raw data and let the model sort it out
Clean the data by removing duplicates and corrupted records and dropping or redacting the unneeded sensitive data before training
explain: Data quality and privacy practices require removing corrupted and duplicate records and applying data minimization: fields the model does not need, especially sensitive identifiers, should be removed or redacted before training. Training on raw data bakes in errors and needlessly exposes PII to breach and memorization risks.

q: A streaming service's recommendation model was trained on years of engagement data containing clickbait placements the company itself created, plus large gaps for newer regional content. The model now keeps promoting low-quality titles and rarely surfaces regional content. Which analysis best explains this outcome?
options: Poor data quality and biased historical patterns in the training data are reproduced and amplified in the model's outputs
The model's temperature is too high for a recommendation task
The endpoint lacks enough provisioned throughput for peak hours
The model has too many parameters for the catalog size
explain: Models learn the patterns in their training data, including the distortions: engagement data shaped by the company's own clickbait placements teaches the model to repeat them, and missing regional examples mean regional content is systematically undervalued. Output quality problems with this signature trace back to data quality, not inference settings.

q: A government agency is improving the data practices behind a benefits eligibility model. Which TWO practices most directly support responsible AI? (Choose two.)
options: Using as much personal data as possible because more fields always help
Verifying that the training data represents the full population the model will serve, including smaller communities
Keeping data collection details secret so they cannot be questioned
Applying quality checks to labels and documenting known gaps or biases in the dataset
explain: Representativeness checks and label quality controls with documented limitations are core responsible data practices: they surface bias and errors before they become model behavior. Secrecy, maximal data collection, and stale data all work against fairness, privacy, and accuracy.

q: A custom speech model built by a logistics company transcribes warehouse radio traffic accurately for most staff but fails often for workers with strong regional accents, who were rare in the training recordings. What is the root cause?
options: The workers speak too quickly for any model to handle
The microphone hardware in the warehouses is outdated
The model uses an unsupported audio file format
The training data was not representative of the accents in the actual user population
explain: When a group is underrepresented in training data, the model has too few examples to learn its patterns and performs worse for that group. The remedy is representative data collection and evaluation broken down by group, not blame on the users or their hardware.

q: A healthcare network labels medical images for training. Reviewers frequently disagree on borderline cases, and the network wants dependable labels. Which labeling quality approach is most appropriate?
options: Have a single annotator label each image as fast as possible with no review
Let the model label its own training data without human checks
Accept the first label submitted and discard all conflicting opinions silently
Use multiple annotators per image with consensus rules, expert adjudication for disagreements, and clear labeling guidelines
explain: Label quality for high-stakes data comes from process: clear guidelines, multiple annotators, consensus or majority rules, and expert adjudication of disagreements, as supported by managed labeling workflows. Single unreviewed labels import individual errors and inconsistency directly into the model.

q: A media company fine-tunes a writing model on thousands of news articles scraped from publishers without licenses or permission, then sells the tool commercially. Which risk is the company most directly exposed to?
options: Copyright and intellectual property infringement claims over the training material
Higher latency from the fine-tuning job
Loss of the articles' original publication dates
A SageMaker endpoint scaling limit
explain: Training on protected works without rights or a valid legal basis creates copyright and IP exposure, especially when the resulting system is commercialized. Responsible practice is to use licensed, public-domain, or properly permissioned data and keep records of data provenance and rights.

q: A marketing team uses a generative model to draft campaign copy and discovers a generated jingle closely mirrors the chorus of a well-known copyrighted song. The team is about to publish it. What is the responsible action and why?
options: Publish it, because AI-generated content cannot raise IP issues
Do not publish until the output is reviewed and revised, because model outputs can reproduce protected expression and expose the company to infringement claims
Lower the temperature and regenerate once, then publish without review
Publish it but credit the model as the author to satisfy copyright law
explain: Generative models can produce outputs that reproduce or closely imitate protected material from training data. Human review of outputs for IP similarity before publication, and revising or discarding risky content, is the mitigation; crediting the model does not cure infringement, and a single regeneration is not a review.

q: Criminals clone a CEO's voice with generative AI and use a synthetic call to trick an employee into transferring funds, and a fake video of a public official spreads before an election. Which category of generative AI risk do these incidents illustrate?
options: Model drift in production endpoints
Bias in labeled training datasets
Excessive inference costs from long prompts
Deepfakes and misinformation used to deceive people and manipulate events
explain: Synthetic audio and video that impersonate real people are deepfakes, and their use for fraud and election manipulation shows the misinformation and societal harm risk of generative AI. Mitigations include provenance and watermarking, disclosure of AI-generated media, detection tools, and verification processes for high-stakes requests.

q: An education publisher lets authors draft textbook passages with a generative model. Several passages closely paraphrase a competing textbook and are presented as original work without attribution. Which risk has materialized?
options: A denial-of-service condition in the authoring tool
Overfitting of the publisher's recommendation model
Plagiarism and unattributed reuse of source material in generated content
Excessive redaction by a PII filter
explain: Generated text can closely track source material, so presenting it as original unattributed work is plagiarism with academic and legal consequences. Responsible workflows check generated content for similarity, require attribution where due, and keep human authors accountable for what is published.

q: A law firm offers a Bedrock-powered assistant that drafts client-facing explanations of legal procedures. A draft contains a confident but wrong statement about a filing deadline that a client relies on. Who bears responsibility, and what control best reduces this risk?
options: The model provider bears all responsibility because it built the model
The client is responsible for not verifying the deadline independently
The firm remains liable for outputs it sends, so drafts need qualified human review and verification before reaching clients
Nobody is responsible because the output was machine generated
explain: Deploying organizations remain accountable and potentially liable for the outputs they rely on and distribute; machine generation is not a liability shield. Human expert review, grounding in authoritative sources, and clear scoping of what the assistant may answer are the standard controls for high-stakes professional content.

q: A real estate platform is assessing the legal and societal risks of launching a generative listing-description tool. Which THREE risks should its risk assessment include? (Choose three.)
options: Harmful or discriminatory statements in generated text that create legal liability for the platform
Synthetic photos or media that mislead buyers about a property's condition
A modest increase in monthly inference spending
Outputs that infringe copyright by copying text from other listings or sources
explain: A generative AI risk assessment should cover IP infringement in outputs, deceptive synthetic media, and discriminatory or harmful generated content that creates liability and societal harm. Ordinary operating cost is a business consideration, not a legal or societal risk of the kind responsible AI governance tracks.

q: A hospitality brand wants to reduce intellectual property risk in its generative content workflow. Which practice is most effective?
options: Use material from any public website because public posting implies permission
Remove copyright notices from source material before using it
Rely on the model to refuse any request that might be risky
Train and prompt only with licensed, owned, or public-domain material, keep provenance records, and review outputs before publication
explain: IP risk is managed by controlling inputs and outputs: use content the company owns or has licensed, document where training and reference material came from, and review generated content before it ships. Public availability is not a license, and model refusals are not a substitute for rights management.

q: A news streaming service labels AI-generated segments and is evaluating technical measures so viewers and other platforms can verify that a video genuinely came from the service and detect impersonations. Which approach best supports this goal?
options: Content provenance and watermarking approaches that mark AI-generated media and record its origin
Publishing videos only at low resolution so copies look different
Removing the service's branding from all generated segments
Asking viewers to report suspicious videos as the only control
explain: Provenance metadata and watermarking help audiences and platforms verify origin and identify synthetic media, which is a recognized mitigation for deepfakes and misinformation. Viewer reports alone are reactive, and stripping branding makes verification harder rather than easier.

q: An insurance regulator requires the company to explain individual pricing decisions to policyholders. The data science team's most accurate model is an opaque ensemble whose decisions cannot be explained per customer, while a slightly less accurate model produces clear reason codes. Which decision best reflects the transparency trade-off?
options: Deploy the opaque model but write explanations by hand that sound plausible
Deploy the opaque model because accuracy is the only metric that matters
Deploy the interpretable model, or add explainability tooling and human review to the opaque one, accepting a possible small accuracy cost to meet the explanation requirement
Refuse to use any model for pricing in the future
explain: Transparency often trades against raw predictive performance: meeting a genuine explanation requirement can justify a modest accuracy sacrifice or investment in explainability tooling. Fabricating plausible explanations is deceptive, and ignoring the requirement exposes the company to regulatory and trust consequences.

q: A bank rebalances its training data and adjusts its credit model so approval rates are more equitable across demographic groups. Overall accuracy falls by a small amount while the fairness gap closes substantially. Senior leaders ask whether the change is acceptable. Which evaluation approach best supports this decision?
options: Judge the model on overall accuracy alone and revert the change
Measure both accuracy and fairness metrics by group, weigh the regulatory and ethical cost of the disparity against the small accuracy change, and document the trade-off decision
Increase the marketing budget to offset any complaints about the old model
Hide the group-level results so the accuracy debate stays simple
explain: Fairness interventions commonly trade a small amount of aggregate accuracy for materially more equitable outcomes. The responsible approach quantifies both sides with group-level metrics, considers legal and ethical exposure, and documents the rationale rather than optimizing a single headline metric.

q: A research team wants to publish its custom generative model's weights and full system prompts openly to maximize transparency and reproducibility. The safety team objects. What is the core trade-off they must weigh?
options: Openness has no effect on misuse because safeguards are stored in the model card
Keeping the model closed eliminates all bias from its outputs
Publishing weights reduces the model's inference cost for the team
Openness improves transparency and external scrutiny, but releasing weights and prompts can enable misuse such as generating harmful content or bypassing safeguards
explain: Openness and transparency help the community audit and improve a system, but the same artifacts can be repurposed to remove safeguards or generate harmful content at scale. Responsible release decisions weigh scrutiny benefits against misuse risk and may use staged or gated access instead of a binary choice.

q: A government agency selects a model for screening benefits applications partly because caseworkers can understand and challenge its reasoning. Which characteristic most supports this?
options: The model's vendor refuses to disclose any limitations
The model retrains itself nightly without version records
The model uses billions of parameters with no documentation
The model relies on interpretable features and produces explanations a caseworker can review for each decision
explain: Transparent, explainable systems use meaningful, interpretable features and produce per-decision explanations that affected people and reviewers can understand and contest. Undocumented complexity, silent retraining, and undisclosed limitations are the opposite of transparency.

q: An energy company must be able to reconstruct, months later, exactly which model version and which data produced a grid load forecast that is now under review. Which property of a transparent system makes this possible?
options: High inference throughput on the forecasting endpoint
A large context window in the forecasting model
Automatic scaling of the prediction service
Auditability, supported by versioned models and data, logged decisions, and complete documentation
explain: Auditability means decisions can be traced and reproduced after the fact through model and data versioning, decision logs, and documentation such as model cards. Performance characteristics like throughput and context size do nothing to reconstruct a past decision.

q: A retail company wants its product tagging model to qualify as transparent and explainable. Which TWO characteristics should it look for? (Choose two.)
options: A design whose internal logic is deliberately kept secret from the team operating it
Documentation of the model's purpose, data, and limitations that stakeholders can inspect
Predictions that change randomly so no pattern can be inferred
Features that have clear business meaning and whose influence on predictions can be shown
explain: Transparent and explainable models combine interpretable, meaningful features with inspectable documentation of purpose, data, performance, and limits, so stakeholders can understand and question decisions. Secrecy, randomness, and no-recourse outputs undermine both properties.

q: Which statement best describes a common trade-off when an organization prioritizes model transparency and explainability?
options: Explainable models are always both faster and more accurate than opaque models
Transparency requirements apply only to models that are already inaccurate
There is no relationship between explainability and any other model property
Simpler, more interpretable models may give up some predictive performance compared with complex opaque models
explain: A well-known tension in responsible AI is that the most accurate models, such as large ensembles and deep networks, are often the hardest to explain, while inherently interpretable models can be slightly less accurate. Teams manage this trade-off deliberately based on the stakes and regulatory needs of the use case.

q: A hospital network can deploy a highly accurate but opaque triage model, or a slightly less accurate model whose per-patient explanations clinicians can inspect, with a plan to monitor outcomes by patient group and keep clinicians as final decision-makers. Regulators require explainable recommendations for this use. Which deployment decision is most defensible?
options: Deploy the explainable model with clinician oversight and group-level outcome monitoring, because the use case's stakes and regulatory requirements make verifiable reasoning part of safety, not an optional extra
Deploy the opaque model and generate explanations afterward with a separate tool that clinicians are told not to question
Delay all AI use indefinitely because any trade-off is unacceptable
Deploy the opaque model only for patients whose cases look straightforward
explain: In high-stakes, regulated settings the defensible choice weighs total risk, not accuracy alone: an inspectable model, human final authority, and group-level monitoring satisfy the explanation requirement and catch disparate harm. Post-hoc explanations for an opaque model that staff cannot question do not provide the same accountability.

q: A logistics firm retrains its delivery-time model monthly. After each retraining, the predictions change noticeably, but stakeholders receive no updated information about the model's performance or limitations. Which practice corrects this?
options: Only document the first version because later versions are similar
Stop recording which version produced each prediction
Update the model's documentation, such as its Model Card, with each new version's evaluation results and any changed limitations
Freeze the model permanently so documentation never goes stale
